How to read this book? Dungeons and Kittens

is a complete game and everything you need is contained in this book. The introduction, the rules of the game, how to create a Kitten, and the Players’ Book can be read by everyone. On the other hand, what comes after that—the universe, The Storyteller’s Book, and the scenarios—is reserved for the Storyteller only. Dungeons and Kittens is not a particularly secretive game, and you can play with multiple Storytellers who each contribute, but it’s more fun to discover some things as your adventure unfolds…

pages.name: p.5
pages.html:
Dungeons and Kittens is an adventure game that blends animal tales and Medieval fantasy in a post-apocalyptic world.

It follows the journey of a group of Kittens who have been driven out of their native land by a ridiculous law and the whims of a tyrant.

Nature has reclaimed much of the world, maybe because she had had enough of concrete slabs, acid water pools, and the lack of rainfall. Humans have disappeared from the planet, leaving only a few remains dotted around the newly lush vegetation. Nobody knows what happened to them. Rumors are told of the “big-bare-butts”— it is said they are hairless giants who live alone, hiding out far away. But very few have actually seen one. Maybe it is just another legend...

However, humans did leave some things for the animals: the gifts of speech and imagination, the ability to anticipate and predict, and the power to invent. But not all creatures accepted those gifts. So, there are animals, who speak, walk, and can use objects and tools; and there are beasts, who remain speechless and fierce, and have retained their original nature.

But there is a universal law that is respected by all, with no exceptions: “An animal that talks eats not another animal that talks”. Other than that, beasts provide leather, milk, and meat for the animals that need those things—not everyone eats only fruits and roots.

Animals have formed societies with rudimentary technologies and some basics of magic. By copying old images from the human world, some have kitted themselves out with strange, colorful clothes that they rescued from the ruins. They have also started to build their own dwellings.

Could this also be another effect of the gifts the humans left behind? Some animals have even begun to behave as badly as the former masters of the planet. They are greedy, violent, and hungry for power. Will our brave Kittens manage to convince them of the error of their ways, or will they have to be more forceful?

pages.name: p.6
pages.html:
Dungeons and Kittens is a roleplaying adventure game.

It is a boardgame with multiple players, where the idea is to all tell a story together.

It’s best with 4 to 6 players.

One of the players is the

Storyteller.

“Hello!”

“My role is to bring the world of D&K to life, to play the parts of the inhabitants, and to referee the game.”

“We are going to play parts of the Kittens who have been chased from home by the naughty

Walter. We are the heroes of the adventures...”

“... and these are the characters that we have made up.”

Everything happens around a table, with talking and rolling dice.

Most important: There are no winners or losers. We are playing to share an adventure together!

pages.name: p.7
pages.html:
An easy way to think of how we play is like a little computer program.

The Storyteller describes a situation:

“You arrive in a copse made up of dark, strange-looking trees. There’s a strange smell and you can hear a grinding noise that goes on and on.”

1 The players ask questions... ... or they say what their characters will do.

“What is the smell? Where is the noise coming from?”

“I take out my scarf and make it into a mask, and I light a torch.”

2 The Storyteller answers the questions: “When you light the torch it seems like the trees draw back a bit.”

When the Storyteller and the players don’t know how to continue (or go back to step 1)...

... they can read the rules and the advice in this book.

Or she says what happens:

And then we go back to step 1.

“The smell is toasted gingerbread.”

Thanks to Jerome Larré for the roleplaying game program

pages.name: p.8 - Why play Dungeons and Kittens?
pages.html:
Why play Dungeons and Kittens?

You are going to play Dungeons and Kittens because:

You want to spend some fun, exciting, social time with friends. You love cats and dogs, ; this also means you have millions of potential friends to play the game. You want to explore a universe that is both familiar and exotic, and has an interesting outlook. You have a taste for adventure, twists and turns, danger, and action—all done safely from home, curled up in your armchair. You want to tell a story, and also create some legends with your comrades, while you uncover the secrets of a new, changing world.

Feminine and masculine

In Dungeons and Kittens, both feminine and masculine pronouns are used as indicators. In general, we use the feminine (she/her) to indicate the people who are sitting around the table eating cookies and cupcakes while they talk: the players and the Storyteller. And we use the masculine (he/him) to indicate those who exist in the game world: the Kittens and extras. Why did we do this? Simply to avoid confusion when we were writing the rules—it was much easier for us to do it that way. For example, when a player describes the actions of her Kitten: It is he who acts, but it is she who rolls the dice.

And this goes without saying: A Kitten can be a

male or a female, and a player can be a boy,

a girl, or whatever she wants to be.

Kittens

The Kitten is the avatar of the player in the world of the game. It is he who acts, but she rolls the dice.

Creating the players’ Kittens is the starting point for every adventure, but before we get into that, let’s start by learning what the terms on the character sheet mean, and how to use the dice. See page 12 for an example of a blank character sheet and page 13 for an overview of Kitten creation.

To play Dungeons and Kittens, each player and

Storyteller needs four six-sided dice (written as d6), and a few other items: pencils, erasers, sheets of paper, and, of course, a character sheet for each player.

pages.name: p.13 - Kitten Creation Overview
pages.html:
Kitten Creation Overview

1. The Kitten’s name It is essential to have a cool name (see page 43).

2. The Kitten’s childhood Where did they come from? How were they raised? What did they learn? (see page 25).

3. The Kitten’s abilities These measure a Kitten’s strengths and weaknesses (see page 15).

4. Heart points These measure a Kitten’s mood and its physical health (see pages 18 and 53).

5. Furr-endship points These are a Kitten’s morale and luck (see pages 18 and 54).

6. The Kitten’s skills What they learned during childhood (see page 19).

7. Meowgic These are the spells a Kitten knows (see page 37).

8. Cattributes These are a Kitten’s special abilities (see page 22).

9. Backpack This includes the useful objects and Purr-ecious items carried by a Kitten. (see page 23).

10. Character traits Every Kitten has a distinct character, don’t they? (see page 24).

All the information to create your own

Kitten can be found from page 14–54.

Some ready-to-play Kittens are available at the end of the book.

pages.name: p.14 - Creating a Kitten
pages.html:
Creating a Kitten

To create your Kitten: 1. The player first chooses a childhood from the eighteen available, then writes down the Kitten’s Cattribute and the objects he carries in his bag (see page 25). 2. She then divides 8 points between the Kitten’s three abilities, which are Strong, Smart, and Cute, so that each ability has a minimum value of 1 and a maximum value of 5 (see page 15). 3. She chooses two skills for her Kitten (see page 19–21). 4. She chooses two spells from any branch of Meowgic and of any level (see pages 37–41). These are the two spells that the Kitten learned when he was little. 5. Finally, calculate Heart points (see page 18) and Furr-endship points (see page 18), then choose a character trait for the Kitten (see page 24).

The Kitten and his companions Before creating their Kittens, the players should talk to the Storyteller about what kind of group they would like at the gaming table. The simplest kind is to choose only Kittens of the Kingdom—there is less choice, fewer surprises, and the adventures will be easier for the Storyteller to make up. Odd Ones Out bring more fantastical, strange, and mysterious elements to the universe, so the Sto- ryteller may want to save them for use as extras, unless the players really want to be a litter of Meowgician Kittens roaming the world in search of magical items. Finally, it is recommended that the group should include no more than one animal that is not a Kitten, unless the players really want to be a troupe of acrobats of all species, wandering from city to city performing their shows.

pages.name: p.15 - Describing a Kitten
pages.html:
Describing a Kitten

Abilities

A Kitten is Strong, Smart, and Cute. Now obviously, some Kittens can be more Strong than Smart, or more Cute than Strong—no two Kittens are the same.

Strong, Smart, and Cute are the Kitten’s three abilities. They are shown by a score between 1 and 5. The higher a Kitten’s score, the better they are. A score of 1 indicates that the Kitten is not very good at all—maybe they are even bad. A score of 5 indicates that the Kitten is one of the best.

Strong is the ability of bold, physical Kittens. They are faster, stronger, and more agile. Kittens with a high score in this ability are usually pushy and headstrong, but also very brave and unselfish.

Smart is the ability of resourceful and knowledgeable Kittens. They are vigilant, focused, inventive, and thoughtful. These Kittens always seem to know everything about every thing. It can be unbearable! But they do have nerves of steel and manage to find a solution to almost any problem.

Cute is the ability of adora ble, charming Kittens. They are subtle and attentive, diplomatic, and cunning. And they can be shameless, purring and making big eyes to seduce and persuade; but they are actually skilled negotiators who get what they want.

pages.name: p.16 - Mechanics: Actions
pages.html:
Mechanics: Actions

Before we go any further with the description of the Kittens, let’s take a look at what all these numbers are for and how the players will use the dice.

When a Kitten tries to do something, the Storyteller must decide the consequences.

Most of the time it’s very easy: either the task is simple enough for success to be automatic (talking to someone, packing a bag in the morning, walking along a track, and so on); or the task is clearly impossible (lifting a huge rock alone without any tools, changing the course of a river by blowing on it, emptying the sea with a bucket—that sort of thing).

The rest of the time, when the success or failure of a task depends on the Kitten’s abilities or skills, or (good and bad) circumstances that are difficult to measure—maybe even luck— the Storyteller can ask the player to roll the dice.

The player rolls 3d6. The result of each die is compared to the appropriate ability. If a die’s result is equal to or less than the ability’s score, it is a success.

There are some other small mechanics that we will explain later (starting on page 45).

pages.name: p.17 - Example:
pages.html:
Example:

Example 1: Bobbin wants to chase a thief, and says: “I climb the tree and jump from branch to branch to catch the thief and get my favorite saucepan back.” The Storyteller asks Diane, Bobbin’s player, to roll for Strong to see if the Kitten can do it. Bobbin’s Strong score is 3 and Diane rolls 4, 4, and 6 on the dice. None of these results is a success for Diane, so Bobbin watches as the bird flies off. "Bad-luck bird!" he says, out of breath.

Example 2: Mookie tries to distract one of the Yardogs’ poodle guards so his friends can make a crafty getaway. Mookie talks about how important it is to be careful when grooming such a nice, curly coat… Mookie has a score of 3 in Cute and Lucy, his player, rolls 3, 2, and 6 on the dice. That's two successes! The poodle listens attentively to l’il Mookie’s advice on shampooing and does not realize what is going on right behind him…

Example 3: Bib, a Were- kitten, is trying to find the trail of his friends who were kidnapped earlier in the day. With his muzzle in the air, he sniffs out the fragrant residue of Mookie's favorite shampoo: cinnamon and vanilla! Bib has a score of 2 in Smart. Gerry, his player, rolls the 3d6 and gets 1, 2, and 2. That’s a great roll! Three successes! Were- kitten Bib’s senses focus intensely and enable him to visualize a thin, golden trail in the air: Mookie’s scent. Bib sets off in pursuit of his friends.

pages.name: p.18 - Heart points
pages.html:
Heart points

Heart points measure a Kitten’s mood and health:

A Kitten loses Heart points when he gets tired, when he is stressed or attacked, or when he loses hope. However, he regains Heart points when he rests, is taken care of, and when he gets a little tenderness or friendship. A Kitten’s maximum Heart points equals the sum of his Strong and Smart abilities.

More information on Heart points, and how to lose and gain them, can be found on page 53.

Furr-endship points

Each Kitten has a reserve of Furr-endship points, equal to its Cute score. These points measure, in a way, a Kitten’s morale, his mood, and his luck.

More information on Furr-endship points, and how to lose and gain them, can be found on page 54.

pages.name: p.19 - Skills
pages.html:
Skills

During their childhood, Kittens have all learned various useful skills—and they will learn many more during their adventures, gaining experience or finding teachers on the way.

The Kitten either has a skill or does not—skills do not have a score. When a Kitten wants to make an action and one of his skills can help, then the player gains an advantage for that roll of the dice (see page 46). Each skill is described below (this list continues through pages 20-21).

Care of Beasts. The skill of Kittens who love beasts (animals without speech and imagination), who know about caring for and training them, and who find them endlessly interesting—and useful. Cook. A skill for gourmet Kittens, who can turn any ingredients into a hearty, delicious dish fit for a king, treating all their friends. Draw & Paint. A skill for observant Kittens; artists who always have pencils, watercolors, and paper, to record what they see. Find Your Way. The skill of adventurous Kittens, for finding their way in the wild, locating paths and shortcuts, and following tracks left by others. Find Information. The skill that urban Kittens have for finding their way around town, sniffing out a bargain, and getting the information they need.

pages.name: p.20
pages.html:
Heal Wounds & Diseases. The skill of doctor and healer Kittens, from preparing simple medication to sewing deep wounds. Herbology. A sorcerer-like skill, for the alchemist Kitten with a knowledge of obscure plants, strange stones, and all kinds of ways of using them. Hide in Shadows. The skill for sly, crafty Kittens, staying still, moving slowly from one shadow to another, or waiting patiently for a long, long time.

Hiss & Growl. The skill for brawling Kittens, raising their hackles, showing their fangs, growling, and insulting their opponents—without touching them.

Hunter-Gatherer. The skill of a

Kitten who is comfortable in nature and knows about fruits and berries, edible insects, dangerous mushrooms, moss that heals, etcetera. Keep Calm & Carry On. The skill of brave, willing, patient, and enduring Kittens, who resist pain and stress without giving in to any hardship.

Knowledge of Laws & Legends. The skill of Kittens who were listening attentively to the elders as they talked of legends—and all manner of other things. Knowledge of People & Places. The skill of Kittens who have traveled the world and visited many inns, listening to wanderers from all over. Make Music. The skill of singing, musical Kittens, who know popular tunes, dances, and ditties, as well as music for battle—or for parties. Move Silently. The skill of graceful, sneaky Kittens, who can cross grass and stone without a noise, drawing no attention to themselves. Pickpocket. The skill of light-mittened Kittens—both mischievous and cheeky—for making small objects disappear in their paws. Read Sky & Stars. The skill for Kittens with their eyes on the sky, who know how to find their way around, tell the time, and even find the answers to cryptic questions.

pages.name: p.21
pages.html: Read, Write, Count. The skill of scholarly Kittens who have learned to read, write, and count fluently—not just sign their name with a crude pawprint. Scratch. The skill of Kittens who are ready to use claws and weapons to draw blood— hurting or even killing (such violence!) Seduce & Charm. The skill of the cutest Kittens, who get what they want by purring and nuzzling, not hissing and scratching. See & Search. A skill for Kittens who always pay attention: alert, with eyes, ears, and noses wide open. Shake Your Booty. A skill for athletic and acrobatic Kittens, helpful for climbing trees, running far and fast, jumping long and high, and even swimming (yes, swimming!) Sweet-talk. A skill for the Kitten who was born with a silver tongue in his mouth. Never at a loss for words, these Kittens are usually full of confidence. Tinker with Bits & Bobs. A skill for resourceful Kittens who are good with their paws; for making, repairing, modifying, inventing, and fiddling with all sorts of things.

pages.name: p.22 - Cattributes
pages.html:
Cattributes

Cattributes are special abilities unique to the Kitten’s childhood, which may allow him to perform extraordinary actions (more or less well).

A Cattribute is a bit of a Swiss army knife for the player and the Storyteller. There are not really strict rules for Cat- tributes: the most common use of a Cattribute is to provide a re-roll (see page 47); but sometimes it will be impossible to do something if the Kitten does not have the Cattribute; other times, the Cattribute makes it possible to automat- ically succeed with an action without rolling the dice; the Cattribute can also give or increase an advantage. The way a Cattribute is used all depends on the circumstances. The Storyteller must rely on her instinct and judgement, but in all cases, a Kitten’s Cattribute should be something a little out of the ordinary, a little meowgical, that the player can mold or adapt to make certain decisions, to go along with the story or even to cheat reality—it is the spirit of the Cattribute that counts. And if necessary, the Storyteller can always make the player spend a Furr-endship point on the weirdest or most powerful Cattribute effects.

Meowgic

All kittens practice some meowgic and know spells (see pages 37-41).

pages.name: p.23 - Backpack
pages.html:
Backpack

When the Kittens are exiled from the kingdom by Walter, they each leave with a small bag that contains their possessions:

A wooly blanket so they can sleep warm and dry, a sharp pen-knife, a wooden spoon, a small cooking pot, a large leather flask, a tinderbox, a few candle stubs, a bar of soap, a brush, a packet of kittysnacks for the road.

They also each carry five Purr-ecious items. These items are so important that Kittens can only have five of them at most. During their adventures they can lose them or find new ones they prefer, but they can never have more than five. When the character is created, these five Purr-ecious items are dictated by the Kitten's childhood. He can change them later if he wants to.

Whenever a Purr-ecious item could help with an action, the player gets a re-roll (see page 47).

Kittens can never carry more than five Purr-ecious items. So what can they do if they have too many?

You can sell a Purr-ecious item to a merchant, who will usually offer half a gold coin for it. You can buy such objects for the price of one gold coin on average. One item can be swapped for another, if someone is interested. Later in their adventures, there is the possibility for the Kittens to have a large chest somewhere—in their base, or at the home of a trusted person. All unused objects can be stored there, and used another time. Finally, there is always the easy way: Throw the extra object away, leave it by the side of the road, or even give it to someone else. Last bit of advice: Do not forget that Kittens can also swap or lend objects to each other if needed for a particular action.

pages.name: p.24 - Character traits
pages.html:
Character traits

All Kittens have a character trait; some useful, some not so useful:

Once per game session, the Kitten may use his character trait in a positive way. He gains an advantage with 1 roll of the dice (see page 46), as if he were using a skill. On the other hand, once per game session, the Kitten may allow his character trait to mess something up or prevent him from making an action. When this happens, he may give 1 Furr-endship point to one of his comrades. Example: Luner is a scaredy-kitten. During a session, he uses his character trait to help him escape a dangerous situation: he gains an advantage for a Strong roll, so is able to run as fast as possible. During another part of that session, he remains motionless during a rather lively Fang Catfight, and stands back to let his companions settle the situation. At the end of the conflict, one of them comforts him and receives 1 Furr-endship point in exchange.

1d6 1-2 3-4 5-6 1 Loving Uncertain Domineering 2 Loud Unruly Scared 3 Angry Sad Bold 4 Cold Naive Scatty 5 Greedy Proud Stubborn 6 Snobbish Lazy Shy

A player can either choose their Kitten’s character trait or generate one using this table. Roll 2d6, first for the column, then for the row, then read the result.

pages.name: p.25 - Childhood
pages.html:
Childhood

A Kitten’s childhood defines what he is, how he grew up, what he learned, and what he knows how to do. The childhoods below are separated into three broad categories and described on pages 26-32.

Kittens of the Kingdom are the children of craftsmen, farmers, guards, and nobles of the kingdom. They are regular Kittens, resourceful and courageous, and who will soon be exiled because of the tyrant Walter’s unjust laws. Odd Ones Out are those Kittens who have more alternative origins and powers, and who live on the fringes of society. They are very rare (there shouldn’t be more than one Odd One Out in a typical group), very mysterious, and they always display very… strange behavior. Other Animals allow the players to play something that’s not a Kitten—usually a different young creature. That’s not unusual of course, but the game is called Dungeons and Kittens after all. Not Dungeons and Cutiepies or Dungeons and Puppies… So, it is recommended that there be no more than one Other Animal in a typical group.

pages.name: p.26
pages.html:
Young Noble This Kitten was born with a silver kittysnack in his mouth. From birth, he learned all about the finer points of etiquette and how to speak properly. Despite his young age, he has the self-confidence that comes from high birth. But this did not protect him from Walter’s law, and he must now leave the Kingdom.

Cattribute: Inheritance. At the begin ning of each game session, an animal (carrier pigeon, tunnelling mole, or migrating turtle) brings the Kitten 1 gold coin stamped with King Walter’s profile. It’s worth a fortune on the road, and is proof that his parents have not forgotten him (a Purr-ecious item that does not count towards a backpack’s limit).

In the Young Noble’s back-

pack (Purr-ecious items):

Fancy clothes; special soft fur shampoo; a finely carved walking cane; fragrant and exotic spices; a

“bling” object—to be selected.

Country Kitten A tough and resourceful farm Kitten, this one is probably the best prepared for the long journey that awaits. He knows the seasons and the trees, what is edible and what is poisonous. And although he has none of those good city manners, sleeping under the stars does not scare him at all.

Cattribute: Animal Companion. The Kitten is accompanied by a beast of his choosing, which is loyal and friendly to him. It is a little smarter than other beasts and can help the Kitten, respond to simple orders, and even take the initiative—but it is a friend, not a servant. It could be a big-eyed spider, a huge turkey or a large, colorful lizard.

In the Country Kitten’s backpack (Purr-ecious items): A bird call that sounds like birds singing; cereal bars; a large hat; a walking stick; his animal companion’s favorite food.

pages.name: p.27
pages.html:
Kitty Merchant This Kitten grew up in the middle of caravans and souks, his nostrils filled with the smell of spices and eyes full of wonders from all over the world. He learned about the value of goods, how to choose them, and how to trade them. By chasing him away, Walter forbade him to stay with his parents, but he will find another way to make a fortune!

Cattribute: Make Friends. As soon as he arrives somewhere, the Kitten quickly learns who he needs to see for business, who he should be wary of, who is really in charge, and where he can find what he is looking for. It only takes him a few questions, a please, a thank you—and a friendly smile.

In the Kitty Merchant’s backpack (Purr-ecious items):A perfumed silk scarf; trinkets to exchange or gift; a small set of scales with weights; a compass; a time-estimating machine.

Soldier’s Child Walter’s soldiers are often bullies, crushing even the smallest resistance group in the shadows of the city. This Kitten grew up in the barracks, learning how to use weapons and mimicking the combative nature of his elders. But he was mercilessly rejected, and banished by his own parents, on Walter’s orders.

Cattribute: Heroic Lineage. The Kitten is the child of one of the Kingdom’s great military heroes. His parents’ enemies fear them; their friends are indebted to them. It is not always easy to live up to such a big reputation, but it can have its advantages when looking for allies or confronting enemies.

In the Soldier’s Child's backpack (Purr-ecious items):Armor; a guard’s spear; healing balm for fast recovery from wounds; a pipe and pipe-weed

(stolen from the old company sergeant); spicy sauce for food.

pages.name: p.28
pages.html:
Apprent-hiss This Kitten has learned to be thorough and precise. Passionate about objects, materials, and machines, he was just starting to master the many techniques a craftsman needs when he was banished. On the road, and without a workshop, he seems helpless. But don’t write off his creativity and crazy ideas.

Cattribute: DIY Superstar. The Kitten seems be able to make or repair anything, even the strangest or most wacky objects. Usually it just takes a lot of time, the right tools, and the right materials.

In the Apprent-hiss’s backpack (Purr-ecious items): A three-inch wrench; a jeweler’s magnifying glass; a leather apron; an oil can; dish soap.

Abandoned Kitten Not all Kittens are born into good fortune and safety. Many are simply abandoned by their own parents. They will join up with the orphans who roam the streets of the kingdom, and learn how to get by—sometimes even resorting to shady or even criminal exploits.

Cattribute: Blend In. It only takes a moment for the Kitten to escape the attention of those who are looking for him. He can slip from shadow to shadow, tuck in behind a plant or a rock, ruffle his fur to change color, climb up high, or find a little hole to hide in quickly.

In the Abandoned Kitten’s backpack (Purr-ecious items): A dark hood; a light rope and a grappling hook; some mismatched (but useful) tools; a collection of handkerchiefs stolen from rich people of the kingdom; a good, sharp knife.

pages.name: p.29
pages.html:
Meowge Kittens who possess the gift of meowgic pursue extensive studies in the most prestigious meowgic school (even if it is the only one in the kingdom). They live there, keeping apart from other Kittens, and they never go out—unless Walter decides to banish some of them, of course.

Cattribute: Mystic Mentor. The ghost of a former teacher from the Meowgic Academy decides to accompany the Kitten—such a young student should not be out on the road without an adult. The ghost gives good advice and is super knowledgeable, but may never intervene physically. He also has very strong ideas about good manners, being extra careful, and compulsory study time.

In the Meowge’s backpack (Purr- ecious items): A small meowgic spell book (with two additional spells); a meowgic wand; a large hat covered with strange symbols; an odd broom that is also used as a walking stick; a china tea set.

Hooting Kitten Although they are very old, Hooting Kittens suffer from a strange affliction that prevents them from growing and ageing. They live in the countryside, in large, lonely mansions, and are the root of all kinds of rumors and fears. However, they are actually really nice, even though they usually only go out at night.

Cattribute: Mysterious. A Hoot ing Kitten has many powers, but they only work at night. He can transform into an owl; he can reflect moonlight and can shine the light around him, as if carrying a lamp; he can walk on water; and when he reads tarot cards, he sometimes gets surprising answers.

In the Hooting Kitten's backpack (Purr-ecious items): A long, dark cape; sunglasses; a large bone flute; tarot cards; a small, unbreakable mirror.

pages.name: p.30
pages.html:
Were-kitten Were-kittens date back a long, long way, to an ancient line of cats—it is said that they were the first of all the animals to receive the gift of speech. However, it didn’t turn out well: These Kittens have strange dreams and are bad-tempered, grumpy, and angry—traits that keep them away from towns and their inhabitants.

Cattribute: Overexcited! Were-kittens are very fast: They are quick as a flash, they take half as much time to complete a task or a job, and they can perform an action even when it is not their turn. When they are scared, angry, or very excited, they turn into a strange kind of creature that is a bit doggy and a bit kitty, which can be quite frightening.

In the Were-kitten’s backpack (Purr-ecious items): A hairstyling brush; thick, warm, waterproof boots; a wooden mask with a (slightly scary) smiling cat's head on it that he wears when everything gets to be too much for him; a big bell tied around the neck by a silver chain; a long chef ’s knife.

Meowmy In ancient human history, Kittens were worshipped as gods and buried alongside their kings. And when the humans disappeared, the Meowmies awoke. These hairless Kittens have an odd appearance and tend to think of themselves as great lords, but they are still as cute as they were at the time of their divine reign.

Cattribute: Children of the Sun. Meowmies do not need to eat, drink, or sleep. They are not affected by heat or cold. They are utterly tireless and never get worn out. Exposure to the sun puts them in a good mood, making them more radiant and admirable. On the other hand, they hate getting wet and if they do, either because of rain or falling into water, they are unable to speak and they feel awful.

In the Meowmy's backpack (Purr-ecious items): An ornate golden chestplate covered with precious jewels; paint brushes and paints; a comfortable embroidered cushion to sit on; a whip; a small wooden statue of a strange cat with a dog’s head.

pages.name: p.31
pages.html:
Catnut Some Kittens are born with marks or differences that Walter finds terrifying. So, they are exiled as soon as they are old enough. They learn to fend for themselves quickly, often wandering to the borders of the kingdom just to watch other Kittens, and play at looking like them.

Cattribute: Disguise. Catnuts have developed the intriguing gift of disguise by observing other cats from afar. They can take on almost any appearance, using colorful material, old clothes, or mud on their fur. They can become a Kitten, a Yardog, a royal pig—even a slimy swamp monster!

In the Catnut’s backpack (Purr-ecious items): Winter-dried acorns; bug armor; a cape of leaves; a bow with arrows; a large black cauldron full of rags and ribbons.

Future Kitten Some Kittens say they come from the future.

They have come back in time to change the past and share some of the wisdom of the era they came from. But their equipment isn’t very good, they suffer from memory problems and lapses, and are often confused. They could be lying, but what about that strange equipment? Cattribute: Foresight. A Future Kitten sometimes seems able to anticipate events or foresee disasters. He can never be surprised. His pockets are stuffed with little gadgets which he does not always remember exactly what to do with. But they may well prove very useful in many circumstances (the player is encouraged to invent all the wacky future-tech she can, and to describe them all to the Storyteller).

In the Future Kitten’s backpack (Purr-ecious items): A badly set up multifunction analyzer; very high magnification binoculars; a full-face helmet with visor and breathing apparatus; photo of a strange house with oddly dressed cats in front; a long-distance communicator (there is never a reply).

pages.name: p.33
pages.html:
Puppy More playful and active than a Kitten, always busy, always happy and unable to slow down, the puppy makes for a tiring companion. But nobody is more loyal and friendly than one of them, nor more protective. His powerful bark carries much further than the meows of a Kitten and makes his opponents think twice about approaching.

Cattribute: Guardian. Growing up and playing frequently with Kittens, the puppy has always considered himself a bit like a protective big brother or an ever-present best friend. Whenever one of his companions is in danger or in an impossible situation, the puppy can take their place by sheltering them and suffering the consequences instead of them.

In the Puppy’s backpack (Purr-

ecious items): A necklace with a personalized nameplate; a brush to keep his fur in order; an old record player and some records; a soccer ball; a set of wrenches.

Sparrowchick These little sparrows have barely left their nest and are only just starting to spread their wings. Thoughtful and curious, they are pleasant companions, but can be a bit chatty. They make excellent scouts, but flying tires them out quickly and they may need to be carried for a while.

Cattribute: Imitation. Sparrowchicks have a gift for imitating voices and noises. They can speak with any accent or tone, from the deepest boom to the highest squeak, and can imitate a person they only heard speaking for a second, or mimic any natural or manmade sounds you can think of.

In the Sparrowchick’s backpack (Purr-ecious items): Cream for his fragile feathers; a pair of aviator sunglasses; a colorful smoke cannister (which seems to refill all by itself); a compass, a local map.

pages.name: p.34
pages.html:
Raccoon This is the Kittens' word—and it is a bit dismissive—to describe all the children of rats, mice, voles, dormice, ferrets, and all other small animals from fields and hedges that their ancestors used to hunt. These days all these animals get along much better, and it is not uncommon for a Raccoon to be part of a group of exiled Kittens.

Cattribute: Tiny!. Raccoons are so small and fast that they can slip anywhere, through any hole, or through the thickest undergrowth. It is almost impossible to catch, grab, or stop them. This speed does not make them quiet, but it certainly makes them more mobile.

In the Raccoon’s backpack (Purr- ecious items): A rip-proof cape in a color that blends in anywhere; a long spider-silk rope; a pair of good pliers; a small, thick, comfortable rug; a roll of duct tape.

Bearcub These are the largest and most striking animals that sometimes accompany Kittens in exile. Bearcubs nearly all come from families of acrobats or lumberjacks, depending on whether they are from the city or the countryside. They are massive and powerful. Bearcubs are also brave and tireless, and they have a big heart to match!

Cattribute: Porter. The Bearcub can carry two additional Purr-ecious items!

In the Bearcub’s backpack (Purr- ecious items): A unicycle; a lumberjack’s ax; a yellow plastic raincoat; a smoke device to make bees sleep; a pillow; two additional items of the player’s choice (discuss with the Storyteller).

pages.name: p.35
pages.html:
Kittenfish Although they need to spend part of the day in water (especially when they sleep), Kittenfish are able to live on dry land thanks to meowgic, and they get around using their strong fins. Calm, patient, and silent, they usually remind Kittens to be careful under all circumstances. However, nothing excites them more than climbing trees.

Cattribute: No Fear. Of course Kittenfish can breathe underwater and they can swim like, well, a fish. But above all, they are never afraid of anything or anyone. Threatening them never works and they do not ever back away from danger (which can sometimes be dangerous itself).

In the Kittenfish’s backpack

(Purr-ecious items): A large, old fishhook; a solid rope; a large fishtank (to cool off); an inflatable inner tube (just in case)

a car headlight

(powered by a hand dynamo, shines a long way).

Hoglet A bit short-sighted, a bit absent-minded, and always hungry, a little hedgehog is usually good-natured, even-tempered, and eager to please. But don’t rub them the wrong way!

You do not want to mess with a Hoglet, for they are argumentative and totally unforgiving. It is said that they each keep a notebook containing the names of all those who have ever annoyed them.

Cattribute: Perfect Pal. By being careful about how he handles his sharp quills, the Hoglet has learned to help his comrades in the most effective way. He always wants to lend a hand; he anticipates the needs of his friends, and is usually in the right place at the right time.

In the Hoglet’s backpack (Purr- ecious items): A notebook to write down the names of those who annoy him (and those who help him); flavored cooking oil; a pair of glasses; a skeleton key; a set of darts.

pages.name: p.37 - Meowgic
pages.html:
Meowgic

A long, long time ago, the cats of the kingdom developed their own way of casting spells: meowgic of the kingdom. Every Kitten in the land—even the wildest ones—learn a few spells as part of their education. The most gifted go to the Meowgic Academy and undertake a much deeper study of the subject.

Meowgic is difficult to master and has effects that are not always easy to control—it is supernatural, strange, and weird. Meowgic works when it wants and rarely as expected, but it can certainly be effective and useful whatever the circumstances.

Spells

Spells are classified by different meowgic paths:

Tower Meowgic and Great Hall Meowgic are

favored by the strongest cats and are often used by soldiers, guards, mercenaries, or nobles of the realm. Craft Meowgic and Country Meowgic are used by the smartest cats, including workers and labourers. City Meowgic and Caravan

Meowgic, which the cutest cats use, are always very practical on a day-to-day basis.

Kittens are free to mix the paths.

pages.name: p.38 - Casting a spell
pages.html:
Casting a spell

To cast a spell, a Kitten must first learn it by heart. The player then makes a roll for the related ability—Strong for a Tower Meowgic spell, for example. She must roll a number of successes that’s at least equal to the difficulty level of the spell—2 successes for First Aid, for example.

If the roll is successful, the spell works as including.

If the the roll is unsuccessful, the Kitten has two choices: —They can choose that the spell works no matter what, so they must make a meowgic accident roll... —They accept that the spell simply does not work. Succeed or fail, once a spell has been cast, the Kitten no longer has enough energy to cast it again before the next morning, after they have a good night’s rest. However, they can reset a spell they have already cast that day at any time by spending 1 Heart point!

1d6 Meowgic accident 1 The spell works normally, as if the roll was successful.

2 The spell does not work, but the Kitten can try to re-cast it during this day without spending 1 Heart point.

3 The duration of the spell is random—it can last much longer or stop after a few seconds (the Storyteller decides). 4 The Kitten loses 1 Heart point and the spell works normally.

5 The spell affects a completely different target than the one chosen by the Kitten. Select randomly or the Storyteller can choose. 6 The spell does not work at all.

The player can spend experience points to improve her Kitten and teach him new things. See the table below. When abilities increase, the same applies to Heart points or Furr-endship points.

Abilities 2 experience points times the level to reach (one level at a time).* Skills 2 experience points per skill. Spells 2 experience points per new spell learned. One additional Purr-ecious item in the backpack
