pages.name: p.45 - Mechanics
pages.html:
Mechanics

Actions

Reminder

In D&K, when a Kitten wants to perform an action that could fail and possibly change the course of the adventure, his player rolls 3d6. She compares the result of each die with the Kitten’s ability indicated by the Storyteller: Strong if it’s to do with muscles (physical actions); Smart if it involves his intelligence (thinking actions); or Cute if it involves charm (social actions). Each die result that is is equal to or lower than the ability’s score is a suc- cess—the more successes the player gets, the better!

pages.name: p.46 - Advantages and disadvantages
pages.html:
Advantages and disadvantages

In some cases, a Kitten may benefit from an advantage or suffer a disadvantage in an ability roll.

An advantage happens when the circumstances are positive, when the Kitten is well positioned to act, when he receives help from his friends, or when he has just the right skill. Instead of rolling 3d6, the player rolls 4d6! A disadvantage occurs when the circumstances are particularly unfavorable, when the kitten is injured or poisoned, when the ground is slippery, or if it is dark, wet, or cold. Instead of rolling 3d6, the player rolls only 2d6! Whatever the circumstances, the player can never roll more than 4 or less than 2 dice. If several advantages apply, only 1 more die is rolled; likewise, if several disadvantages apply, only 1 less die is rolled. If, during the same action, one or more advantages are balanced out by one or more disadvantages, everything cancels out and the player simply throws 3d6—no more, no less.

Example 1, Advantage: Finn has made his way into the store room of a merchant he suspects of handling stolen goods, and who may have an item he is looking for. He tries to be careful (the Storyteller decides this is a roll for Smart) and, as he has the

Move Silently skill, he gets an advantage for the roll.

The player can roll four d6.

Example 2, Disadvantage: Sud denly, something jumps on Finn’s back! It is the shop’s great big toad-guard. He tries to dodge the big amphibian that could squash him into the ground. It is a roll for Strong. However, Finn suffers a disadvantage because he was surprised. The player only rolls two d6.

Example 3, Advantage + Dis advantage: Finn tries to escape from the shop, chased by the toad. The toad is big and heavy (the Storyteller decides this gives Finn an advantage), but he knows the shop much better than Finn, including its corridors, doorways, and passages (giving Finn a disadvantage). In the end, Finn’s player gets to make a Strong roll with three d6—the advantages and disadvantages cancel each other out.

pages.name: p.47 - Re-roll
pages.html:
Examples of advantages: The Kitten receives help, he is in a stronger position than his opponent, he takes everyone by surprise, his reputation precedes him, or he is famous, and so on. Examples of disadvantages: The light is bad (it is night- time, foggy, glaring light, etc.), is is slippery under paw, the Kitten is stunned or surprised, hungry or thirsty, he has a bad reputation, he is dirty or messy, someone has snuck up on him, he’s not sure how to react, and so on.

Re-roll

The player may re-roll one or more dice of her choice whose result she does not like—usually a die that did not get a successful roll. It is possible for a player to get multiple re-rolls on the same throw of the dice.

A Kitten can get a re-roll when:

He uses a Purr-ecious items from his bag. His Cattribute relates to the action. The Storyteller thinks that the player had a good idea or found a clever solution to accomplish an action.

Example: Feeder is trying to get away from three big poisonous toads in the marshes, so he hides in some dense bushes. The player rolls for Smart and Feeder’s score is 4: 2, 4, and 6. Two successes! But as Feeder is wearing a wood- colored hood—one of his Purr-ecious items—his player can re-roll the 6 to get... a... 3—another successful roll, making a total of three successes!

pages.name: p.48 - Difficulty level
pages.html:
Difficulty level

Actions that Kittens want to perform can be more or less complicated, so they will need greater numbers of rolled successes to overcome a task that is harder. These are difficulty levelsand can be set as the Storyteller determines.

Easy actions: Must roll at least 1 success— Examples include steering a raft in gentle waters, observing a bird's strange behavior, climbing a tree, getting a small discount from a traveling merchant, convincing a guard to talk to his boss, etcetera. Medium actions: Must roll at least 2 successes— examples include balancing on a wet and slippery branch, following a trail, spotting a spy hidden in some branches, convincing a Yardog to cross the road, etcetera. Difficult actions: Must roll at least 3 successes—examples include: escaping from a hungry bear, deciphering the human language written on an old sign, discreetly entering Walter’s city to see their parents, calming a very angry Yardog, etcetera. Legendary actions: Must roll at least 4 successes— examples include: riding on a hungry bear, diving from a high cliff into the foaming rapids below, running day and a night to deliver a message, getting help and protection from a Yardog… These are rarely seen events!

pages.name: p.49 - Success and failure
pages.html:
Success and failure

The consequences of an action are determined by the Storyteller. She compares the number of successes the player rolled with the number required by the difficulty level of the action.

As many or more successes than difficulty—the action succeeds exactly as the

Kitten wanted it to. Nice one! Fewer successes than difficulty—the player can choose whether her Kitten fails to accomplish the action, but without additional negative consequences, or whether her Kitten succeeds anyway, but will have to pay for the cost of this success with complications. No successes—it’s a failure! The action is completely messed up.

Example 1, Success Equals Difficulty: Tsuki tries to steal some apples from a merchant’s stall to bring some food back to an injured comrade. This is a medium action, requiring 2 successes. Tsuki rolls 3 successes. He manages to do it. He is able to steal some apples without the merchant noticing.

Example 2, Fewer Successes than Diffculty: Fuzz tries to make a harness so he can de scend with a rope into a deep chasm. This is a difficult action, requiring 3 successes. Fuzz only rolls 2 successes. The Storyteller gives the player the choice of two consequences: Fuzz realizes that the harness is not quite strong enough so he will have to find another way down into the chasm; or, Fuzz manages to get down safely, but the harness comes apart a few feet from the bottom so he won’t be able to get back up. This lets the player choose what is most important to her Kitten: Staying safe or reaching the bottom of the chasm.

Example 3, No Successes: Munch tries to negotiate crossing a small bridge that's guarded by a Yardog. Usually a large piece of cheese or a basket of fruit is enough to pay your way across. The dog is in a very bad mood, but it is still an easy action, requiring 1 success. The player completely misses her roll! No successes. It is a complete failure. The Yardog will not be convinced, and Munch will have to take a long detour or get his fur wet.

pages.name: p.50 - Open actions
pages.html:
Open actions

Some actions have no set difficulty level. The Kitten must try to do their best and see what happens. The player makes a roll for the appropriate ability and tries to get as many successes as they can. The Storyteller then assesses the overall success of the action based on the circumstances and the task.

Example: Roxy has taken her lute out of her bag. She is going to give a small concert for her hosts, to thank them. The player rolls the dice for Cute/Make Music (skill). She rolls four dice with results of 2, 4, 5, and 5. Roxy’s Cute ability is 3, so she has only one success. Roxy, however, gets a re-roll because she used the lute, one of her Purr-ecious items. The player re-rolls the 5 and gets a 2. That’s two successes. The storyteller thinks Roxy played pretty well, but that she missed a few notes in the most complicated parts of some songs.

However, everyone was very happy with the performance.

Opposing actions

When a Kitten goes up against an opponent directly, to see who is the best at something—a race, an eating contest, a woolball match, etcetera.—each character makes an appropriate ability roll. Whoever gets the most successes is the winner. In the event of a tie, the

Storyteller may ask for another roll or declare a draw. In some cases, a Kitten can go up against an opponent over multiple rounds.

Example: Pepper wants to race Frenzy the squirrel by climbing up one of the highest trees in the forest. The player rolls for Strong/

Shake Your Booty, while the Storyteller rolls for Frenzy. Pepper gets two successes, but Frenzy gets three, so the squirrel get to the top of the tree first, with a very slender lead.

pages.name: p.51 - Long tasks
pages.html:
Long tasks

Some tasks take a long time to complete and so time can run out—examples include repairing an old elevator to rescue a friend deep in a mine, harvesting fruit in an orchard before the Yardogs return, or searching every box in a warehouse before it gets dark. The Storyteller has to decide:

The number of successes needed to finish the task: usually 4 for a relatively fast task and up to 20 for a long and difficult one. The time required to perform a roll: from one roll per minute of work to one roll per hour, or even one roll per half-day. If necessary, the Storyteller can also define the maximum time available to gather the number of successes or the consequences of the time that elapses. Some of these tasks can be performed by all the Kittens together, in this case add up the successes of all the die rolls. Other times, only one Kitten can work at a time (but they can take turns).

Example 1: Blueberry, Hammer, and Avenger need to build a makeshift raft from salvaged materials. It’s a roll for Smart/Tinker with Bits & Bobs. Each Kitten can perform a roll every working hour and it takes at least 12 successes to make the raft. But every hour that passes there is an increased risk of the arrival of the band of giant rats that are chasing the Kittens.

Example 2: Miniboo tries to clear the roof that has collapsed on his little group as quickly as possible—his friend Pawline is trapped under the rubble. He needs to get six successes, making one roll for every minute that passes, while Pawline loses 1 Heart point each time.

pages.name: p.52 - Group actions
pages.html:
Group actions

Sometimes Kittens all perform an action together, helping each other out: examples include climbing a cliff; moving silently through the forest, and so on. When this happens, all players make an ability roll with the appropriate ability as set by the Storyteller. If the majority of Kittens succeed, then they all succeed together.

Example: Milo, Luna, and Sneezy need to dress up for the big ball this night, and are searching through boxes of costumes in the old theater. Their goal is to be dressed well enough for the guards to let them through. The Storyteller sets the difficulty as 2 (medium). Milo and Sneezy each roll two successes and manage to get dressed up in line with current fashions, but Luna finds it more difficult and does not succeed. Fortunately, because it is a group action, his two friends help him and find just what he needs in his size. Everyone will be able to go to the ball.

Triples

When a roll of the dice ends up with 3 identical numbers, there is always a positive effect for the Kitten, whether or not the action itself was a success. It can be just a little something that makes the action a tiny bit better, or lessens slightly the consequences of a failure. It could be a bonus that has nothing to do with the action itself but that adds a little to the story.

pages.name: p.53 - Heart points
pages.html:
Heart points

Heart points measure a Kitten’s health—including their tiredness, stress, or injury. Remember that a Kitten’s maximum Heart point equal the sum of his Strong and Smart abilities (see page 18).

A Kitten loses Heart points when:

He suffers a loss during a Fang Catfight or is wounded during a Claw Catfight (see page 59). He decides to re-cast a spell that he has already used that day (see page 38). When a Kitten’s Heart points fall to 0, he is out of play until the end of the scene, or until he has rested or received care. He could have been knocked out, forced to leave, was scared, become frozen, etcetera. In any case, that Kitten can not make any actions for the time being.

A Kitten recovers Heart points when: He rests—he recovers 1 Heart point when having lunch and 1 after a good night’s sleep. If he cannot rest at those times, the Kitten does not regain Heart points.

He is looked after—a successful ability roll for Smart gives 1 Heart point to another Kitten, but this can only be performed once per half day.

He is pampered by his comrades—by spending 1 Furr-endship point, a Kitten can immediately give 1 Heart point to a friend in need.

In Dungeons and Kittens, Kittens cannot die—except in very exceptional circumstances, for example a Claw Catfight! They can be bullied, injured, or knocked out. They may find themselves out of action, but they will always come back into play.

pages.name: p.54 - Furr-endship points
pages.html:
Furr-endship points

Furr-endship points measure the morale and happiness of a Kitten, his pleasure of being surrounded by his comrades, and living his best Kitten life (even if it is on an open road far from home).

A player may spend these points to achieve certain effects:

1 Furr-endship point gives 1 automatic success for 1 roll of the dice. Counting successful die rolls, a player cannot achieve more than 4 successful rolls in this manner in total during the same test. A player can spend 1 Furr-endship point on her own Kitten or to help a companion. 1 Furr-endship point allows a Kitten to give 1 Heart point to another Kitten, simply by giving him a big hug and purring in his ear (see page 53). Being in a Claw Catfight always leads to the loss of 1 Furr-endship point (see page 56). However, a Kitten does not recover Furr-endship points simply by resting or letting time pass. Nor do they return to their maximum at the beginning of a gaming session. To recover 1 Furr-endship point, a Kitten must:

Spend a quiet night in a secure and comfortable place, in good company, and away from the worries of adventure. They must be able to take it easy and forget about the dangerous world around them. Spend a pleasant evening in the company of friends—new or old—telling stories, eating a nice meal, or sharing a little warmth and happiness. It doesn’t work if Kittens spend their time hissing at each other or never agreeing on anything. Attend an interesting, fun, exciting, or moving show in the company of friends.

It could be a concert, a display of acrobatics, or a magnificent sunset over a breathtaking landscape. Chooses to get into trouble because of his character trait (see page 24). This allows that kitten to choose 1 of his companions to recover 1 Furr-endship point.

pages.name: p.56 - Catfights
pages.html:
Catfights

Unfortunately, the life of a Kitten does not only involve the happy times spent in the company of friends. Sometimes a Kitten has to defend himself or fight to impose his will: these are Catfights.

There are two types of Catfight:

The most common type of fight for animals is a Fang Catfight (because Kittens bare their teeth). They bristle, flatten their ears, snarl and growl, trade insults, argue, puff out their chests, make themselves seem big, and arch their backs. In a Fang Catfight, a Kitten does not seek to physically hurt an opponent, only to frighten, intimidate, convince, or force them to give in. The most rare and violent type of fight, is a Claw Catfight (because the opponents claw for blood). In this fight claws, knives, or other weapons are drawn. The objective is to hurt or even kill the opponent! Very few animals get involved in a Claw Catfight—most flee as soon as the situation threatens to escalate. Every time a Kitten enters a Claw Catfight, the stress it causes him is so great that he immediately loses 1 Furr-endship point. If he doesn’t have any left or if he doesn’t want to fight, he must run away!

A Fang Catfight and a Claw Catfight use the same mechanics, but the consequences are very different.

pages.name: p.57
pages.html:
In general, animals almost never engage in a Claw Catfight, unless they are really, really angry, filled with hatred, or are extremely violent. When an animal becomes angry enough to want a Claw Catfight, the other animals present flee as quickly as possible or, if there are enough of them, all set upon him—friends and enemies alike—to stop him and calm him down, so there can be some odd situations. Predators are something else: They are monsters who want to eat animals and they attack without asking questions. Kittens must either flee or defend themselves in this situation!

It is possible for a Fang Catfight to take a turn for the worse, when one of the participants decides to raise the stakes: A simple argument on the road can become a Claw Catfight to the death. If it is one of the Kittens, he must lose 1 Furr- endship point. His comrades can then choose to support him, leave him alone and get out of the Catfight, or jump on him to stop him—then everyone loses 1 Furr-endship point, but their combined weight may be enough to prevent him from doing something he can never come back from.

pages.name: p.58 - Initiative
pages.html:
Initiative

When a Catfight occurs, it quickly escalates to be a big deal between a Kitten and his opponent! But at the gaming table, we need to keep things a little more orderly so that all players can take their turn to talk and resolve their action. We call this initiative.

The players can decide which Kitten acts first before any opponent acts, or if the players can’t agree, the Storyteller can decide, unless all the Kittens were surprised , in which case the Storyteller chooses an opponent to act first. He can perform an action of his choice and even move a little.

If the Kitten’s action is an aggressive action—that is, an action that directly targets an opponent—the player must complete her action and then hand the initiative to the Storyteller, who will play the part of the enemy. If the Kitten’s action is a non-aggressive action—that is, an action that helps an ally, moves a bigger distance, or accomplishes something that does not threaten an opponent— the player must complete her action and then can pass the initiative to another player. It is the same for enemies: Depending on the enemy’s action (aggressive or non-aggressive), the Storyteller can keep the initiative or pass it to one of the players. One complete turn of a Catfight ends when all players and all their opponents have each performed an action.

Tactical actions

It is impossible to measure the number of possible actions in a Catfight—anything can happen. There are, however, a number of very common actions. There’s no need to learn this list by heart; these actions use the same mechanics that you have already seen.

Help. This is a non-aggressive action. The goal is to use the action to give an advantage to a comrade who will make an ability test during his own action. The help action is automatically successful.

Hinder. This is an aggressive action. The goal is to give an opponent a disadvantage. For this to work, it is usually enough to roll at least 1 success on an appropriate ability roll, depending on the method described by the player. A successfully-cast spell can instead be used for this action if that spell does not cause the loss of Heart points.

pages.name: p.59 - Attitude
pages.html:
Attack. This is an aggressive action. The goal is to inflict a loss of Heart points on an opponent, to force them to give up, or to render them unable to act. Each success on an attack ability roll causes the opponent to lose 1 Heart point. In a Fang Catfight, the player can make either a Strong or Cute ability roll. Almost any Skill can be used, depending on the circumstances: Hiss & Growl, Seduce & Charm, Shake Your Booty, Sweet-talk, Keep Calm & Carry On, etcetera. In a Claw Catfight, the player may make a Strong or Smart ability roll. Only the Scratch skill can be used. Weapons give re-rolls, as long as they are listed as Purr-ecious items. Defend. This is a non-aggressive action. The Kitten tries to defend himself or his comrades.

He makes a Strong or Smart ability roll, using the Keep Calm & Carry On or Shake Your Booty skills. He can use successes he rolls to cancel an opponent’s successes on any attack in that turn. Interact. This is a non-aggressive action. The Kitten interacts with the scenery or with other creatures, without attacking or acting aggressively. He can talk, pick a lock, heal a comrade, and so on. Move. This is a non-aggressive action. The Kitten makes a big movement, perhaps some acrobatics or a stunt, or leaps over a large obstacle. Sometimes it may be necessary to perform a roll for Strong or Smart/Shake Your Booty. With this action a Kitten may hide, or move silently, by using the appropriate skills.

Attitude

At any point in a Fang Catfight, a Kitten can lift its paws in the air and concede victory to their opponent—the opponent may also do the same. Once out of a Fang Catfight you may not return to the fight—especially after resolving any post-fight healing, for example. Generally speaking, conceding victory prevents the consequences of a total defeat (zero Heart points). The opponent is magnanimous in victory and an arrangement can be negotiated.

The only ways of withdrawing from a Claw Catfight are to flee or lift paws into the air. Generally, you have to succeed with a roll for Smart/Shake Your Booty in order to flee, or a roll for Cute /Seduce & Charm to give up with no risk.

pages.name: p.60 - Consequences
pages.html:
Consequences

Here’s what happens when a creature falls to 0 Heart points during a Catfight:

In a Fang Catfight, the Kitten raises his paws in the air, puts his tail between his legs, or runs away. Whatever they do, they accept that the opponent won there and then, and can no longer make actions, at least until the end of the scene. It is universally understood that after a Fang Catfight, one party accepts defeat. But it is also understood that their opponent will not seek to profit from that beyond the subject of the Catfight. If it was a Catfight about, say, who goes first across the bridge, there is no question afterwards of taking advantage and stealing the loser’s money or taking them prisoner. In a Claw Catfight, the consequences are much more serious. A creature that drops to 0 Heart points is seriously injured! A Kitten that drops to 0 Heart points rolls for a wound from the table below:

1d6 Consequence

1 Bruises The Kitten escapes with only a few scratches and a little less hair.

2 Minor injury The Kitten gets a disadvantage for all its rolls until the end of the next rest stop (see page 53).

3 Major injury The Kitten gets a disadvantage to all its rolls until the end of the adventure. 4 Serious injury The Kitten cannot do anything for 1 full day.

5 Very serious injury

The Kitten cannot do anything for at least 1d6 full days and cannot use meowgic until the end of the adventure.

6 Critical injury

The Kitten cannot do anything for 1d6 days and cannot use meowgic until the end of the adventure. He also permanently loses 1 point in one of his abilities (the player chooses); if the chosen ability is Strong or Smart, the Kitten therefore loses 1 Heart point.

pages.name: p.62
pages.html:
Example Catfight: Jacko, Spinnit, and Veralynne are three Kittens who were exiled by Walter a few weeks ago. After a few adventures, they find themselves in Clarin, the city of sheep, a place where much woolen clothing and blankets blankets are produced. They are strolling through the market when they see another small band of exiles, and Jacko, a young noble, recognizes one of the other band as Ruby-Chewsday, another noble Kitten from Cat Tree City. Jacko reflects for a second: Ruby-Chewsday was older than him, and used to bully him. Spinnit, the daughter of a craftsman from Chopton, quickly realizes that the other exiles seem to be harassing and stealing from the merchants! Veralynne is, the daughter of Vizir Chilli, the officer in charge of the Cat Tree City Fair, sees red. It is undignified for Kittens to behave like this and she rushes over to put a stop to it.

That’s how a Fang

Catfight starts!

These are our heroes, the players’ characters: Jacko, Young Noble // Strong 1 / Smart 3 / Cute 4 // Heart points 4 // Furr-endship points 4 // See & Search; Seduce & Charm // Cat’s Eyes (1); Enchanting Voice (2)

Spinnit, Apprent-hiss // Strong 2 / Smart 3 / Cute 3 // Heart points 5 // Furr-endship points 3 // Cook; Treating Beasts (1) // Leather Apron (1); Breathe Under Water (1)

Veralynne, Soldier’s Child // Strong 4 / Smart 2 / Cute 2 // Heart points 4 // Furr- endship points 4 // Shake Your Booty; Hiss & Growl // Fearless (1); First Aid (2)

And here are the bad boys and girls of the Ruby-Chewsday gang, played by the Storyteller:

Ruby-Chewsday, Arrogant and brutal noble // Strong 2 / Smart 1 / Cute 3 // Heart points 3

Flounder, Rude, hot-headed ferret // Strong 2 / Smart 2 / Cute 4 // Heart points 4 // Hiss & Growl

Fulstop, Aggressive, mocking little Kitten // Strong 3 / Smart 1 / Cute 2 // Heart points 4

Furnace, Large hedgehog with ginger quills // Strong 3 / Smart 2 / Cute 3 // Heart points 5 // Keep Calm & Carry On.

pages.name: p.63
pages.html:
Initiative! The players get to take their turn first. They decide that Jacko will act and open the hostilities. He calls out to Ruby-Chewsday: “That’s not how decent creatures do things, Ruby- Chewsday! You should be ashamed of yourself.” // The Storyteller decides this is a roll for Cute, and Jacko rolls 3 successes! Ruby-Chewsday loses 3 Heart points straight away and steps back, stunned and humiliated—he is out of action for the moment!

As Jacko carried out an aggressive action, the players must pass initiative to the Storyteller, so it is her turn to play the actions of her extras. She decides that Flounder will answer back. The ferret has a strong lisp, but that does not stop him from making a nasty comment: “Do you weally fink you got thomething to thay to uth? Go and wash yourselfth, you thmelly thothageth!” // It’s also a Cute roll for Flounder, but he gets an advantage because of his Hiss & Growl skill. However, on four dice and despite a Cute score of 4, he only rolls 1 success. That’s very poor… but Jacko still loses 1 Heart point.

The enemies took an aggressive action, so initiative must pass back to the players and it is their turn. Veralynne steps forward and puffs up her chest underneath her leather breastplate, to make an impression on Ruby-Chewsday’s comrades. That’s a defense. // It is a roll for Strong, and she gets an advantage since she has the Shake Your Booty skill, and a possible re-roll thanks to her leather armor (one of her Purr-ecious items). Amazing! Veralynne rolls four successes and stuns her opponents with a death stare, as if challenging them to say something.

As it was a non-aggressive action, the players still have the initiative and it is Spinnit’s turn. She stands there, indignant and fuming. She turns to the Ferret. “Really? Wash? You should wash your mouth out with soap! Or do do you need your mom to do it for you?” // It’s a straightforward roll for Cute, with no advantages or re-rolls. Spinnit’s player is: 3 successes on the three dice! Flounder loses 3 Heart points, feeling his cheeks redden and burn from the insult.

All of the Kittens have acted, so initiative must pass back to the opponents. The last two villains, Fulstop and Furnace, can now act and finish the first round of the Catfight. Furnace stays where he is and bristles the hair on his back. He is calm and confident, and looks straight into Veralynne's eyes. // It is a roll for Strong, with an advantage thanks to his Keep Calm & Carry On skill. The Storyteller rolls two successes, which knocks the young soldier’s defenses, but doesn’t affect her morale.

pages.name: p.64
pages.html:
Fulstop goes for Spinnit, bristling the hair on his back and tail, "Get out of here, fishface. Go back to counting beans!” // It's a straightforward roll for Strong. The Storyteller only rolls one success, but Veralynne’s defense from earlier allows him to absorb it, even though Spinnit was the target.

All Kittens and enemies have acted, so the second round starts. Jacko gets the initiative and turns, smiling, to Flounder and his pals: “I’m sure Ruby-

Chewsday promised you hot baths, sweet perfume, and a place by his side in

Cat Tree City. But you should know that he is no longer welcome there, since he stole cakes from Walter… I wouldn’t be surprised if he never sees the capital again, and neither will you.” // It’s a roll for Cute, with the

Seduce & Charm skill and a possible re-roll, thanks to the sweet smell of Jacko’s special fur shampoo (his Purr-ecious item).

Jacko’s player rolls three successes on the first throw, and the re-roll brings a fourth. Flounder is eliminated when he falls to

0 Heart points and turns, ungracefully, to Ruby-Chewsday. Fulstop loses his 3 remaining Heart points as soon as he sees the ferret give up the fight.

Furnace lifts his paws into the air, glaring at the sheep’s wool merchant (with the implicit promise that they’ll be back) and drags the rest of the sorry band off with him, toward the market’s exit. The tension lifts, and Jacko sits down quickly to catch his breath. The wool merchant hands him a large cup of warm milk and thanks him with a big smile.

pages.name: p.65 - Extras
pages.html:
Extras

Extras and monsters are created in a similar way to Kittens, but in a simplified manner. They are shown like this:

Tiramisu. Big tabby cat; patron of the Honorable Kittysnacks Society; intimidating and generous // Strong 5 / Smart 3 / Cute 4 // Heart points 8 // Cook; Find Information; Hiss & Growl; Knowledge of People & Places // Clean and Tidy (1); Preserving resources (1); Slice and Dice (1) // Large butcher’s knife; thick apron; box of spices.

First the name is shown. Then a line or two of description is given—typically appearance and character. The extra may get re-rolls if this description applies to an action they make. Then come abilities, Heart points, skills, spells, and Purr-ecious items. Some extras also have the equivalent of Cattributes or other special abilities.

The same rules apply to extras as Kittens: How they roll the dice, advantages and disadvantages, re-rolls, and so on.

The table below is a guide to help the Storyteller create extras and creatures based on their difficulty as opponents (similar to the process on page 14):

Extra Abilities Skills Spells Purr-ecious items Weak 6 points 1 0 1 Average 8 points 2 1 or 2 2 or 3 Strong 10 points 3 2 or 3 3 or 4 Very strong 12 points 4 3 or more 4 or 5

pages.name: p.67 - Player’s book
pages.html:
Player’s book

My dear playing pals, the pages in this section are filled with tips and good advice. This is not the only way to play, but it’s a great way to get started: You and your friends will learn how to find the way to play that suits you the best.

First of all: don’t worry

Dungeons and Kittens is a game. There is nothing real at stake, you don’t have to achieve anything. Nobody is expecting anything from you. There are no winners or losers. You can stay quiet or participate a lot. In fact, you don’t even have to have fun—but it would be better if you did. And you can leave the gaming table whenever you want.

There is no skill difference between a beginner and an experienced player. Everyone can take their turn to shine with bright ideas and intelligence, and then make the dumbest mistakes possible (believe me, when you think you have seen and heard everything, players who have been gaming for years will find a way to surprise you). And it really doesn’t matter: Dungeons and Kittens is a game, and even the most awful errors are ones we can laugh about afterwards, since they have no consequences in real life.

And that is the beauty of telling stories together: they’re just stories, and everyone brings something to them. There are no wrong decisions or wrong ways for your Kitten to act. All the bumps, all the adventures—be they comic, dramatic, heroic, sad, or joyful—add to the story and take us in often surprising, but always interesting, directions.

Also, it is impossible for you to play badly, or to misunderstand your Kitten. If you want to, you can lie and deceive, try impossible or stupid things, make plans, leap in without thinking. It’s a bit like kicking a ball: you don’t have to be skilled to have fun—just follow it and keep kicking.

pages.name: p.68 - A little word about etiquette
pages.html:
A little word about etiquette

However, just because Dungeons and Kittens is a game where anything is possible for the characters, it does not mean that the players can do just any old thing, however they want. It is strictly forbidden to behave rudely around the gaming table!

A game of Dungeons and Kittens is a pleasant pastime, played by friendly people. And everything that is judged to be bad behavior outside—laughing at or insulting your friends, scapegoating someone, harassing each other, blowing your nose on the tablecloth, picking your toenails, disrespecting the Storyteller and so on—all of that is absolutely, strictly forbidden.

Similarly, you can laugh with someone, but you must never laugh at someone! Some people are actually very sensitive and you should always be careful that your comrades are laughing along with you and are happy. Also remember not to drag a joke on too long.

After all, Dungeons and Kittens offers good times and a lot of fun, whether it is with friends at home or with strangers at a convention, or on the internet. And everyone should behave as they would like others to behave with them.

Of course, this rule comes down to the question of characters and customs—what is acceptable at one gaming table may be seen as bad form at another. Also, eventually, players will learn to pay attention to others in the group, not to want to mark their territory by spraying their scent everywhere, or imposing their point of view by talking over everyone else. Remember to introduce yourself to players you don’t know—it’s always nicer to be on first name terms (and to know the preferred gender pronouns) of your neighbors at the table.

And if a player behaves really badly and gets a few warnings, it is perfectly acceptable to ban them from the table and to no longer play with them.

In short: behave well, pay attention to your human sisters and brothers and everything will be fine.

pages.name: p.69 - The player and her Kitten
pages.html:
The player and her Kitten

To follow on from what is stated above: the player is not her Kitten and the Kitten is not the player. That may seem obvious, but it can be anything but. As a game takes place, and as you play your character, you get into the game quickly and it often happens that you begin to feel your Kitten’s emotions yourself.

After all, although the adventures and stories are imaginary, and the Kitten is a fictional character, the time you spend around the table is real, and some of the things you experience there are as real for your brain as if you were the Kitten himself. Which is fine.

However, you must remember that the other players are not their Kittens, and the Storyteller is not the extras she brings to life. A Kitten can do stupid things, behave badly, and have the manners of a grumpy hippopotamus; extras can be aggressive, rude, cruel, and mean. All this is part of the story.

We recommend you not take this too personally, even though the story can beco me intense. However, players are always en couraged to say when a situation is really becoming upsetting (see page 70). Sometimes a player can get angry after someone says something nasty to their Kitten. A little humor and detachment, a little perspective, and some dramatic irony do a lot to keep play gentle and calm. You can still let your emotions and feelings rise, but at the same time, keep a critical view of what’s going on. It’s like reading a good book or watching a good film that really involves you: it may bring a little tear to the eye, but there should be a pleasant smile at the end.

pages.name: p.70 - Play safe
pages.html:
Play safe

However, there are times when all these precautions are not enough, so players should always be ready and willing to make an extra effort to make sure everyone is having a good time.

There may be situations in the game that can touch a sensitive nerve or provoke sudden emotions in a player. Nobody will know in advance which situations can trigger bad feelings. The most common one is a phobia: it is never a good idea to have a horde of giant spiders come crawling out of the woods when a player has chronic fear of spiders. But there are also many other sorts of life events (big and small) which may be recalled during a session: bad memories, disastrous experiences, loss, or trauma.

When this happens, there is only one thing to do: The player must tell the others at the table immediately, or, if she is not able to, other players should be attentive enough to notice and react. You have to stop the scene, get rid of the problematic elements of the game, take a break and have a snack or drink, talk about something else, and alleviate any discomfort. This is just as you would do with a nightmare, by waking up and taking care of yourself for a few moments.

It’s not a question of pampering, being ultra-sensitive, or anything else: If a player doesn’t feel good, it is a serious matter, and it is up to everyone to make it better.

Choose your game

In fact, it even goes a little further than that. Dungeons and Kittens allows you to create all kinds of stories, with very different atmospheres, but players don’t necessarily like all the same things—or not in the same amounts. Different players prefer a little drama, a little action, a little mystery, a little horror, a little investigation, a little romance, some chills, laughter, serious stuff, and so on.

It is not easy to agree in advance on the genre you want to make more of—it is difficult to anticipate how the story will evolve and it is easier to know what you don’t want than things you do.

It is therefore important that everyone pays attention to everyone else, and nobody makes final, unilateral decisions alone in their corner and without asking their

pages.name: p.71 - Time to talk
pages.html:
comrades’ opinions. Imagine if you had a Kitten who wanted to betray an extra and who acted behind his friends’ backs, while everyone else in the party wanted to help him. It’s perfectly possible if it’s part of the story—after all, it is the Kitten that acts, not the player. But only on the condition that all other players accept the consequences and have fun with the reversal of the situation. Otherwise, it’s just a way of disturbing the peace.

Once again, as you can see, it is predo minantly a question of paying attention to your comrades in order to enjoy the same game, all together in a group.

Time to talk

Playing Dungeons and Kittens is kind of like a very long conversation between the players and the Storyteller. There’s a lot of talking required.

However, here’s an example: a Storyteller and four players are having a gaming ses sion one Saturday afternoon for four hours. Assuming there are no long interruptions to go and heat up some hot chocolate or raid the stash of chips in the cupboard, the Storyteller will probably talk for half the time. She will be describing situations and settings, speaking for the extras, answering the players’ questions, managing the me chanics and the rules, and so on. That leaves two hours of speaking time to be shared be tween the four players—half an hour each.

Dungeons and Kittens is a game where, in fact, you listen much more than you talk. However, listening does not mean that you are passive—on the contrary.

To begin with, you can take notes. Notes are important: Names of extras and places, the chronology of events, details in a story and clues in an investigation, maybe what your Kitten is thinking, whether your comrades are in good spirits, a humorous exchange, or a hilarious slip of the tongue. All of this adds up to a gaming memory that can be very useful when you play regularly.

Then you can prepare your Kitten’s actions, think about the choices that come up, the goals you want him to achieve, what he can do to achieve them, and so on. So, when the Storyteller gives you the floor and asks you what your Kitten wants to do, you can react immediately: You know the questions you want to ask, you have already thought about what actions to take. That means time saved for everyone and makes the gameplay fast and dynamic—the turns go quickly as a result.

pages.name: p.72 - Speaking out
pages.html:
Speaking out

It is usually the Storyteller who decides the order of speaking around the table— this is good practice that we will discuss in the chapter dedicated to her (pages 183-200). However, that does not mean that each player is not responsible for both the discipline required and knowing what works best in taking turns.

Fortunately, in Dungeons and Kittens it is not the case where you talk for half an hour and then stay silent the rest of the time. The game is organized in the form of a dialog: between the Storyteller and the players, and between the players themselves.

Generally speaking, you should wait for the Storyteller to let you know when to speak. She will go around the table and talk to everyone in turn. This is all the more important when every Kitten has something they want to do. And this ensures that the loudest players do not talk over the shy players, or those who are a bit less good at speaking out. That way, the game is faster, tighter, and more energetic, as everyone takes it in turns to speak without hesitation or interruption.

But do not hesitate to show that you want to intervene, offer an idea or an alternative, ask a question, or ask to clarify something. The Storyteller will let you talk if it does not interrupt another player or the situation she is describing.

You can of course make comments, jokes, smart remarks, or reactions that accompany the Kittens’ actions, but it must not distract from the game or come at a bad time. So avoid distractions that have nothing to do with the game, like talking about your cat’s fleas or the latest unmissable TV show with the person next to you at the table when another player is taking their turn.

Another sort of thing happens a lot and it is often involuntary: When the Storyteller has just given you your turn and she moves on to another player to continue around the table, do not interrupt her by wanting to ask a new question or make another action! It’s a bit rude and, anyway, the Storyteller will be back to you shortly. So rein in your eagerness and wait your turn…

The previous advice remains valid when another player is talking. But when it is the Kitten speaking and talking to an extra, it is a little different; that will be a more free-form discussion, so everyone can take part, join in, and even interrupt their neighbors if necessary. Just remember, everything that is said around the table actually comes from the mouths of the Kittens. So beware of blunders, etiquette errors, lapses of civility, or impoliteness! What’s said is said!

pages.name: p.73 - Choices and decisions
pages.html:
Choices and decisions

In Dungeons and Kittens, the story unfolds because the players make choices and decisions, and because their Kittens make actions. In fact, this notion of choice and decision is at the very heart of the game and its mechanics.

A story is like a snake that keeps on moving forward around a maze without ever being able to go back. It is a maze with as many possible exits (the end of the story) as there are paths that can be traveled. The story snake changes its path largely through the choices and decisions of the players (and a little through the results of the die rolls).

The Storyteller, and the players, cannot know in advance what the snake’s path will be or what exit it will take—that’s the whole point of playing together around the table instead of reading a novel or watching a TV series. Whenever the snake arrives at a junction, the players choose one of the paths available to them (or invent a new one).

Should we cut through the forest, where there are giant spiders, or take the old road, where we’ll have to negotiate with the Yardogs in order to cross the old bridge? Do we have time to help Mother Fox who must feed her little ones, or do we absolutely have to get to the village before dark so we can talk to the mechanic at the Great Clock? Should we stay hidden from the troop of badger mercenaries who are marching up the road, or shall we ask them if we can travel with them? How can we deactivate this terribly dangerous trap without getting hurt? How do we get the essential information out of the gang of thieves who are based at the Satellite Inn?

A choice is interesting because it always has consequences, good and bad, and it is these consequences that drive the story. So, think before you make a decision—but also be decisive and determined! And don’t forget that you have multiple brains around the table to discuss matters, weigh up the pros and cons, and make joint decisions.

pages.name: p.74 - Ask questions
pages.html:
Ask questions

The secret is that you only have a choice if you have information about the possible consequences check spacing between senten ces here you have to choose between two identical doors it’s not choice, it’s luck. But if you can investigate the doors and one of them has nice kitchen smells coming from it and the other is cold and damp, you can start to weigh up your options.

So you will have to ask a lot of questions, be very curious, and keep constantly on the lookout for the slightest clues that the Storyteller may give.

Your Kitten is immersed in the delicate world of the story: he sees, he hears, he breathes, he smells, he feels textures under his paws, he tastes things in his mouth. You only have what the Storyteller tells you and explains for information—and she will never be more precise than the interest you show in the details. If you ask questions, she’ll give you the information you think you will need. It’s like zooming in on an object: If you choose to get closer, then you’ll have more and more detail. However, it’s unlikely that the Storyteller will give you answers to questions you don’t ask.

So when your Kitten arrives in a new situation—whether at the start of a story, when you are discovering what’s happening in a new situation, or during the game at times that may be difficult to anticipate— your job as a player is to ask questions to identify and understand all the elements in place. This is what will allow you to make decisions and make your Kitten act.

Sometimes you’ll just need to ask the Storyteller for information—it may be common knowledge that your Kitten already has, or the answer may be in his visible environment. Other times, your Kitten will have to make an effort: questioning people, reading a book, searching a location, examining an object, and so on. Some information is easier to get than others.

First: Identify. The storyteller always gives you few details to start with, the start of the trail of breadcrumbs you can follow. So listen carefully to everything she says: She will slip in some small important things—that might initially sound unimportant—hidden inside other things. From there, you can ask her what a place looks like, about particular elements of the decor, the weather, humidity, the brightness, and so on… Ask if there are useful resources for your Kitten: some tools or materials, a place to hide, food, and water. You can also observe extras and creatures you

pages.name: p.75
pages.html:
meet, and try to read their state of mind or their emotions, their body language, and the words they use. But you will only get this if you ask the Storyteller questions.

Then: Understand. Armed with this initial information, you can now try to understand the ins and outs of a situation. Again, you’ll need to ask the Storyteller some questions. Compare this information to what you, the player, already know and what you have learned so far (now is the time to have another look at your notes). You can also call on your Kitten's knowledge: He knows a lot of things you don't know (yet). Ask the Storyteller to clarify you understand things correctly. You can use all this information to work out what motivates an extra, what a location is like, the side stories, and the big secrets. You can learn the best way to negotiate, the right order to do things, or how to address certain extras that your Kitten may need to charm in a particular way.

pages.name: p.76 - Make your Kitten act
pages.html:
Make your Kitten act

Every time your Kitten acts, it changes the direction of the story snake. And then it is up to the Storyteller to determine what the consequences of that action will be in the world of Dungeons and Kittens. Some actions are automatically successful: tying your laces or closing your bag. Other actions automatically fail: uprooting a hundred-year-old tree with a single paw. Many actions have very limited consequences. In these cases, your Kitten manages to do what he wants to do or not, maybe wastes a little time, gets tired, or breaks something.

Sometimes the consequences of an action (or a sequence of actions) are much bigger and can influence the whole world. Getting angry with a powerful creature of the woods doesn’t have quite the same long-term effects as forming an alliance or making friends with it. The ideal is to always try to choose the actions that will have the most positive consequences both for your Kitten and for the world of Dungeons and Kittens.

When your Kitten has to act—open a strange door, negotiate with someone, flee through the woods, and so on—try to work out the best way of doing it. Look for objects in his backpack that could help; look at his surroundings to see if there is help available; ask the other Kittens if they can lend a paw (or four). If the Kitten needs to ask someone a favor, it is usually better to say hello, please, and thank you (in fact, it’s just like in real life—you always get more with a smile than a scowl).

The more ideas you can come up with to make the action a success, the more likely you are to convince the Storyteller that your Kitten is capable of doing it (and doing it better). Similarly, you can offer compromises: The action may take a little longer than expected, the Kitten may get tired or use resources, he can take extra risks, and so on.

Don’t just say something like: “My Kitten jumps over the ditch.” Explain to the Storyteller precisely how he is going to get a bit more momentum by taking a run-up from the best possible angle after you have had a good look around. Tell how he first gets rid of his backpack by throwing it across to the other side to lighten the load— and all those kinds of little ideas that will make it easier for him to succeed. Generally speaking, Storytellers will tend to imagine big challenges for the slightest of actions, but as soon as you explain to them exactly how the action will be accomplished, it gets easier.

pages.name: p.77 - Elaborate and make stuff up
pages.html:
Elaborate and make stuff up

Which leads us to an important element: The Storyteller controls her world of Dungeons and Kittens and she is responsible for its consistency, but that doesn’t mean that you can’t invent things and bring elements into the game universe.

In fact, the opposite is true. You have great powers of invention, if you choose to use them. You remember that the Storyteller is the eyes and ears of your Kitten: It is she who describes the surroundings. Sure, but what if she misses some detail? Can you just add them yourself?

When your Kitten needs something to help him carry out an action, you can, of course, make specific suggestions. Imagine that while lost in the middle of some fields, your Kitten needs to repair an object. The Storyteller could certainly tell you that it is impossible, or at least very difficult. But nothing is stopping you from asking if your Kitten could maybe use parts taken from that old, rusting car that’s half-buried in the hedge. The Storyteller never mentioned this old wreck, but nothing is stopping it from being there if the Storyteller accepts it. She may well be open to it if the suggestion is made.

And if you want to make sure the Storyteller agrees, you could also explain to her how the wreck is tangled up in some roots that will have to be cleared first, and then tell her about the odd feeling your Kitten gets from the wreck, as if there may be a something living in there.

In one go, you get the spare parts for the repair your Kitten wants to make, and you give the Storyteller a little idea for a side story! Everyone is happy. But then you are faced with a new choice: Shall we just leave the object broken, or shall we take the risk and explore the roots and the rusty car?

Of course, all this works as long as you respect the limits and laws of the universe and do not make up fanciful, im possible, absurd, illogical, or unbelievable things. The secret? Get the Storyteller and the other players on your side.

pages.name: p.78 - Channel your Kitten
pages.html:
Channel your Kitten

There has been a lot of talk about what the player says in Dungeons and Kittens, but what about what her Kitten? How can you understand it, speak for it, and express its emotions?

There are plenty of ways to do this:—You can talk about him in the third person (“being very careful, and using his rope, my Kitten climbs the biggest tree on the edge of the field to look into the distance…”). —You can talk in the first person (“I run up behind the Yardog to push him and grab the backpack he just stole!”). —You can move from one register to another according to the circumstances and how you feel.

Generally speaking, when your Kitten is talking, everything he says is spoken aloud in the game world. If there are extras listening, he should be careful about what he says, or face the consequences. You can't go back.

Playing a Kitten is not like acting in a play. Even if the story may be funny and the players joke around, the Kitten’s words and actions are serious things that may have consequences.

pages.name: p.79
pages.html:
But there’s no need to make a meal of this drama. It is usually better to describe the tears running down the sad Kitten’s cheeks than to sniff loudly at the table while sobbing miserably.

Similarly, you should always try to think of your Kitten as a regular person (like you), although, of course, he’s an adventurer and he takes risks that you would never take. However, you may conclude there are in-game reasons for your Kitten to make decisions you would not. If you think that your Kitten would act in a certain way, you should be ready to pursue those actions to the end and face the consequences.

This notion of seriousness is important: Dungeons and Kittens is a game and the players have fun, but their Kittens are immersed in what can be dark and difficult stories, and you have to maintain a measure of gravitas to keep up with the mood.

However, you have a huge advantage: the principle of dramatic irony. This is like when the hero in a film approaches a closed door. The audience knows that there is a monster behind the door, but the hero doesn’t. Everyone shudders in anticipation or is about to laugh at the character’s surprised face.

You know things your Kitten doesn’t know. You understand what may happen if your Kitten acts in this or that way. But you can still make choices, and take the time to think. You can enjoy the humor of a situation, but you must not forget that for your Kitten, it is all serious and important!

And that’s it—we hope that all these tips and advice will help you play Dungeons and Kittens and make your games more enjoyable and thrilling.

pages.html:
The Kingdom of Cats

pages.name: p.82
pages.html: Cats believe they are the center of the world. And they’re not far wrong! The Kingdom of Cats is at the forefront of Meowgic Studies, agricultural production, and technological development.

pages.name: p.83 - Meowgic and everyday life
pages.html:
Taking advantage of the temperate climate and land now clear of human pollution, the rise of the cats was rapid and seemingly impossible to stop. All eyes are on Cat Tree City, the capital of the kingdom, where King Walter rules.

From high in his tower, King Walter governs his land and his subjects. That is to say, he spends his days watching the animals work, beavering away to fill his coffers, and put ever more sumptuous dishes on his table. King Walter, with his seemingly insatiable royal belly, is just the latest in a long line of large, lazy louts who, through all manner of false promises, made it onto the throne and then turned tyrant.

The majority of animals that live in the kingdom are cats, but it is not uncommon to meet, say, a merchant ferret, a vagabond dog, or even a little minstrel skunk. But as you would imagine, rodents remain rare. And although cats live off the the land and are always respectful of the universal law—an animal that talks eats not another animal that talks—historic enmity ensures a line is still maintained between former prey and former predator.

Meowgic and everyday life

The Kingdom of Cats features an incessant soundtrack: the beating of tools and materials in the workshops; off-key singing in the fields; and the clashing of swords in the Royal Guard’s courtyard. Meowgic amplifies this daily melody. Meowgic is not reserved solely for the ancient archmeowges in the tower, although they are the only ones to fully master the art. Meowgic is ever-present and can be useful to all: threading a needle, healing everyday wounds, and helping to keep tidy the rooms of even the messiest Kittens!

pages.name: p.84 - The Exile of Kittens
pages.html:
The Exile of Kittens

Every kingdom has its ruler and it could be said—honestly—that cats are not lucky. King Walter is enormous, bad-tempered, unfair, stupid, and bone idle, unless it comes to plotting and intrigue. He made it to the throne through cheating and trickery, and ever since has remained in power through the help of his faithful Royal Guard, who blindly follow his every order. And to ensure that he wants for nothing, he rules by fear. Taxes are excessive and cruel, the Royal Guard is all-powerful, and justice is swift and merciless.

And King Walter’s most unfair law is surely the Exile of Kittens. Under the false pretence of an initiation quest, the exile is in fact a punishment for families and a danger for every child who is sent far away. Following a ca lendar that only he understands, King Walter organizes a draw (which everyone knows is rigged) in order to pick the Kittens who will be cast out. This is followed by a sham celebration, during which a quest is assigned to those Kittens. Following that: good riddance!

The mission given to the Kittens is to return with treasure—amazing treasure—if they want to see their loved ones again and return to reside in the relative security of the kingdom. Unfortunately, Walter’s instructions are often imprecise, incomplete, and even downright dishonest…

And so, sadly, it is not uncommon to see young cats grow up in exile, alone in the wild world beyond the city walls, having given up on the ridiculous royal quest.

And with the threat of exile for their children or grandchildren at the slightest sign of dissent, King Walter has created such a climate of fear that none dare question him. And that is a price that he, and the members of his court, are more than willing to pay for their lasting luxury. The rest of the kingdom must simply submit, whether they agree or not.

However, his nastiness does not stop at the exile. Walter plots with the Yardogs as a way of keeping useful enemies close by— and another threat he can use to silence his subjects…

pages.name: p.86 - Cat Tree City
pages.html:
Cat Tree City

The capital of the Kingdom of Cats is affectionately named Cat Tree City—but it is ultimately the name of Walter’s gigantic fortress. It is a huge, vertical city where the floor you occupy indicates your social position—the richest and most powerful cats wanting to reach ever higher for themselves, and to lord it over the other noble families.

For these cats, the social elevator operates at full speed, whereas the poor and downtrodden are not even allowed in the tower and must live in the suburbs, the sprawling neighborhoods at its feet.

In the tower itself, luxury is everywhere and, despite its relative narrowness, each floor has been tastefully decorated with care and a sense of grandeur. Mechanical elevators make their way up and down the various microcosm levels, each of which is stranger than the last, as they compete to see which can be the most original and eccentric.

Six floors under—the dungeons. If a Kitten is caught stealing bread from the market, he risks spending time in the dungeon, where he will remain unless he can find a way out, or waits for the goodwill of the guards or Walter (fat chance!)

nd floor—the fine Spice Market. Its delightful scents fill the entire stairwell. Somewhat isolated from the other stores in the tower, this market occupies the entire floor and comes under the direction of a mysterious, hairless cat named Bareboddy.

th floor—the library. Knowing their time of departure is near, some Kittens may want to learn more about the outside world and may try to “borrow” maps, atlases, and spellbooks. The librarian, Lamia, keeps guard, watching over everything.

th floor—baths and thermal pools. This is a labyrinth of bathrooms and swimming pools, pipes, and boilers. Cats meet there at all times of day or night, in bathrobes with a towel under the paw, and an array of masseurs and beauticians are happy to groom and scratch them.

pages.name: p.87
pages.html:
rd floor—the school for nobles. Here, Kittens learn about the arts, music, mathematics, speaking, and so on. Obviously, most Kittens prefer breaktime. There are often a few Kittens from the outside who come to take part in marbles matches or frenzied games of dodgeball.

st floor—the dance academy, frequented by all the Kittens of Cat Tree City. The knowledge and practice of formal dance is what differentiates noble cats from the inhabitants of the suburbs (who are more content with spinning around to crazed tarantellas).

nd floor—the large greenhouse of exotic plants, all ripe with strange fruits. The meowges of Highcastle look after this place, and keep it at a warm temperature.

th floor—the Hall of Mirrors, where hundreds of mirrors of all shapes and sizes, made of glass or silver, framed or bare, hang all higgledy-piggledy on the walls.

Around the 80th floor—the Heights is the name given to the upper levels of the grand tower of Cat Tree City, consisting of palaces, sumptuous restaurants, and shops filled with Purr-ecious items (not to mention Bobbins', the toy store). Suburban Kittens love hanging out there, although the guard is not quite so keen about their presence.

th floor (and above)—these are Walter’s apartments, never seen by the public apart from the throne room, and even then, only in truly exceptional circumstances. Far from the eyes of the people—and even the members of his court—Walter has a vast pantry filled to bursting, a group of discreet bodyguards that changes every three hours, and his own private elevator that allows him to secretly entertain the most villainous individuals of the Kingdom of Cats.

pages.name: p.88
pages.html:
Encounters in the upper floors The Heights of Cat Tree City are reserved for nobles from the Kingdom of Cats, Walter’s courtiers, but it also happens to be the Kittens’ favorite playground: the view is superb, and there are plenty of nooks, crannies, vast rooms, and forbidden places (at least for the public) to wander. In short, it is a paradise for all Kittens that are at least a little bit adventurous. Obviously, the Royal Guard tries to keep an eye on them and chase them off, but that makes up part of the game.

1d6 Rounding the corridors, Kittens may find:

1 Walter in an alcove, whispering with a hooded figure.

2 A troop of guards on a tour of the ramparts.

3 The meowge’s laboratory, which is temporarily abandoned.

4 Walter's favorite fine pastry shop—closed to the public! 5 A glass gallery full of distorting mirrors.

6 Behind the scenes of a theater where the latest fashionable play is being staged.

Licorishi, member of the Royal Guard Licorishi entered the Royal Guard when he was still a Kitten, like his father and seven siblings before him. Serving the king is no joke in that family! Wearing the uniform of the Royal Guard is a great honor and Licorishi is very proud of it. He rigidly respects the values of the guard, which are honesty and loyalty, but it is sometimes difficult to unite the two when you are in Walter’s service.

pages.name: p.89
pages.html:
Lamia the librarian Lamia is an elegant young cat. She is passionate about old books, leaflets, scrolls, and other antiquities. She has made it her mission to know everything about everything—and to do this, she reads everything in the library, starting with the letter A. She does not like to lend out the books, preferring to keep them with her, but if she can be convinced that someone shares her passion for old writings, she will probably make an exception.

Strong 1 / Smart 5 / Cute 2 // Heart points 6 // Knowledge of Laws & Legends; Knowledge of People & Places; Read, Write, Count // Heart Charm (1); Words of Wisdom (2) // A pair of glasses; a solar powered lamp.

Taro, from Bobbins’ toy store Taro is an old grey cat who always wears a colorful checked coat that makes him look like a harlequin. When his wife is watching, he tries to scare Kittens who hang around too long between the shelves of the famous shop, but in truth he really likes them. As soon as she is no longer around, he gives them sweets and lets them play as they please.

Strong 2 / Smart 2 / Cute 4 // Heart points 4 // See & Search; Sweet-talk // Cat’s Eyes (1); Summon Tools (2) // A colorful yo-yo; some candy; a wooden pencil and a notebook.

pages.name: p.90 - The suburbs
pages.html:
The suburbs

Piled up at the foot of Walter’s fortress are many small houses and huts. These make up the popular suburbs of the capital. This is where the traders, workers, and craftsmen live. This is the vibrant heart of the kingdom—where they play, meow, and sing, far from the silence of the plush apartments above. However, even the suburbs are subject to Walter’s greed. Taxes are high; houses and dwellings are regularly knocked down to strengthen or extend the base of the tower, or to build smoky, stinky factoriesfrom which emerges the explosive noise of machinery.

In fact, for several years now Walter has increased his portion; not only of food— military spending also! This is under the pretext of improving security and defense. The kingdom is arming, ready for expansion. Craftsmen of all types—tailors, watchmakers, carpenters, masons—have been bullied, taxed, and forced to work in factories to prepare for a war of conquest that has not yet been declared. And as pressure increases on suburban residents, inequalities become more and more evident.

There are three main districts in the Cat Tree City suburbs: the Marketplace, Chopton, and the Soot District.

pages.name: p.91 - The Marketplace
pages.html:
The Marketplace

Cat Tree City ’s main marketplace is a bright and open suburb, with many beautiful houses with vine-covered gables. On the ground floor, the houses have covered arcades with rows of shops and boutiques dedicated to the sale of all kinds of useful or precious items: fabrics and veils, pots and pans, bags and baskets, jewelry, toiletries, and scented soaps. In short, everything that is manufactured in the kingdom, and beyond. The inhabitants of the region inevitably end up meeting here and even Walter himself deigns to go down here and do a little shopping sometimes.

The Showground In the center of the market lies the vast Showground, where the (frequently vandalized) statue of Walter is situated. Here there are all sorts of wandering merchants from the kingdom and elsewhere, who do not own a shop in the neighborhood, and who come from afar to sell and swap their goods. Most of the time, there are no more than two or three peddlers passing through, but once a month, for three days, traders flock from all around, and the square is crowded with tables and stalls. This is the time to get your paws on some exceptional objects, or fill your pockets with goods. Kittens in exile can even take advantage, if a merchant is willing to help them to enter the city incognito, hidden in the trunks and boxes at the back of a cart. 1d6 Examples of unique marketplace objects

1 A human-made, folding multifunction tool 2 A pair of high magnification binoculars

3 A photo of a (clothed) big-bare-butt with a cat on their lap

4 A rock-solid rope of or spidersilk; I’d choose a consistent spelling

5 A small, domesticated octopus in a large jar of water

6 A plastic tiara with shiny gemstones (very precious!)

pages.name: p.92
pages.html:
Vizir Chilli Vizir Chilli is the royal officer in charge of organizing the Showground, locating merchants, granting pitches, settling quarrels, enforcing good business laws, protecting customers from swindlers, and collecting taxes and levies. Vizier Chilli was once an enthusiastic, loyal cat. But since his daughter was exiled by Walter—possibly on the pretext that the Vizir never managed to prevent the defacing of the royal statue—he no longer puts nearly as much effort into his work. He stops a bit too often in the drinking dens that surround the square, and he lets infringements go that he would never have previously ignored. Anyone who is able to give him news of his daughter is likely to attract his good favor.

Ptolemeow's Bazaar There are valuable, precious, and useful things, beautiful and essential items, rare and sought-after objects. And there’s everything else too: stacks of chipped mugs, bundles of yellowed waste paper, drawers of mismatched socks, buttons of all colors and sizes (but never two of the same), boxes of bent nails, old wooden pencil stubs—in short, everything that was thrown away and forgotten, nothing that is of much use any more. However, there is plenty of tidy, well packed stuff in this shop, which is is nestled in one of the market’s narrow alleys. It looks smaller from the outside—with its narrow shopfront and faded paint—than from in, where it is deep, with many levels and half-levels. Visitors will not find anything interesting or particularly useful here and will leave with the impression of having wasted their time and energy: Really, it is a pretty plain old flea market.

pages.name: p.93
pages.html:
Ptolemeow Ptolemeow is an old cat with silky hair , and with his eyes hidden behind thick glasses. He is a poor merchant, although his shop has been open for many years, but he is an excellent spy. He is in fact Walter’s chief spy, in charge of gathering information on all the region's powers: Selene, Corktown, Bigwheel, Huggle, and so on, as well as stirring up trouble and causing problems all over the kingdom. He’s the head of a vast network of bad boys and girls who do whatever he says: attacking merchants caravans, writing anti-Walter graffiti (and blaming locals), terrorizing the creatures of the kingdom with a thousand and one unpleasant acts and petty crimes. None of these threats are really serious, but just enough to to keep people worried, to keep an air of distrust (especially of Kittens in exile, who are accused of the worst crimes), and to keep obedience to the regal Walter.

Strong 3 / Smart 5 / Cute 4 // Heart points 8 // Find Information; Hide in Shadows; Knowledge of People & Places; Seduce & Charm // Feel the Path (3); Leave no Trace (1); The Color of Grass (1) // A dark cape; a bunch of false skeleton keys; a watch.

Chopton Chopton is the center of the kingdom's food production. All agricultural production ends up here, and is treated and transformed into portable snacks or treats, which are then exported worldwide. Countless breeders and growers cross the bridge every morning to bring their products and sell them in the trading halls. The bosses of the family canning factories come to buy goods and obtain the best produce (or worse produce, for those who create what is subsequently sold to those with smaller purses). Then the chopping, folding, mixing, and cooking begins, in order to fill pots, cans, and bags. Some manufacturers are very famous; for Kittens in exile, finding a box of such snacks when you are away from home is always a spe cial treat...

pages.name: p.94 - Regina and Sadie
pages.html:
Roundpaw, Incorporated Roundpaw, Inc. is one of the kingdom’s most famous producers. They don't make large quantities, but their pies and snacks are famous everywhere: poultry pasties with delicate herbs, roast-chili termite crackers, frog's liver paté, cricket croquettes, crispy crayfish just like Mama used to make, and so on. It is a family business and four generations of Roundpaws work in the offices and kitchens, or the market and distribution center, under the direction of the matriarch and founder of the establishment, Regina Roundpaw.

Roundpaw, Inc. also engages in social works and a small part of production is reserved for the elder cats of the city who can no longer fend for themselves (and who receive no help from Walter. Fortunately they don’t eat much, otherwise Walter might exile the old cats too!) Regina and her grand- daughter Sadie use this as an opportunity to make their way around the city three or four times a week to meet people.

Regina and Sadie

Roundpaw The grandmother and her granddaughter also organize, with the help of Grandma Scramble (see page 207), a postal network that enables exiled Kittens to keep in touch with their families. Grandma Scramble has a number of fake wooden eggs—just the right size and color—which can be hidden in the middle of the egg baskets that she takes into Cat Tree City every week. The wooden eggs are hollow and are easily unscrewed to place the letters inside. Grandma Scramble’s one and only client is, of course, Roundpaw, Inc., and they buy all her produce. And the letters Regina and Sadie just need to distribute them to the families as they go on their charity tour: Two birds with one stone!

Regina—Strong 1 / Smart 4 / Cute 3 // Heart points 5 // Cook; Heal Wounds & Diseases; Keep Calm & Carry On // Slice & Dice (1) // Small first aid kit; portable inkstand. Sadie—Strong 3 / Smart 2 / Cute 3 // Heart points 5 // Cook; Hiss & Growl // Quick as a Flash (2); Clean & Tidy (1) // Large scarf; running shoes.

pages.name: p.95 - Saint Purina’s Orphanage
pages.html:
Saint Purina’s Orphanage

Not all abandoned or orphaned Kittens end up on the street. Some are lucky enough to be taken in at Saint Purina’s orphanage, an ancient, well-regarded establishment. Kittens receive a solid moral and intellectual education, as well as technical instruction, and many later find employment in the city’s workshops. Some of them disappear, and the Reverend Mother Barbiecute tells the other Kittens that they were adopted and went to live in the countryside on a nice, welcoming farm.

The truth is that Reverend Mother Barbiecute is a horrible person. She chooses the cutest Kittens (never the smartest) and sells them to a trafficker in Corktown—the despicable Loonie Rinswith-Gutrotter—who takes them away to sea, to distant, sunbaked shores. Since it is impossible to prove that the trafficking goes on—it is quite normal that you don’t hear anything from an adopted orphan—no one has ever noticed.

Reverend Mother Barbiecute This old cat is very greedy and has little affection for the Kittens she sells to Loonie, but she does have a good reputation in the neighborhood. This is because she takes good care of the other residents of her institution: She feeds them, educates them, does not beat them, or make them live in fear. She is fairly kind to everyone and it's not as if she wishes harm to come to the Kittens she sells. But she's greedy. She has amassed a massive fortune. So much so that she has difficulty finding a place to keep it—there is no more storage space under her wooden bedroom floor.

Strong 4 / Smart 3 / Cute 3 // Heart points 7 // Find Information; Heal Wounds & Diseases; Sweet-talk // Cat Haven (2); Fearless (1) // An embroidery bag; colorful handkerchiefs; cream for aches and pains.

pages.name: p.96 - The Soot District
pages.html:
The Soot District

The Soot District was once lively and buzzing, but is now little more than a ghetto for those who have nothing. The faces are sad and hardened, their fur is dull, the curtains drawn. You are more likely to hear crying than laughing here. Formerly, it was known as “The Canvas”, and it was the craftwork and artistic heart of the city. Some of that is still the case, but factories have replaced the workshops, and their large chimneys belch out black smoke that stains the houses. King Walter insisted upon a great industrialization of the city and the kingdom: production, production, and then more production. Machines, weapons, equipment,

pages.name: p.97 - The Smoking Cat
pages.html:
vehicles, shiny buttons for uniforms, and buckles for harnesses… and everyone is working in hellish conditions. The presence of the Royal Guard, who watch everything and everyone, hunt down spies, and have begun a curfew, has not improved the daily lives of workers and their families.

The Smoking Cat

Tavern Located in the Soot District, one of the poorest neighborhoods of the capital of the Kingdom of Cats, this tavern is an unusual plact that attracts visitors from afar, including a large number of Cat Tree City nobles. The Smoking Cat is a modest tavern that serves all kinds of roasted and grilled vegetables and fruit—the food is good, but it may be the setting and the owner that really attract people.

Ignatius, the boss, does not differentiate between his clients, noble or needy, and he treats all the same way. Everyone eats until they are full, regardless of their budget. Inside, the atmosphere is warm: People willingly mix by sitting on long benches around three large tables. The large kitchen works flat out for the whole service, so smells of frying and roasting food float through the air and stir the taste buds. A little further away, there’s a table reserved for children and young people. It is always lively, and surrounded by shelves full of wooden toys and a few storybooks.

When the weather is nice, the tables are dragged out into the garden and the Kittens play on swings, rope, and the jungle gym.

1d6 Smoking Cat Dish of the day

1 Grilled corn-on-the-cob and mushroom skewer with garlic and parsley

2 Barbecued sweet potato fries with sliced tomato and zucchini
