Despite many arguments, the fox never managed to convince his new friend that he was not a sheep, but actually a goat. Horn believed there was no way his sheep mother could have lied to him and hidden his origin! That was ridiculous. Meanwhile, Casper and Horn traveled extensively through the country. Wandering here and there, working, hiding, and generally getting by.

And then came the first part of the tragedy: While wandering randomly on an icy winter night, the fox and the goat sought refuge in a remote farm. It was inhabited by a goat and her family. She recognized Horn as the child she had abandoned in her miserable youth, who had been taken in by Mrs. Bloomunday.

And so, one morning in the middle of winter, in an isolated farmhouse in the kingdom of Walter where they had come to ask for shelter, Horn met his real mother. But the goat now had another life altogether. She had become someone else. She had a husband, children, a family… She recognized her son, who had the same beautiful, shiny coat as her. But she turned her back and asked him to leave. Horn couldn't stay here. He was not part of her life!

pages.name: p.164
pages.html:
Horn fled, tears in his eyes, tense and angry. Casper set out after him, but at night, on icy ground and moving too fast—he fell to his death at the bottom of a steep slope.

All at once, Horn had lost his sheep family, his goat family, and his best friend. He wandered around the wasteland for weeks, deep in one of the big-bare-butts’ trash heaps, bashing his goat horns against the walls over and over again.

When he got back onto the road, he was different—tougher, harder, with his anger evolved into a pure rage that burned in his heart. From that point on, he took the name Dark. Cunning and powerful, he became the most feared and cruel mercenary on the other side of the world. He quickly rose to be a renowned mercenary leader, at the head of formidable forces.

Later he traveled with his army. But he tired of service to employers and wanted to rule, give his own orders, and tell others what to do. And after a long absence, he made his way back to the gates of the Kingdom of Cats and settled in the Misty

Valley, with the firm intention of conquering and bullying others!

pages.name: p.165 - The Dam
pages.html:
The Dam

The Black Horns’ camp is right at the top of the dam, on the shores of the water retention zone near the ruined hydroelectric plant that once operated here. The setting is majestic. The position gives Dark a big advantage. He may decide to flood the valley, along with any army that may come for him. This prospect worries the beaver community that lives below. Gnawbert, the leader of the beavers, doesn’t know what to do.

Encounters Dark/Horn Dark is a goat with fur as black as soot. He has a beautiful pair of curved horns, one of which was broken in a horrific fight. He has long, shiny hair, and a carefully-tended goatee. Dark is angry and sad. He is annoyed at the whole world and often wanders off alone to stew with rage in his stronghold at the top of the dam.

Strong 5 / Smart 4 / Cute 3 // Heart points 9 // Find Information; Find Your Way; Hiss & Growl; Keep Calm & Carry On; Shake Your Booty; Scratch // Balancing Cat (2); Bug Swarm (2); Fearless (1); Long Night (3); Quick as a Flash (2) // A large black sword that seems to talk to him; high- quality chain mail.

pages.name: p.166
pages.html:
Black Horn mercenaries These mercenaries are a small army under Dark's command. They will do truly horrible things for gold or to satisfy the anger of their revered leader. Black Horns are not all goats, or even horned animals, but they all proudly wear their company’s coat of arms on their armor.

Strong 4 / Smart 2 / Cute 2 // Heart points 6 // Hiss & Growl; Scratch; Shake Your Booty // Various weapons; armor; tabard with the symbol of the black horns on it.

The Bloomundays Horn adoptive parents are a couple of unremarkable sheep. Mr. Bloomunday is very proud of the fact: He doesn’t like to cause trouble and would prefer to forget the whole affair. Mrs. Bloomunday has always blamed herself for letting Horn leave. She loves him as one of her own and would be willing to help him if she could. They heard no news of him and did not realize he had turned into Dark, the ruthless warlord. It’s up to the Storyteller to place the small Bloomunday house where she wants geographically, according to the needs of the plot. It could be somewhere in the middle of some meadows—nice and simple.

Strong 2 / Smart 2 / Cute 2 // Heart points 4 // Herbology; Hunter-Gatherer // Summon Tools (2); Treating Beasts (1) // Some big hats.

Mrs. Bighorn Horn’s biological mother married a wealthy farmer and now lives on a plush farm in the Kingdom of Cats. She has drawn a line under her old, sad, frightened existence—a life that her husband and new family know nothing about.

Strong 2 / Smart 2 / Cute 4 // Heart points 4 // Care of Beasts; Cook // A farmer's apron.

Adventure trails What if a few Kittens came to remind

Dark that he is, in fact, Horn? It could just take a little something, some compassion and understanding, acceptance of yourself and others, for everything to change. Until now, Dark's story has been a tragedy. Perhaps some brave Kittens can come and add some hope and laughter?

To start with…

The Kittens are staying in The Crossroads

Motel, an inn (formerly a railway station in the olden days). Some of the Black Horn mercenaries are there, talking about Dark over a drink or two. Everyone is frightened. Maybe the family of one of the Kittens was friends with the Bloomundays; maybe he even met Horn before.

pages.name: p.167
pages.html:
The Kittens defend a community against

Dark's troops (maybe even an invasion of Corktown?). They make a prisoner reveal who his master is. Perhaps one of the Kittens had previously encountered the nice Horn and Casper, when they performed at Walter's court? How could it be that the singing kid goat who was so nice became such a brutal character? The Kittens cross the Misty Valley.

They see the big military camp and all the guards. They meet the beavers (see page 165), who tell them about Dark.

And maybe…

The Kittens end up travelling to the

Misty Valley to find out for themselves. Once there, they could spy, meet the beavers, or ask to speak to Dark directly. This way they can learn more and eventually have a first meeting with Dark. The outcome of their meeting will depend on what’s been happening in the adventure.

The “easiest” solution to calm Dark down and put a stop to the madness is to find Mrs. Bloomunday and Mrs. Bighorn and talk to them. Maybe convince them to meet so that they could then go and see Horn. Only meeting and talking to both his birth and adopted mothers will dissipate the rage he feels against the world and himself. A slightly more fantastic turn of events could involve an intervention from the ghost of Casper the fox. Maybe this could be through Selene (see page 131). Casper could be a fun guide or some sort of playful support if the players and their Kittens are finding it hard to make a plan. The Kittens’ adventures can involve lots of incidents: an attack by the Black Horn mercenaries; trouble at the dam; a counterattack against the forces of Dark; helping captured Kittens escape; and so on.

pages.name: p.168 - The big-bare-butt in the
pages.html:
The big-bare-butt in the

valley of statues

All the animals know that humans once ruled the world. They were super-smart and super-powerful and all the animals—and beasts— worshipped and feared them. They were inventors and artists, scientists and engineers, philosophers and dreamers. Whenever it was needed, they had the power to change the world around them, to make it safer and more beautiful. They would also fight, quarrel, waste things, and be selfish, and they did not always pay attention to the people around them, or to nature, or the world. And since they could do anything, why would they about such things?

One day, everything collapsed. The humans disappeared. They left behind a wasteland full of useless gifts, uninhabitable cities, and terrifying and fascinating memories. But above all, animals received the

pages.name: p.169 - The humans of yesteryear
pages.html:
gift of speech. Why? How? No animal knows the answer to these questions. And neither do the last humans.

Now, animals talk about the big-bare-butts in taverns, markets, and palaces. Some naked giants are occasionally seen wandering aimlessly, mumbling to themselves. But you always hear it from someone who heard it from someone else… in fact, no animal can boast of actually seeing a big-bare-butt in real life.

The humans of yesteryear

The big-bare-butts lost their memory and with it a large part of their intelligence. They babble and make old gestures at nothing in particular, for no good reason. One plays a tune on a violin that does not exist, another repairs an invisible car, yet another marches up and down, every now and then stopping to salute. They are like big children or really ancient old people. They don’t even communicate. They drink rainwater and feed on pollen and fond memories. In actual fact they are harmless— little more than decoration, wandering evidence of a time long forgotten.

There is, however, a place where the big-bare-butts gather. A legendary city in the mountains, tucked away in a secret valley: Cavetopia. The animals claim that this utopian city was built by humans before their fall and that they have kept their intelligence and science there, and that they have been welcoming back their lost, naked cousins.

pages.name: p.170
pages.html:
Greenshore A big-bare-butt sought refuge in a secluded valley alongside a raging river. Several wandering merchants and other explorers in search of new discoveries have glimpsed him in the distance. Shaggy and solitary, he lives in a ruined old mansion in the middle of a garden that's lined with statues. He keeps to himself and does not leave his safe haven, but the rumors increase and spread: He prowls around at night, he eats animals, he has terrible powers, and so on.

These sightings have happened not far from a village of simple fishermen, on the banks of the river at the entrance to the valley. Greenshore is rustic, pleasant to live in, and is a stopover for ships heading towards Corktown and the sea... Well, it used to be a pleasant place. Since Bruno the hamster, and wandering merchant, found out about the existence of the nearby big-bare-butt, everyone has been afraid.

Some of the inhabitants, mostly wading fisherfolk, decided to feed the big-bare-butt in the hope that if he was full he would stay in his valley. They regularly come to drop off fish offerings at the foot of the statues. The big-bare-butt likes to watch the ritual from afar, and he is more than happy to fill his tummy.

The children of the village have taken up the habit of visiting the valley in order to scare themselves. The young hedgehog Spikey is particularly bold. He goes on increasingly daring expeditions to the ruins with his small gang. He made a bet with his friends that he could steal a strand of hair from the big-bare-butt.

Encounters The big-bare-butt The big-bare-butt of the valley of the statues is a stray. He traveled for a long time, fearful, before ending up here, seemingly attracted by the ruins of the manor and its park that is decorated with many white marble statues. These sculptures fascinated him. He seems to recognize the features. They remind him of something. Perhaps he was an artist himself? Maybe he lived there a long time ago? This big-bare-butt now looks after the garden. Gradually, his hard work has

pages.name: p.171
pages.html:
paid off and the valley looks beautiful. He lives on fresh water, roots, berries, and, in particular, apples from the huge orchard next door. He lives in the least damaged part of the mansion, in an old wing that's crumbling but still solid.

Strong 5 (or more) / Smart 1 / Cute 2 // Heart points 6 // Care of Beasts; Herbology.

Mayor Eve Eve is the lively fox who leads the community of Greenshore. Her one desire is to protect the citizens, so she encourages all projects that help repel the threat of the big-bare-butt and send him as far away as possible.

Strong 2 / Smart 5 / Cute 3 // Heart points 7 // Herbology; Knowledge of Laws & Legends; Knowledge of People & Places // Heart Charm (1); Words of Wisdom (2) // Mayor's chain around her neck.

Rebecca, the superstitious fisher Rebecca has declared herself the leader of the village fisherfolk. She is an ambitious grey heron who wants to take the place of Eve as mayor. Highly superstitious, she is convinced that the big-bare-butt must be worshipped, and that doing so will help her to achieve her goals.

Strong 3 / Smart 3 / Cute 2 // Heart points 6 // Hunter-Gatherer, Knowledge of Laws & Legends, Knowledge of People & Places, // Various talismans and meowgic protection charms.

Magnificus the meowge Magnificus the meowge roams the world in search of artifacts. He is a specialist in the olden days and their mysteries. He has a rather condescending air of superiority. Now that he’s heard about the big-bare-butt, he intends to capture it so he can study it.

Strong 3 / Smart 4 / Cute 3 // Heart points 7 // Hiss & Growl; Knowledge of Laws & Legends; Seduce & Charm // All spells // A big hat; bag; whip; pocket watch.

pages.name: p.172 - Adventure trails To start with…
pages.html:
Adventure trails To start with…

Kittens in exile who are on their way to Corktown pass through Greenshore. They will hear talk of the big-bare-butt at the Golden Barge inn. The Kittens have been employed by Baron

Embergrunt in Corktown (see page 143). They must travel to Greenshore to learn more about the big-bare-butt rumors. The Baron wants the brave heroes to approach the giant to see how dangerous it is. Lost on a foggy night in the valley by the river, the Kittens seek refuge in the ruins of the mansion. One of the statues starts to move! How will their meeting with this strange man turn out? And maybe…

Spikey has disappeared (see page 170)! His friends are worried. The hedgehog went out alone into the valley to show how brave he was. In fact, the youngster was injured when he fell into a well in the mansion’s grounds. He was rescued by the big-bare-butt. But given the tense atmosphere of fear in the village, a kidnapping was suspected. What will the Kittens do?

Everything is going wrong in Greenshore! Some of the villagers (mainly fisherfolk) led by Rebecca, the grey heron, are opposed to Mayor Eve, the fox. They say that the big-bare-butt must be fed regularly in order to avoid his wrath. The mayor and her camp think this idea is dangerous. The ambitious Rebecca plans to take advantage of the opportunity to overthrow her rival and take power. After all, Greenshore exists because of the river, the domain of the bird fisherfolk. Magnificus the meowge is on an expe- dition to Crimsonfief (see page 247). After hearing about the big-bare-butt, he decides to stop off at Greenshore. He lands with his band of tough guys to capture and study it. His henchmen create a ruckus in Greenshore, which leads to more friction with the fisherfolk. In addition, Magnificus’ expedition looks like an ill-fated trip. Both Eve and

Rebecca call on the Kittens to help restore calm and protect the giant out of fear that his capture will cause the village to be cursed.

pages.name: p.173
pages.html:
And then…

The big-bare-butt is actually a nice giant.

After the first encounter, he may offer the Kittens a nearly intact object from the olden days (a dynamo flashlight, a powerful magnet, a polaroid camera, and so on). This is a relic that’s of no value to him, but which will no doubt attract much envy: Dark’s attention, Bojosar’s greed, Suzanne’s visions, and maybe even Walter will hear about it? The big-bare-butt keeps for himself what he considers to be his greatest treasure: a crude drawing of a city where several big-bare-butts are dancing together. A rough map is drawn on the back of the sheet of scuffed paper. Some geographical landmarks are identifiable (the sea, mountains to the north, the river, the dam at Misty Valley, and so on). Could it be a clue that leads to the legendary Cavetopia? The Iron Loins (see page 148)

have captured the big-bare-butt. They transport him in a vast iron carriage. Baron Embergrunt intends to rid the region of this terrible threat. Why not exile him to the Isle of Evimettal? Dualeaper, the owner of Bigwheel (see page 155), has heard about the operation. He is ready for some tough negotiation with Corktown so he can make the big-bare-butt one of his fairground attractions. Naturally, the Kittens will have a part to play in all this. Does the gentle creature really deserve to live life in a cage? Will the animals reverse roles by creating a new type of zoo, or will they behave better?

pages.name: p.175 - Doctor Mojo’s Isle of
pages.html:
Doctor Mojo’s Isle of

Evimettal

The Isle of Evimettal, just off Corktown’s coast, is kept hidden by mist and sea spray. This steel and cast-iron building is suspended above the water, supported by a number of vast rusty pillars. Sinister-looking cubic buildings are constructed all over its raised platform. In high winds, the structure moves and makes long, deafening, squeaking noises. It is salt-eaten and rusty.

This old oil rig has become the lair of a half-crazed scientist, Doctor Mojo. With the help of Lemi, his parrot assistant and servant, the doctor performs experiments on beasts that are brought to him by unscrupulous pirates. His goal is to make them talk! He wants to make them into animals that are capable of thinking and speaking, reproducing the miracle that occurred when the big-bare-butts disappeared.

For this, the “scientist” uses somewhat strange methods, combining the drinking of seaweed potions at fixed times with the learning of words and gestures. The Isle of Evimettal is a zoo, a laboratory, and a school all at the same time, driven by the joint insanity of Mojo and Lemi. However, the atmosphere is more bizarre and ridiculous than worrying. For example, Lemi gives poetry lessons to chickens while Doctor Mojo feeds blue soup to reluctant pigs. You may also come across Doctor Mojo trying to show clumsy goats how to waltz, while Lemi throws strange red pills made with extracts of coral at them.

The island constantly vibrates, pitches, and rolls. It is a dangerous maze of wind- and sea-battered rusty beams and pylons. Crabs and oysters have moved in, as well as countless noisy, nosy sea birds—everything is slippery, slimy, and unstable. And there is still plenty of machinery for drilling and pumping scattered around. An old crane is decomposing in a corner; loose barrels float around in the swell. Inside, the rig is full of airlocks, corridors, and stairs. Useful rooms are few and cramped: dormitory, crew’s mess, infirmary, galley, meeting room, bridge, engine room, control room, etc.

pages.name: p.176 - Lemi, the overzealous assistant
pages.html:
Encounters Doctor Mojo Doctor Mojo is an octopus in a colored diving suit who speaks with the accent of someone from high society (although he does not have much high society to mix with). He takes advantage of his island’s sinister reputation, and the mysterious stories and rumors, to frighten away the curious and to earn the respect of the pirates who trade with him. It doesn’t hurt that he can pay them in rubies, thanks to some treasure he happened to find in a nearby shipwreck. Mojo is convinced that it is his destiny to discover the secret of speech—a project that may be unattainable, but he thinks is ultimately commendable: He wants to make every beast the equal of an animal! Mojo purchased the Isle of Evimettal and, during one of his stays in Corktown, he recruited Lemi, who became his assistant. He goes into town once a month to make deals with pirate crews to provide him with beasts, food, and scientific equipment and machinery. These days, the project is well-established and the experiments are well under way.

Strong 2 / Smart 5 / Cute 1 // Heart points 7 // Knowledge of People & Places; Read, Write, Count; Tinker with Bits & Bobs // Animate Object (3); Slice & Dice (1); Summon Tools (2) // A diving suit.

Lemi, the overzealous assistant

Lemi is a sea parrot—a puffin—who helps Mojo out with his crazy projects. Lemi is secretly in love with Mojo but does not dare to open up about his feelings for him. He is fascinated by the brilliant mind of the octopus, his ambition—and his extremely good manners. Mojo does not suspect a thing, and sees Lemi only as a faithful assistant who is there to do the dirty work.

Strong 2 / Smart 4 / Cute 2 // Heart points 6 // Care of Beasts; Cook; Herbology // Leather Apron (1); Quick Fix (2); Treating Beasts (1) // Kittysnacks and sugar cubes in his pocket.

pages.name: p.177 - Adventure trails To start with…
pages.html:
Captain Blueclaw Captain Blueclaw is a pirate crab who lives around the waters off Corktown. His name comes from the many tattoos that cover his claws. One for each adventure at sea, he claims. He is dirty, badly behaved, and smelly. He smells so bad that a colony of mussels live on his back and he doesn’t even notice. Aboard his ship, The Arch, he is surrounded by his band of tough guys who terrorize the fishermen and inhabitants near the coast.

Strong 5 / Smart 3 / Cute 2 // Heart points 8 // Shake Your Booty; Hiss & Growl; Read Sky & Stars // Breathe Under Water (1); Long View (2); Feel the Path (3) // Sword; telescope.

Adventure trails To start with…

Caught in a storm while aboard ship, the Kittens are washed up on the Isle of Evimettal! The Kittens are staying in a farmhouse by the sea. The Nysoof family of donkeys is very friendly. As the night falls, a black cloud appears on the horizon. For their hosts, it is the sign for all hands on deck! For some time now, farms have been attacked and all their beasts stolen by pirates.

pages.name: p.178
pages.html:
At Corktown, Kittens hear strange rumors about an octopus in a colorful suit who hangs around in the dodgiest taverns. It is said that the animal is in cahoots with the worst ruffians of the seas. Maybe the Kittens would like to know more? The Kittens eventually meet Captain

Pokkay, the crab boss of The Scoffer. He tells them about his recent discovery of a mysterious iron island (see Corktown, page 152), and recruits them for an expedition in search of some hidden treasure. The Kittens are captured by nasty pirate crabs. Captain Blueclaw is in cahoots with Doctor Mojo. On board The Arch, a cargo of beasts is waiting to be delivered. A few more little Kittens will be a welcome addition to the cargo!

And then…

The Kittens can get involved with the story of the strange doctor and his assistant. After all, their project is in some ways commendable and the beasts are not harmed—the creatures are actually a fun group who enjoy spending their time playing around with eccentric scientists. There's plenty to laugh at! But the problem of the pirates remains. The Kittens may want to persuade the doctor to continue his experiments in a quieter environment—for example, within the confines of Bigwheel. The Kittens may decide to free the beasts instead, and put an end to the madness. They will have to come up with a plan, because the doctor won't let that happen, and nor will Lemi. And the two scientists could use pirate muscle to rid themselves of the Kittens.

pages.name: p.180 - The White Paradise
pages.html:
The White Paradise

of Lost Children

The White Paradise is a place out of space and time where Kittens can go when they are feeling low, lost, tired, injured, exhausted, or sad. The Storyteller can introduce this place the first time the players seem discouraged; when their Kittens have suffered badly during an adventure but still have things to do; when they are low on Heart or Furr-endship points; if they have run out of kittysnacks; or if they don’t seem to know how to solve a problem they are confronted with. Later, the players themselves will be able to reach the White Paradise whenever they choose.

When the Kittens seem to hit rock bottom, they can be transported on Sola’s back. She is a giant manta ray with a luminous mandala on her belly. This silent creature glides gently through the air, appearing only to animals that have lost hope.

When they arrive in this pristine, white environment, animals do not age, all fear disappears, and all their wishes come to life if they draw them. A kitten can sketch a swing, and it will take shape and start to move. Drawing the shapes of a sumptuous banquet will cause it to materialize in the form of succulent, fragrant dishes.

It is easy to lose yourself and forget you are here—there is no pain, no hunger, and no sadness, just a quiet, peaceful feeling of happiness. Exhausted kittens can quickly top up their Heart and Furr-endship points, heal their wounds, and maybe even find an object they thought they’d lost.

It may prove difficult to find the courage to leave, to go back out to the world and its problems! Many animals live there, slowly forgetting their lives, friends, family, hopes, and dreams.

And although the place is not a trap or an illusion, it can prove to be a prison for Kittens who realize their tasks are not over.

To get out, Kittens have to shake themselves up, and get motivated. Sola does not mind if they decide to leave—the Storyteller can subtly guide the players to, help them find answers and solutions.

pages.name: p.181 - Sola, the giant manta ray
pages.html:
But as you would imagine, relaxing in the White Paradise has a cost: time does not stop. When the Kittens are ready to go, Sola can drop them off wherever they want, but things will have changed. The Storyteller should make slight changes to the world— just enough for the Kittens to be forced to deal with new circumstances. Perhaps Walter came up with some new laws that were even more wicked than the previous ones; maybe Dark has laid siege to Corktown; or the big-bare-butt of Greenshore has been captured by Brutus.

Sola, the giant manta ray

Sola does not speak and does not seem to have consciousness. She simply feels pain and sadness and feeds upon it, taking it away from the Kittens. It is impossible to know if it is empathy or if it is simply instinct. In any case, she silently watches over her white, peaceful hidden world, without ever giving advice or counsel to the Kittens.

Jojo, the lost kitten Jojo is a Kitten who was exiled by Walter. One day, he fell seriously ill. He became too much of a burden for his companions, and he awoke one morning with a fever, to find that they had all left without him. Shivering, exhausted, and drained of energy, he was picked up by Sola. He saw many Kittens and other animals pass through since but he always refused to leave the refuge of the White Paradise. He’s been there for so long that he doesn’t even know if anyone is still waiting for him outside…

Strong 1 / Smart 2 / Cute 3 // Heart points 3 // Draw & Paint; Seduce & Charm // Sound & Vision (1) // White pyjamas; colored pencils; paper.

pages.name: p.183 - The Storyteller’s Book
pages.html:
The Storyteller’s Book

Congratulations and good luck if you have chosen to become the Storyteller for a game of Dungeons and Kittens! Here are some tips, reflections, and advice that should be of much help to you.

pages.name: p.184 - Do not worry (again!)
pages.html:
Do not worry (again!)

Becoming the Storyteller for a game of Dungeons and Kittens is a big responsibility, a lot of work, and a fair bit of pressure. Or is it?

Remember: Dungeons and Kittens is a game. First, it is meant to be fun.

For this reason, you have nothing to prove to anyone: Your players are there to have fun, but it is also their shared responsibility that everything goes well and everyone has a good time—they are not there to simply sit at the table and have everything handed to them. And if that does happen, you can (and should) remind them about why you are all gathered together! The weight of the world does not rest solely on your shoulders.

Finally, the amount of work needed is relative. You can arrive at the gaming table with ten minutes—or ten days—of preparation and still find that you haven’t done enough. The most important thing, in truth, is that you more or less remember the game mechanics, (they are also summarized on the character sheets), the names of the Kittens around the table, and the advice from these pages. The rest will come on its own, very naturally, as long as you don't freeze or panic.

Dungeons and Kittens is a game that evolves as you play it. It is the dialogue with the players, the spur-of-the-moment inventions, and the opportunities for narrative development that creates the story. The time you spend on preparation before playing is only a bit of support so you feel comfortable— and is by no means absolutely essential. We will come back later to talk about how you can easily prepare.

In short, what you have to remember is that you are no more or less important than any of the other players. It’s not all about you: neither the content of the game, the good atmosphere, nor the pace. You are a facilitator, and all of the players around the table—yourself included—are part of what makes a successful game.

pages.name: p.185 - The heart of the matter
pages.html:
The heart of the matter

What is the dynamic of a Dungeons and Kittens game and what is the Storyteller’s role at the table?

In Dungeons and Kittens, players all create the elements of a story together, collaborating to combine ideas and actions. There’s literature in there—mathematics too—and all sorts of things that come from each player individually, as well as the book you hold in your paws, the numbers on the character sheets, and the notes you've taken. It is a whole bunch of imaginary objects placed in the middle of an imaginary imaginary canvas and put together gradually to create a timeline that is the story.

Everything that existed before the game is played is potential; what exists when it is played is an organized fiction with a notion of time passing, of before and after, of causes and consequences. It is a fiction that we can follow, and tell as a story with a beginning and an end, and with as many details that we want to add.

And what allows the transformation of the bits of the game into a story is the constant dialog that takes place between all the players—including the Storyteller.

This dialog begins with the introduction of the Kittens by the players. These are the first elements of the fiction: Who are the protagonists of the story, the heroes of the adventure? Then, the Storyteller describes their surroundings and the universe: Where are the Kittens? Why are they here? What happens to get them moving?

The dialog continues between the players and the Storyteller. Players ask questions about what their Kittens can see, what they know, and what makes them act, in order to get more information or to interact with things—such as the group, items, or extras. The Storyteller answers these questions and reveals the consequences of actions, saying how the game world evolves around the Kittens.

And then we repeat that dialog across the story.

This is usually where the Storyteller starts to worry. Most of the time, it is easy to respond to the players; other times, it is more complicated and, without some method, the Storyteller will not always know how to cope when faced with wild ideas, unexpected events, and a multitude of possibilities.

pages.name: p.186 - The decision tree
pages.html:
The decision tree

This is the first tool you will need. It is something very simple, but it will help you easily determine the consequences of a kitten’s actions.

When a Kitten acts, it’s your job to tell the consequences. However, it is not simply to give the answer “it succeeded” or “it failed,” instead you are meant to explain how the game universe has changed, or how the extras adjusted.

The first reference that will help you make a decision about the consequences of an action is what you know about the game universe and its consistency. In Dungeons and Kittens, if an animal throws a stone in the air, it falls back down; if he puts his legs into water, they get wet; if he drinks hot tea too quickly, he burns his tongue. It is impossible for him to lift a two-ton rock on his own without machinery. If he is rude to a Yardog, he is unlikely to get any help. All you have to do is be logical and look at how the real world behaves around you.

Most simple tasks are automatically successful and require only a little time and effort. Their consequences are easy to measure. A Kitten will have no difficulty sweeping up in a cabin in the woods. The obvious consequence is that the cabin is clean and it will be nicer to spend the night there.

This means that the vast majority of the actions the Kittens and extras make can be resolved quickly and clearly, without much need for thought. Saying please and thank you go a long way for animals who may decide to help the Kittens; using a suitable tool can transform an impossible action into an automatically successful action (for example, using the right-sized wrench to loosen a nut).

The second reference when deciding the consequences of an action is the Kitten himself. He knows things, he has some education, he’s got some useful objects. His character sheet contains lots of information to help you decide: his abilities, skills, and Cattributes. Usually, these elements will allow you to adjust what your understanding of the game universe is already telling you.

Similarly, the Storyteller may decide, using logic and being consistent, that an action is successful, but that a skill, an object, or a suitable ability will improve the result—and therefore the consequences.

pages.name: p.187
pages.html:
A Kitten wants to lift a sheet metal plate to free an injured comrade. It is not so heavy as to make the action impossible, but a particularly Strong Kitten will not need a lever. An especially Cute Kitten will still get the same information as another Kitten by talking to people in the street, but they may get it faster. The Knowledge of People & Places skill will be enough to help a Kitten who has it remember some useful information.

Finally, the third reference for determining the consequences of an action is the game mechanics and the dice. At this point, if you have not already made a logical decision based on the universe or the character sheet, you may ask your players to roll the dice based on the ability and skills you think are relevant.

You will soon realize that this method is very natural and helps you make quick decisions. At first, however, it’s OK to take your time to think carefully and do things in order. You will realize that you will not need to ask for die rolls all the time; that the players’ words and their explanations are often enough to determine the most likely consequences of an action; that it is easier to say “yes” than “no”; and that you can let the game flow in a very flexible manner.

pages.name: p.188 - The golden rule
pages.html:
The golden rule

A little secret: Sometimes, dice are also a good way to make minor yes-or-no decisions, because whatever that decision is, it’s just a way to advance the story by taking one direction instead of another.

Is the Old Bridge still guarded by a dog when night fell hours ago? Does the owner of the scarf shop agree to be paid with small items instead of gold coins? Does the Lost Tower library have a copy of the book that the Kittens are looking for, to check some information? Is there a large tree that is easy to climb nearby? Does that stream lead to the river?

A game of Dungeons and Kittens is full of simple, circumstantial questions like these, and players will ask them all the time. Sometimes there are a lot of decisions for the Storyteller to make, even though the answer is not very important: If it’s yes, the story moves in one direction; if it’s no, the Kittens are forced to do something else.

The easiest, most practical, solution is to roll 1d6. On a score of 1 to 3 the answer is no; on a score of 4 to 6 the answer is yes. All you have to do is ask the right question.

If the bridge is still guarded, they will have to make a plan or a detour; if it is no longer guarded, the Kittens will move quickly and easily. If the owner of the shop demands gold, the Kittens will have to find a way to get it; otherwise, they can simply swap scarves—or maybe ask the Kittens to do something for them… and so on.

pages.name: p.189 - The question of failure
pages.html:
The question of failure

This idea that the story is always moving forwards, one way or another, is essential to fully understand the dynamics of the game, and how the Storyteller reveals the consequences of an action.

Whether an action succeeds or fails is just a way of telling how the story progresses, according to what was expected. Also, you must always be careful that a failure does not result in a dead end that prevents the story’s progression.

When a Kitten fails, it is a setback or a complication, never a punishment. For example, they may waste time or break some tools; they may have to start over from scratch; they may have to find a completely different solution to the problem, because they have hurt themselves or annoyed someone important.

Imagine a Kitten at the foot of a large wall. If they fail to climb it, they must either be able to walk around it (losing time in the process) or try and get through a door (which may be guarded). In short, there must be alternative solutions if the Kitten wants to reach the other side. Maybe they just need to buy a rope or borrow a ladder? Maybe the Kitten asks a comrade for a foot-up! Players can be inventive and crafty.

But if the Storyteller decides that there is no door, that they can’t go around, or that there is no way to get a ladder, what happens? The story ends at the foot of the wall.

That means that you can never say “no” if there isn’t another way to solve a problem or get past an obstacle that absolutely prevents the story from continuing. There should either be several solutions (from the simplest to the most complex) or if there is a single solution, it has to work.

pages.name: p.191 - The pleasure
pages.html:
The pleasure

of success

A good reason to try and say yes (or a no that doesn’t close anything off) is that players like to succeed. It’s not a matter of giving instant gratification but acknowledging the effort they put into the game. Players try things, make plans, and show interesting ways to find solutions and solve puzzles. And there is nothing more unpleasant than to fail when you have worked so hard.

On the other hand, most players are also aware of the times they did not make much effort, when they just made something up quickly, or had an obviously silly solution—failure is not really an issue when that's the case.

However, when a player spends hours trying to solve a situation or makes her way through a whole adventure, she knows that she may fail because she has not understood all the ins and outs, because she did not see some of the pitfalls, or because she maybe didn’t dig deep enough. But it can be unpleasant and frustrating to ultimately fail through the roll of a die or an arbitrary decision from the Storyteller, without the chance to influence the decision through discussion or a plea, or a chance to change the circumstances and reattempt the task.

An adventure can be as difficult or as complicated as the Storyteller wants it to be, as long as the players know they can achieve something if they give themselves the means, such as if they think, help each other, seek support from extras, and ask questions.

That is why, as much as possible, you should say yes more often than you say no to your players.

pages.name: p.192 - In between, a little
pages.html:
In between, a little

more, a little less

Saying yes does not mean accepting everything and anything. Remember: First there is the logic of the world, then the abilities of the kittens, and finally the rules and the dice.

So there are three types of “yes”. The simplest, in Dungeons and Kittens, is the basic “yes”. The Kitten wants to do something and eventually he manages it. And that’s that. The Kitten wants to jump over a ditch. It is not automatic, as he does not have the right skills. The player rolls the dice and if the throw is successful, the Kitten gets to the other side. Quick and easy.

There is also the exceptional “yes”, the “yes and.” Not only does the kitten succeed in what he wanted to do, but he is so successful that he gets additional benefits. Most of the time, this happens when the player gets high numbers in a dice roll, but nothing prevents them from also coming up with ideas that are so good and so creative that the Kitten gets an exceptional success without even rolling the dice. This can occur when the Storyteller and the other players are so impressed or wowed by an idea, or something makes them laugh so much, that they reward the player with a “yes and.”

Finally, there is the “yes but”, perhaps the most common and most-used yes in Dungeons and Kittens. It is a yes that looks a lot like a no—a “no, but.”

The “yes but/no but” is the most powerful tool available to the Storyteller! It allows a yes when the Storyteller should really say no, and it gives the player a chance to accept a no when a yes really isn't an option. This flexibility makes it very powerful.

Let's take an example: A Kitten is trapped in a corner of the Junkyard. The Yardogs have not spotted him yet, but he has no obvious way of escaping. The player tries a lot of things, but none of them quite work, so the Storyteller offers the player a “yes but/no but” situation. Yes, the Kitten manages to get out of his hiding place, but he was seen by the dogs, who give chase… Or no, the Kitten remains stuck all day long, until dusk, but the dogs did not notice he was there.

Many things can be handled like this, following the decision tree: Whenever you want to say yes, but something within the game world prevents you, you can say “yes but”! It’s not complicated, it keeps the players happy, and it forces them to find solutions.

The advantage of this approach is the Storyteller isn’t constantly saying no, and the players never feel it’s too easy.

pages.name: p.193 - Choice
pages.html:
Choice

So this is also where one of the most powerful elements of Dungeons and Kittens comes into play: Players are forced to make choices.

Basically, pushing players to make difficult choices is the goal for every Storyteller. The more choices there are, the more responsible the players will be for the story and the more failures or tragedies that the Kittens encounter will be dependent on their own decisions and not those of the

Storyteller. In this way, the Story teller is only a facilitator as the story advances, and she will not need to force its twists and turns.

With this goal in mind, a choice is a time when the story can advance in a different direction, not because the Kittens fail or succeed in an action according to the consequences the Storyteller decides, but because the players themselves have decided what they want to succeed at and what they want to fail at. It takes the decision out of the Storyteller’s hands, so it is the easiest and least stressful position to be in.

A choice can be limited and without much scope: take the path on the right that goes through the fields or the one on the left that heads into the hills. It can be a bit more serious: Who is trying to open the trapdoor, the strongest Kitten or the fastest Kitten? It can be critical: Does the Kitten save a merchant’s precious trunk and drop all his Purr-ecious items in the water, or does he let the results of a lifetime’s work on the road float off down the river?

The question is no longer whether the Kitten can manage to hold onto the trunk (an action that can simply succeed or fail), but whether the player is prepared to lose everything—although her character will make a friend for life—or does she care too much for the mementoes of his parents that the Kitten keeps in his bag.

pages.name: p.194 - Information
pages.html:
Information

and predictability

A player can only really make choices under two conditions: Either she has definite information about the consequences of her choices or she can predict, with near certainty, what those consequences will be.

Faced with two identical doors, a Kitten does not really make a choice when he has to open one of them. It’s just luck. Instead, if one of the doors is made of metal, reinforced, and padlocked, and the other, is made of light wood with a small, familiar sign on it, then the player is getting some information. Let’s say that the Kitten puts his ear against each door: The metal one is cold and there are loud noises and growls on the other side; the wooden one is warm and smells of herbs and spices. This is even more information. In this example, choice emerges when the doors are different and the player has access to this information.

The information can come from the Kittens themselves (thanks to circumstances of birth or skills), from the questions they ask and the research they conduct, or from the information provided by extras. Sometimes it will be the Storyteller who provides players with the context from which to make a choice; other times it comes from the sum of all the knowledge that the players have accumulated during an adventure.

In either case, the Storyteller must always be careful that the players have the relevant information when she offers them a choice.

The other condition for players to be able to make meaningful choices is when they can determine the most likely consequences themselves. This means that two almost identical choices made under almost identical conditions have almost identical consequences. If the result is random, there is no choice, only luck. If a Kitten throws a rock into the air, it must always come down—it cannot fly away randomly or disappear into a cloud, or continue to float up to the stars. Otherwise, the player can no longer determine in advance the normal outcome of an action or the choice of action.

As Storyteller, you must therefore be careful to be consistent and coherent, unless there is a good reason for a surprising change.

pages.name: p.195 - Questions and
pages.html:
Questions and

answers

In addition to the tools and tips above, each time a player asks a question, the Storyteller must give an answer.

The answer must bring something to the game. It can never be a refusal to answer or a neutral, irrelevant answer. And the Storyteller must not lie—only extras have the right and opportunity to lie. The Storyteller’s answer can be incomplete or ambiguous, or have more than one meaning. But never a barefaced lie.

If a Kitten is not able to get clear and direct information, you should at least give them an idea of how to get it. It could simply be a clue that indicates “you are hot” or “you are cold ”.

This sort of question and answer is especially important when Kittens are conducting an investigation or trying to understand what precisely is happening in a given situation. The players are piecing together a jigsaw puzzle but they don’t have the full picture (because all the pieces are upside down), or know how big it is, or how many pieces there are. And sometimes there are several puzzles mixed up together.

Additionally, the Storyteller cannot hide the answers completely. It’s not fair and it is frustrating, and the players will end up giving up or doing any old thing out of despair. You know what the puzzle looks like, and you know how the pieces fit together. If you want the Kittens to make their way through the adventure, you have to help the players: if they ask questions, give them answers. Always. All the time.

You can give them too many answers. You can mix up the order of the answers. You can answer in riddles. You can make the Kittens run around to look for the answers. But you always have to answer. You cannot hide anything and you cannot lie.

pages.name: p.196 - Word must get around
pages.html:
Word must get around

You now know how to start a good story around the table by paying attention to the words of the players and the actions of their Kittens. So now, how do you organize speaking so that it is nice and easy for everyone?

Not all players are equal when it comes to speaking. They can range from timid to talkative, silent to shouty, and from clammed up to chatty. It is your job to get all of them to express themselves. You have two tools for the job.

Your first tool is your finger. It is up to you to decide who speaks and who doesn’t, and you can do this by pointing at the current speaker. And you must unfailingly and absolutely enforce taking turns to speak. This way a shy player knows that she won’t have to fight to make her voice heard. The louder player knows that no matter what she will get her turn, even if others get to talk too.

Usually, it will be enough to simply go around the table: one player after the other. A quick nod or a glance will show if someone has finished. Then you can answer each player in turn or wait for everyone to talk before responding—just keep the themes together.

The second tool is the matching of location and action. When you let a player speak, it’s always in a specific context—and it’s the same context for all players and for the next pass around the table. “What are your Kittens doing for the next minute? And quarter-hour? Hour? Half-day? What are they doing there now? Arrived in the village? Before you cross the bridge?” And so on.

Each player replies within this precise temporal or spatial framework and states a coherent action or set of actions. When all the players have spoken, it is easy for you to resolve all the consequences of the actions; above all, each player was able to speak without conflict or issue!

pages.name: p.197 - Meeting and
pages.html:
Meeting and

discussing

Things are a little different when it is the Kittens who are talking and not the players. A free-form discussion is not disciplined, planned, or organized: All the Kittens around the table can express themselves freely, through the mouths of their players. It can quickly become chaotic, just like a discussion in real life.

As the Storyteller, you will need to pay attention to two things in particular:

Everything that is said by the players while in character is said by the Kittens! This includes silly jokes, cheek, insults, good and bad ideas, asides, and so on. At first, the players may protest: “But no, my Kitten didn’t say that, he’s not stupid!” Your answer should be: “I’m sure they aren’t. But next time, he will pay attention to what he’s saying!” Just this little habit should allow you to keep some order around the table, when half of the players are serious and the other half just come out with any old nonsense. Extras are normal people with normal reactions: If a bunch of Kittens are all shouting at them, there is a strong likelihood that the extra will leave, or shout back. If the Kittens are disrespectful or rude, extras will refuse to help them or even talk to them. If the Kittens behave normally and take turns to talk, just as we do every day, then extras will usually react calmly, pay attention, and display a genuine desire to help.

pages.name: p.198 - Setting and staging
pages.html:
Setting and staging

To finish with this section, which is all about the Storyteller’s tips and tricks, let’s talk a little about staging. The Storyteller sets the scene and gives the framework for the adventures using description. Players can give directions, such as: “Our Kittens go along the forest road to avoid the grassy knolls.” But it is the Storyteller who will describe that forest road or the grassy knolls.

A good description is not ne cessarily a vast, literary monologue, with complicated, poetic vocabulary (although that can sometimes be good). It is primarily a way to say to the players: this is the general atmosphere of the place, these are the possible dangers, here are the resources you could use to anticipate encounters and possible obstacles— what will you do with it all? What can you do with your Kittens in this environment?

The Storyteller is certainly not the only one who can describe things. She can ask the players questions to solicit answers: What does the path look like? Where is the bridge that crosses the river, and what state is it in? Who are the customers of the place where you want to stop for the night? And so on.

Using this method, when the Kittens enter a new landscape (forest, grassy plains, etcetera), the Storyteller can go around the table: You have heard rumors and stories about this place. What are they? Nobody yet knows if these rumors are true or false, but the players will be happy to give their opinions on the issue (and the Storyteller will get some interesting material to set the scene with).

pages.name: p.199 - Rhythm, continuity,
pages.html:
Rhythm, continuity,

and brackets

The story is framed in a place, but also time. It is the role of the storyteller to maintain a story’s pace.

Sometimes, the story must take

its time. In this style, you decide to play it all out, every small event, every break and stop, the big things and the small things—picking flowers as well as picking a fight with a rude band of wanderers. It is the combination of all these small moments that creates the poetry of the journey and the story, which makes it all interesting— not every story should be filled with constant monumental events. Sometimes playing slowly allows strategies, subtle investigations, and other things to develop. It is often in these circumstances that the longest and deepest discussions take place between Kittens and extras, and we learn more about the world, its stories, and its geography.

Sometimes, the story must move

on, and focus on the important events. The Storyteller can ignore trivial things and split the time into key, meaningful moments. The discussions are shorter, and usually in the third person: “My kitten goes up to the guard and gives him all the information about the group of villains they are chasing.” Players are encouraged to act decisively, on specific and directly relevant points. Sometimes, finally, the Storyteller has to learn to add brackets. In this style, you can skip a moment altogether and talk about it in rough terms only: “A few hours later, your Kittens arrive within sight of the village of Curlybumpington.” This is especially useful when you do not have a very long game session and you need to move on. And nothing prevents you from coming back to it later: “Oh, you remember the trip to Curlybumpington… We didn’t talk about it at the time, but something did happen on the way. " By mixing these various rhythms, even during the same gaming session, the Story teller can keep the attention of her players and maintain tension in the story. It is mostly a matter of how you feel, of trying things out, and of attempting to react to the needs of the story.

pages.name: p.200 - Have a good game, comrade!
pages.html:
And there you go. You know pretty much everything you need to know to get into the role of the Storyteller. First and foremost: trust yourself. Nobody will tell you that you are so bad that you shouldn’t be allowed to play! (And if they do, give us their address!) You are allowed to make mistakes, and whatever happens, you can only improve through practice. And what’s more, we all have our good days and our bad days, and your players won’t blame you. On the other hand, they will blame you for being irrational, giving unfair “no”s, and creating inconsistent storylines. But for that, you now have all the tools anyway!

Have a good game, comrade!

pages.name: p.203 - Adventures
pages.html:
Adventures

All the content of the previous chapters—the mechanics and rules, the description of the universe, the advice to the players and the Storyteller—end up taking shape around the gaming table through adventures!

If you only play the game occasionally to tell a story with your friends in a single evening, additional adventures can be a bit disjointed. But the advantage of this style is that all you need is a place to play and a simple adventure idea. If you play regularly, in the form of a campaign linking the adventures with the same players and the same Kittens, you will need a little more structure.

That’s what we are going to talk about in this chapter, with several examples of adventures, written in slightly different formats. There are also tips to lead them and write others on your own, inspired by all the information from the previous chapters.

pages.name: p.204 - Playing a campaign
pages.html:
Playing a campaign

A campaign is a series of adventures played over several sessions with the same players and the same Kittens. A campaign usually follows a common thread, with episodes that are more or less independent.

In Dungeons and Kittens, the common thread of one campaign will be the Kittens’ relationship with Walter: Will they try to bring some treasure back for him? Will they try to find others to help them overthrow his rule? Will they continue their lives without him, away from their families? A campaign’s common thread is used to connect the episodes to each other and give them a general direction, but Kittens can also simply visit the world, meet its inhabitants, and be interested in the stories that take place there.

The Storyteller is encouraged to use all the material from the previous pages to set up her own adventures—and also to invent her own stories. In the following pages, you will find four different adventures.

pages.name: p.205
pages.html:
The first adventure, The Disappearance of Grandma Scramble (pages 207-215) can serve as an introduction for the Kittens—it is their first night of exile far from Cat Tree City—and presents an opportunity to make new friends and face villains. It is a good way to start the Kittens out on the road. The second adventure, Three Little

Pigs (pages 217-230), is meant to be played afterwards, after a few smaller, in-between stories (which are up to the Storyteller to create), and when the Kittens eventually arrive in Corktown. This is a pivotal moment in the campaign. If all goes well, at the end of the adventure the Kittens will find a patron, a valuable ally, and a base of operations. These are especially helpful if they decide to confront Walter and drive the tyrant away! The third adventure, Selene’s Night mares (pages 233-244), is a kind of re-curring event that Kittens can bring about themselves or that they can discover by accident, depending on the circumstances. This is a dreamlike adventure—the Kittens will be transported inside the dreams of the spirit of the forest and must do all they can to restore calm. It will probably be necessary to return a few times to get rid of those bad thoughts forever—or maybe to bring back some treasure. The final adventure is named for the big dungeon where it takes place: Crimsonfief (pages 247-260). It is a strange, dangerous place where Kittens may find answers to their questions and learn more about the secrets of the world. Whenever they are not sure of what to do, or do not know how to get out of a situation, the Kittens can travel to Crimsonfief using, for example, the secret passages of the GIN (see page 121). By exploring there, they will very likely find all the answers they need… as long as they survive!

entries.name: Adventure: The Disappearance of Grandma Scramble

pages.name: p.207 - The Disappearance of Grandma Scramble
pages.html:
The Disappearance of Grandma Scramble

On a road to exile

Like many Kittens before them, the heroes of our adventures were banished by King Walter. With great sadness, they left their families, their friends, and their homes. Fortunately, there is a secret that is passed down from generation to generation among the Kittens: On the first night of exile, if you take the Old Forest Road, you can stop at Grandma Scramble’s for shelter and advice. The Kittens are deep in the forest, following the old road when they spot—at a small, almost invisible, crossroads—a funny wooden statue in the shape of a hen indicating a small path with its outstretched wing.

Grandma Scramble is an old cat who lives in a large hut in the forest surrounded by hundreds of chickens, who live in hen houses—each more ornate than the last—all built from countless salvaged materials. Once a week, Grandma Scramble sells her eggs at Cat Tree City bridge (see page 93). Tonight, the chickens are worried. Nobody came to fill their feeders and watering troughs. The hut itself is very plain and simple. But tonight the door is open and the fire has not been lit. It’s a complete mess inside. Everything is scattered all over the place. Grandma Scramble has disappeared.

pages.name: p.208 - Scene 1:
pages.html:
Scene 1:

Clues (which can be found with a successful test for Smart— or a few well-chosen questions): Some people came in and attacked Grandma Scramble. There are signs of a struggle: things knocked over or pushed away and tufts of pulled-out hair! There must have been a Claw Catfight! The tracks of a small group of four heavily laden individuals lead into the forest—and there are traces of more than just cats. One of them is very big; another is likely a female cat.

A chair is missing from the house and there are traces of rope fibers on the floor—

Grandma Scramble was tied up!

A pair of pliers was left under a piece of furniture by one of the attackers. It has a small mark engraved on the metal: a moon with what looks like a box hanging from it— the sign of Mr. Mooner, a famous smuggler who is wanted by Walter.

What really happened: Grandma Scramble fainted. She’s getting on a bit in years and she's not as healthy as she once was. Some brave chickens set off into the forest to seek help from an old friend of Grandma’s, Mr. Mooner. He came as quickly as he could and took the old cat with him, but because they were rushing and worried, his team made a mess.

pages.name: p.209 - Scene 2:
pages.html:
Scene 2:

Usually the Kittens will follow the footsteps, but the next encounter can just as well take place at the hut if they decide to stay there for the night.

As they advance into the forest, a voice calls out: “Well, little kittens, going for a late walk are we? Do you need any help? I can guide you if you like. I know this area like the back of my paw."

The offer comes from a suspicious-looking weasel with yellowed teeth, a blank right eye with a scar down the middle, a shabby cape over his shoulder, and some kind of machete attached to his belt. He is accompanied by a huge silent Catnut, as dumb as it is strong, its tawny fur covered with leaves and bits of thorn bush, and carrying a large black cauldron over its shoulder.

Their names are Crowtoe and Greaser. If Grandma Scramble had been there to welcome the Kittens, she would have told them to be wary of these two!

Crowtoe the weasel is a sometime agent of Walter who keeps an eye on the woods and warns him if Kittens come back to hang around near the kingdom. Crowtoe hates Mr. Mooner, who always gets the better of him.

pages.name: p.210
pages.html:
Except that tonight, Mr. Mooner has left a very obvious trail.

Ideally, a Fang Catfight should occur between the Kittens and the two sinister individuals who want to lead them to a place where their accomplices can capture them and send them off to the coast to work on the boats. The Kittens should win, of course, causing the villains to run away. They will go and warn Walter. He will send out the guard to hunt down Mr. Mooner. If they are defeated, the Kittens will have to flee into the forest to avoid capture—where they may stumble across Mr. Mooner’s camp. Crowtie // Dodgy weasel; spy for Walter // Strong 2 / Smart 3 / Cute 2 // Heart points 5 // See & Search; Sweet-talk // A big machete; wood-colored cape; homing pigeon equipment. Greaser // Catnut with low belly and high forehead // Strong 4 / Smart 1 / Cute 2 // Heart points 5 // Hiss & Growl; Hunter- Gatherer; Keep Calm & Carry On // Big cauldron used as a basket and a bag.

pages.name: p.211 - Scene 3:
pages.html:
Scene 3:

The Kittens follow the tracks, which lead them to the small valley where Mr. Mooner and his band of smugglers live, on the edge of a beautiful pond.

Normally, it is a very difficult place to reach. For years, Mr. Mooner has been planting all sorts of shrubs: hawthorn, holly, winged spindle, barberry, scorpion broom, bramble, mulberry hedges, sword grass, and so on. There is a path that leads through all these natural obstacles, but it is very difficult to find. Except tonight, when Mr. Mooner, who was in such a hurry to save Grandma Scramble, came through as quickly as he could and did not take the usual precautions.

Mr. Mooner’s hideout consists of several old transport containers next to each other, hidden by trees and bushes. A little light filters out of one of them and the Kittens can approach without anyone noticing.

Note: Mr. Mooner uses giant dragonflies from the pond to deliver his goods over the city walls at night.

Grandma Scramble is lying on a beautiful carved wooden bed, surrounded by several creatures:

Mr. Mooner// Elegant ginger cat with big amber eyes, dressed as a dandy, cane in hand // Strong 3 / Smart 5 / Cute 4 // Heart points 8 // Find Information; Hiss & Growl; Keep Calm & Carry On; Knowledge of People & Places; Seduce & Charm // An elegant cane; beautiful clothes; pliers (lost); arthropod-language magic stone. Mrs. Lewcy// Young tabby cat in leather armor, large sword on her back, a beautiful colored scarf around her neck // Strong 4 / Smart 3 / Cute 4 // Heart points 7 // Move Silently; Scratch; Shake Your Booty // Leather armor; large sword.

pages.name: p.213
pages.html:
Grenada // Slender, wiry fox with darting eyes, a former resident of Walter's dungeon that a young Mr. Mooner helped escape // Strong 4 / Smart 4 / Cute 3 // Heart points 8 // Find Your Way; See & Search; Shake Your Booty // A skeleton key; solid rope.

Wellington // A big, quiet badger with a chef's apron and a big knife at his side // Strong 5 / Smart 3 / Cute 3 // Heart points 8 // Cook; Hiss & Growl; Hunter-Gatherer; Read Sky & Stars // Chef's apron; large knife; salt & pepper pots; sachet of mushroom powder. Galiena // Giant forest spider, very old, very intelligent, can communicate telepathically // Strong 2 / Smart 5 / Cute 3 // Heart points 7 // Heal Wounds & Diseases; Hunter-Gatherer; Herbology // A cap and a collar.

This encounter can take place in a few different ways. It turns out that Mr. Mooner is one of the very first Kittens that Grandma Scramble took in—on the first evening of his exile—and he is a dear old friend. He gets lots of goods into the city without paying taxes to Walter.

Galiena will heal Grandma Scramble— she’s not very ill, but by eating so many eggs she has become a little fragile. She will have to follow a special diet, with plenty of soup and not many scrambled eggs.

pages.name: p.215 - Scene 4:
pages.html:
Scene 4:

All of a sudden, a hunting horn sounds and shouts are heard. The city guards, tipped off by Crowtoe, are on Mr. Mooner’s trail.

This final scene gives the young Kittens the chance to get involved in a game of hide-and-go-seek with the royal guards (led by the grim sergeant Sikkli), to get away from the smuggler’s base and lose them in the forest.

Each Kitten can come up with their own plan, then describe it and how they will carry it out. Then players can roll the dice to see if they succeed. In order to successfully lose the guards, the players will need to roll a total number of successes equal to 4 times the number of Kittens, in a maximum of two rounds of the table. If, after two turns, the players have not rolled enough successes, Mr. Mooner’s hideout is discovered! Setting an ambush and beating Sikkli in a Fang Catfight is worth 4 successes (regardless of the number of successes rolled for the fight)! It is also quite easy to convince some of the guards to look elsewhere— especially if the Kitten talking to them comes from a family of soldiers.

Sikkli // Unpleasant sergeant of the guard on the Cat Tree City walls // Strong 4 / Smart 2 / Cute 2 // Heart points 6 // Find Information; Hiss & Growl; Shake Your Booty // Royal guard’s tabard; large, heavy stick; pipe and pipe-weed. Royal Guard // Basic Guard, not very brave, not very motivated // Strong 3 / Smart 3 / Cute 3 // Heart points 6 // Hiss & Growl; Shake Your Booty; See & Search // Royal guard’s tabard; large heavy stick; horn for raising the alarm.

In the end

Once she recovers, Grandma Scramble can take the Kittens home, make them a nice meal, and give them plenty of good advice. They will also be able to count on Mr. Mooner and his band to help them get in and out of Cat Tree City should they need to, and he will always be able to send messages to their parents, or entrust them with a few “smuggling” missions.

pages.name: p.217 - Three Little Pigs Urban quest in Corktown
pages.html:
Three Little Pigs Urban quest in Corktown

The Kittens arrive in Corktown (see pages 143-152) and meet Rosie Rosevale, a female pig in need of help to find her three sons. They came to make their fortune in the city but she’s heard nothing since. One thing leads to another, and the Kittens’ investigation reveals a sinister conspiracy that endangers not only the three little pigs but also the Baron of Corktown. Introduction—a mother in distress: while playing heroes, the Kittens meet Mrs. Rosevale. Impressed, she begs them to find her three sons. Chapter one—Straw, sticks, and bricks: The

Kittens make their way all around the city, meeting all kinds of colorful characters on their investigation. They discover that the three country pigs are in serious trouble. Chapter two—the belly of the

Wolfrik: The Kittens reveal Wolfrik’s plan. He’s a brigand who is determined to harm the Baron and who has the three little pigs in his clutches. The Kittens just need to free them and put an end to Wolfrik’s bribery. They must take care, however, for it is a race against time: They must put an end to Wolfrik’s plan before it is too late! Conclusion—a family affair: The

Kittens take part in the reunion between the three little pigs and their mom. New opportunities open up.

pages.name: p.218 - The argument
pages.html:
The argument

This scenario revolves around two groups of extras whose roles must be clearly understood by the Storyteller. Profiles for these extras appear on pages 229-230.

Snorter, Snorfer, and Snorfy are

Mrs. Rosie Rosevale’s three young sons. Their father, Chubbmarine, disappeared when they were still small, so they lived with their mother in a small, simple peasant village. Imaginative and good with their trotters, they pooled all their savings to come to Corktown and set up their own construction business. The problem was that they were never able to agree on how to build things, or even on the best materials to use. Snorter loves straw. It's light, easy to transport, cheap, great insulation, and renewable. Snorfer is a fan of recycled materials, old driftwood, sticks, cardboard, and paper. It costs nothing and you can do what you want with it. Snorfy swears by stone, it is solid, durable, and ideal for this beautiful, modern city and its rich inhabitants. Without the calming presence of their mom, and finding it difficult to get work contracts, the three little pigs ended up arguing. They even came to blows before splitting up, forever angry with each other.

pages.name: p.219 - The date of the inauguration is fast approaching: The Kittens do not have much time to find the three little
pages.html:
Wolfrik is a simple docker by day. At night, he becomes a renowned gang leader who spreads terror in the neighborhood of Hook (see page 230 for Wolfrik and his gang). Wolfrik's real name is Rich. He is a big, powerful pig, who is terribly jealous of the Baron. In fact, Wolfrik is a cousin of the Baron—a cousin whose existence is unknown to nearly everyone. He is the secret son of Lirab, the city’s former baron and the uncle of Embergrunt Rinswith-Gutrotter, the current ruler. Wolfrik would have become the baron if his father had acknowledged him in his lifetime. Wolfrik has amassed a small fortune with his antics and thefts. His one desire is to depose Embergrunt and become the new Baron of Corktown!

And things are looking up for Wolfrik.

In order to consolidate his grip on the city and his restless family, Baron Embergrunt has had a statue built at the very end of the large pier that protects the port, so it will be the first and last thing visitors will see. Wolfrik plans to replace the original rock pedestal with a kind of Trojan Horse: a hollow pedestal in which he can hide with his gang, ready to leap out on the Baron during the statue’s inauguration ceremony. After he saw the three little pigs arguing and discussing building techniques, Wolfrik had them kidnapped to make the false pedestal for him, and has held them prisoner in a warehouse ever since.

The date of the inauguration is fast approaching: The Kittens do not have much time to find the three little

pigs and prevent Wolfrik from carrying out his plan!

pages.name: p.220 - Introduction
pages.html:
Introduction

In the early evening, the Kittens

are walking near the Salt Gate (see page 145) when their attention is drawn by a call for help. A small rabbit with immaculate white fur, who works as a street saleswoman, is attacked by four ruffians from the Red Hook gang. They want to steal her basket full of ribbons, pretty bows, and handkerchiefs. The rabbit, named Snow, tries to hide behind the Kittens when they appear. What follows is a straightforward

Fang Catfight: The baddies want to make a show of strength in the neighborhood, but will run off as soon as the situation seems to be getting away from them.

Whether they win or not, the bravery of the

Kittens when confronted by the robbers gets the attention of Mrs. Rosie Rosevale (see page 229). So she invites them, along with Snow, to The Pink Seagull inn (see page 143), where she is lodging, to buy them a drink and a nice cake. Soon Mrs. Rosevale asks the Kittens for help: Her three children, Snorter, Snorfer, and Snorfy, came to town a few months ago, but she has heard nothing from them since and is worried. She has travelled all the way from her village to find them, but has no idea how to go about it. She can even pay our brave heroes for their time and effort with what little she has, and offers them her life’s savings.

pages.name: p.221 - Chapter one: stone, straw, and sticks
pages.html:
Chapter one: stone, straw, and sticks

The first part of this adventure is an in vestigation: The Kittens gather information about the three little pigs by visiting the city and interviewing its residents. Starting with the few pieces of information given by Mrs. Rosevale, the players will start to follow the thread of the investigation, and should gather as many clues as possible about what is going on, about the three brothers, the reason for their arguments, what happened to them, and their current whereabouts. Use the list of clues provided and feed them to the players, more or less in order, until the Kittens are ready to move on to chapter two.

During an investigation scenario, play- ers gather information by asking the Storyteller questions. Every time a player asks a question, the Storyteller must give a meaningful or interesting answer. Without answers, the players go round in circles, they won’t know what to do, and will get bored. The players act through their Kittens: They are the ones who move around the city, who question the extras and witnesses, who read the letters. But it is the players who think, rack their brains to understand what’s going on, and work out how they can use the Storyteller’s answers to advance their investigation.

pages.name: p.222
pages.html:
Since the Storyteller cannot predict the questions in advance—and she must provide the players with answers—she should not decide that a certain clue will be found in a certain place at a certain time, or from certain extra. That would unfortunately be the way to make players go round in circles and never find the clue. You must be flexible instead: If the Kittens question the old beggar pig in front of the hostel, he should give them the important information; not the owner of the hostel who nobody has talked to (even if that was the plan at the beginning). The important thing is that the information or clue gets to the players. The Storyteller must take advantage of opportunities to reveal information and let the players do something with it, and move on to where the next clue leads them.

This also means that the Storyteller must avoid false leads and false information. She can be ambiguous or confusing—if she wants the Kittens to make some extra effort—but she should not lie or deceive. The players will be quite able to charge off in the wrong direction without anyone’s help!

Throughout the adventure, the Storyteller should set the stage for the preparations of the upcoming anniversary of Baron Ember grunt’s rise to power. The Iron Loins (see page 148) are making the inhabitants clean the streets, pennants and banners are being strung up between houses, big buildings are being decorated, and above all of this the huge statue of the Baron is being constructed at the very end of the pier. The thousands of inns in the city are competing with ideas to attract visitors on the day of the big party: Competitions are announced and extra decks and terraces are being put up.

pages.name: p.223
pages.html:
Mrs. Rosevale's only lead at the mo- ment is a letter she received several weeks ago in which her three children told her they were staying at Madame French's boarding house. They told her about how they were in touch with foremen and workers in the materials market in The Hook. The Kittens can get on with the investigation in whatever order they want. Madame French is a surly, old, can- tankerous duck. It is difficult to get her to talk, unless it is about criticizing her neighbors or telling off the kids who hang out in front of her house. According to her, the three pigs were noisy and argued a lot. However, they paid their rent on time. They left suddenly, but of their own free will. It is possible to persuade her to let the Kittens visit the attic where the pigs were staying—with the right attitude, or maybe a successful Cute test. Madame French has not had time to clean the room yet. The three brothers were not very tidy. There are empty bottles of cheap beer under the beds. They were bought in the Better Here Than There! tavern (see page 146). There are also purchase or ders and scribbled-on invoices for all kinds of construction goods from the market in Hook.

It is possible to question Madame

French’s other residents: Nana Carrot, an old, nearsighted, deaf rabbit; Mrs. Nearsome, the mother of two boisterous, inquisitive young Kittens; Turdi, an Iron Loin who is almost never there; and finally, Click and Clack, a couple of young squirrels. They are acrobats who speak enviously about Bigwheel. They are very confident, and are ready to demonstrate their know-how by performing their routine to the Kittens in the beams of their room.
