One of them (or maybe someone else) may recall seeing a shady individual, who could have been a fox, and who seemed to be watching the attic and the three pigs.

pages.name: p.224
pages.html:
A visit to the materials market in

Hook will give the Kittens the opportunity to learn more about the economic activity of the workers’ district. This is where all the materials that build the city and its ships are bought and sold: Lumberjacks, quarrymen, recyclers, farmers, peasants, smallholders, machinists, workers and bosses all meet there, with a noisy frenzy that fully demonstrates the city’s dynamic nature. The purchase orders found in the attic feature a name, Goldclaw the crab, but if the Kittens ask the right questions in the market they may get his name anyway. Goldclaw is a busy merchant, who has no time to waste helping Kittens. His guards make it very difficult to approach. Kittens will have to be crafty and avoid any form or rudeness or violence, and will need a good excuse to meet him if they want to steal a few of his precious minutes. Kittens can also interview Goldclaw's employees—for example Adan, a big, rough-looking but nice boar. They can eventually learn that the three little pigs never agreed on anything: One would order materials and the other two would cancel the order straight away. They were constantly arguing which techniques and materials to use: Wood or straw? Stone or brick? Human-made, salvaged materials from the olden days? Once, Goldclaw had to call in his guards to separate the three brothers when they came to blows. Someone will probably point out to the Kittens that there was a disturbing figure who seemed to be watching the three pigs: A one-eyed old fox that they know hangs out at Better Here Than There!, the tavern that faces the Daedalus District. Better Here Than There! is a dump.

All the city’s dregs hang out there and if Plonky the skunk, who runs the place, did not have such a strong hand and intimidating look, the fighting would never stop. Neither Plonky nor the customers will answer the Kittens’ questions. The former has no time; the latter are aggressive or silent, with plenty of threatening glances. However, Plonky ends up making the Kittens an offer: If they stay behind after closing and help her clean everything up and put everything away (a task reminiscent of Hercules in Augeas’ stables!) she will tell them all she knows about the three little pigs and the fox.

pages.name: p.225
pages.html:
The three little pigs spent a lot of time drinking cheap beer and arguing— and the more cheap beer they drank, the more they argued. They always had lots of bits of paper and plans with them and endlessly shouted about techniques and construction sites. If the Kittens have not already been there, Plonky will direct them to the boarding house where the pigs lived and the market they visited regularly.

The old one-eyed fox is called Barnaby, and lately he had been watching the three little pigs closely, and following them. Barnaby is a scoundrel who has been arrested by the Iron Loins many times. One day he’s a pirate, another he’s a brigand. But he is always a thief, and always a liar. For a few months now, he has claimed to work for the new boss of the docks, a nasty character named Wolfrik. And, yes, he has been seen hanging out by the warehouses.

pages.name: p.226 - Chapter two: the belly of the Wolfrik
pages.html:
Chapter two: the belly of the Wolfrik

The three little pigs have been missing for several weeks now and no one has seen them anywhere. The only trail that the Kittens have to follow is that of the old one-eyed fox named Barnaby (see page 230). They should get down to the port to try and find him.

To the rescue! The port is bustling. Apparently this afternoon is the inauguration of the new statue. The Baron and his entourage will cross the entire city as they make their way to the end of the pier. Sailors and captains are busy scrubbing their ships and hoisting hundreds of colored flags. The docks are being swept and all the crates and street furniture are being put away so as not to clutter the paths.

The old warehouses are particular- ly busy, since this is where the statue and its pedestal were prepared and built before they were moved to the pier.

By wandering randomly around the warehouses (Smart test) or by questioning the locals (Cute test), the Kittens will eventually spot the fox. They can also come up with plans to find him, approach him, and capture him: set a trap, lure him with the promise of a good deal, use his connections, and so on. Don’t forget that time is running out: Everything must be resolved today! If cornered, Barnaby will try to run or defend himself, but he is not crazy and will surrender if his enemies are too strong. He will definitely not get into a Claw Catfight! The scoundrel is getting on a bit in years, and would prefer to negotiate his freedom by supplying information. He ends up spilling the beans: The three little pigs are imprisoned in warehouse 13, where they have been working day and night to make a replica of the statue’s pedestal for Wolfrik. The leader of the gang has had the original replaced and plans to hide in the replica and surprise the Baron during his anniversary ceremony. Warehouse 13 is guarded by two of

Wolfrik’s tough guys: Vinny, a big pig covered in scars, and Ruddy, a tattooed crayfish (see page 230 for both). The Kittens will have to get rid of them through strength or cunning. The three little pig brothers are locked in three iron cages that are hanging from the warehouse ceiling. In the middle of the floor is the real pedestal, which was swapped by Wolfrik for the fake.

pages.name: p.227
pages.html:
If the Kittens try to get help from the

Iron Loins (see page 148), there is a very good chance that they will be ignored, and even threatened with imprisonment if they insist. The Iron Loins have enough to do, supervising the townsfolk and guarding the ceremony. As soon as the three little pigs are freed

(see page 229), they thank their saviors and will explain Wolfrik's foolish plan (which they are very worried about). At that moment, a fanfare sounds outside! Baron Embergrunt is at the port and heading to his statue on the pier!

Yoohoo! Baron! Step one: The Kittens have to get through the security cordon and reach the end of the pier. They will have to be crafty and clever. The players will probably come up with various plans. The Storyteller should choose the most interesting obstacles, the most relevant tests for abilities, and above all, let the Kittens get to the end with the impression that they overcame the most difficult challenges!

It is really crowded all along the pier, but there are many boats moored next to it. The challenge for the Kittens is to make their way down the pier (more difficult in the crowd but easier when going from boat to boat) and to keep a low profile (easier when surrounded by spectators but more difficult when standing on a boat). There are Iron Loins all over the place, but they have a lot to do and cannot cover all the routes. The three little pigs volunteer to create a diversion, get the attention of the authorities, or cause an incident. Step two: foil Wolfrik's plan. The rogue is hidden in the hollow pedestal with his gang. When the moment comes, he is going to leap out of a secret door and seize the Baron, arrest him and—after ridiculing him—take power!

pages.name: p.228
pages.html:
The Storyteller will have to manage a

Catfight with lots of people: Wolfrik and his gang, the Baron and his Iron Loins, the Kittens and their allies, the crowd, and so on. Don’t worry: A big Catfight is just lots of small Catfights one after the other. You only need to focus on the important Catfights—the ones the Kittens are involved in. You only need to describe the rest of the fighting as if telling a story. To start with, they will only be Fang Catfights: The goal is to better your opponent, intimidate them, force them to their knees, submit, or flee.

Only Wolfrik will want to start a Claw Catfight with his cousin the Baron if things go wrong. The Kittens may have to risk their lives to save Embergrunt! Various options will come up, depend ing on what ideas the players have and what their Kittens do. This list is not definitive: the Kittens block the hidden door and prevent the bad guys from getting out of the pedestal; they manage to get some Iron Loins to help them; they defend the Baron who will only stand up to Wolfrik until a Claw Catfight starts; they get the unsympathetic crowd on their side, and so on. The scene must be massive, with reversals of fortune, the crowd taking turns to back Wolfrik or the Baron, guests and members of the Rinswith-Gutrotter family taking sides or trying to take power themselves. Also, the poorly-secured statue that’s on a weak pedestal could at any time fall into the port and block the way… Depending on the circumstances, Wolf rik will be captured, manage to flee the scene, or he may even win the confrontation. And there are still the members of his gang that need to be taken care of. It will all depend on the level of violence that occurs during the confrontation.

pages.name: p.229 - Conclusion
pages.html:
Conclusion

Assuming the Kittens save the Baron's skin, Baron Embergrunt welcomes them to his palace the next day to thank and reward them. He looks at the Kittens for a while, then makes them a curious offer: He needs some independent secret agents who are willing, courageous, and full of initiative. He explains his plans for the city to them, and talks of his obligation to pass for a tyrant in order to prevent his family from snatching power (as Wolfrik tried). He has plenty of missions for the Kittens if they agree to work for him.

Back at The Pink Seagull, Mrs. Rosevale is absolutely delighted to be reunited with her three little pigs, but she tells them off repeatedly for their arguing, drunkenness, and bad behavior. She asks “Why can’t you work together using all the materials at the same time?” They made the fake pedestal without fighting.

The three brothers promise the Kittens they will build them a house in Corktown one day if they find the land. They’ll do it for free, to thank them!

Extras Mrs. Rosie Rosevale // A desperate, hopeful mom // Strong 2 / Smart 2 / Cute 2 // Heart points 4 // Care of Beasts; Cook // Clean & Tidy (1);Preserving Resources (1) // A canvas travel bag; umbrella. Snorter, Snorfer, and Snorfy // Quarreling but unquestionably ingenious and inventive brothers // Strong 3 / Smart 3 / Cute 2 // Heart points 6 // Tinker with Bits & Bobs; Shake Your Booty // Slice & Dice (1); Safety at Work (1) // Tool bag; notebook filled with diagrams, calculations, and crazy ideas.

Barnaby // One-eyed fox and a dirty, sneaky scoundrel // Strong 3 / Smart 4 // Cute 3 // Heart points 7 // Hide in Shadows; Move Silently; See & Search // Cat Haven (2) // A filthy scarf; bunch of mismatched keys; old piece of cured sausage. Vinny, Ruddy, and Wolfrik’s gang // Brutal, confident ruffians // Strong 4 / Smart 2 / Cute 2 // Heart points 6 // Hiss & Growl; Shake Your Booty // Long Night (3) // Docker’s hooks; old clothes.

pages.name: p.233
pages.html:
Selene’s Nightmare The Kittens are prisoners in Selene's nightmare. They must get out as soon as possible or soothe the spirit of the forest so that the the sun can once again rise in peace.

This adventure is presented as a series of random tables—you will roll the dice a lot to create each encounter that makes up the story. The Storyteller must first define where the encounter takes place by generating two results from the Locations table on pages 234-236. The first result defines the entrance the Kittens find themselves emerging into. The second result defines the exit that leads out of that location.

To generate each location result, you may need to roll 1d6 multiple times to define the type of location and specific form it takes as shown in that result’s columns.

For each result on the Locations table, read the description of that result and then go to the Atmosphere table (pages 238-239) or Adventures tables (pages 241-244) as directed to generate those parts of the encounter. Of course, the Storyteller can also choose herself, without the help of the dice; she can even invent elements if she likes, depending on what the Kittens do, and what ideas the players may have.

Players can try to draw a map, with lines and circles connecting encounter locations, to plot their journey through the restless dreams of the spirit of the forest.

Each encounter within the nightmare will be different from the last. At the end of an encounter, the Kittens can choose to stay in the nightmare or leave it, and end the adventure, perhaps having earned some treasure. Sometimes they will need to fight and defeat creatures in the nightmare, other times they’ll need to release trapped animals. But each victory is one more step towards making Selene better.

pages.name: p.234 - Locations
pages.html:
Locations

Roll 1d6 for the type of place, read its directions, and roll for subtables as instructed.

1-2

A trail that weaves through the trees; roll for each subtable below

(go to Atmosphere, page 238, then Adventures, page 241).

1d6

1 Straight and easy to follow. 2 Tortuous and difficult to walk along. 3 Marked by large stones. 4 Barely visible wild animal tracks. 5 Hidden beneath leaves and brambles. 6 A wet and muddy valley floor.

1d6

1-3 The trail is straight.

4-6 The trail branches off—the kittens must frequently choose to go left or right, and it is easy to get lost.

A steep slope; roll for each subtable below (go to Atmosphere, page 238).

1d6

1-3 Must descend carefully to avoid falling (each Kitten must pass a Smart test or lose 1 Heart point).

4-6 Must climb and scramble without getting tired (Each Kitten must pass a Strong test or lose 1 Heart point).

1d6

1 A rocky, unstable cliff. 2 A wet, slippery mound. 3 A steep, overgrown drop.

4 An embankment with lots of dark burrows.

5 A mound of red earth with large, carved stones. 6 An unstable, paw-breaking scree.

pages.name: p.235
pages.html:
A clearing among the trees; roll for each subtable below (go to Atmosphere, page 238, then Adventures, page 241).

1d6

1-2 Very small, just large enough to catch a glimpse of the sky above.

3-4 Medium sized, big enough for a few tents or a hut.

5-6 Huge, will take some time to cross it.

1d6

1 An ancient, paved square with a fountain and ivy-covered statues of humans and animals.

2

In the middle of an expanse of yellowed grass is a wobbly-looking abandoned shack, filled with things in old boxes.

3 An old tractor from the human era, half sunk in mud, in the middle of a massively overgrown corn field.

4

A beautifully tendered formal garden, its boxwood bushes painstakingly sculpted with a sickle by a big-bare-butt dressed in rags.

5

A wide stream flows through, with white waters that sing to, refresh, and rest the travelers (+1 Heart point to each Kitten).

6

A paved town square, with illuminated, bent-over street lamps, a large, abstract white marble statue covered with ivy, and a few benches.

pages.name: p.236
pages.html:
An obstacle that prevents further travel; roll on the first subtable below (go to Atmosphere, page 238, and then make a U-turn, by rolling on the second subtable below).

1d6

1

The path disappears in a tangle of brambles and impenetrable bushes.

No matter how much they are cut, the plants grow back immediately. 2 A rockfall that blocks all progress.

3 An old, broken bridge jutting out over a swirling, foaming river.

4 A large crevasse, a chasm, or a deep, ominous hole.

5 A noxious marsh, with acidic, polluted waters.

6 A old man-made sign stating trespassers will be shot.

1d6

1-2 The Kittens go back to a place of their choice that they have already visited (or roll another location).

3-4 The kittens go back to the last place they visited (or roll another location).

5-6

The Kittens are lost: throw away their map and start a new one (if they are mapping), then roll a new location.

A door that leads somewhere roll for each subtable below (go to Atmosphere, page 238).

1d6

1 A solid wooden door.

2 A beautiful wooden door painted in a bright or pastel color. 3 A heavy metal door set into a wall.

4 A very small glass door in an embankment. 5 An enormous bronze door.

6 A submarine hatch with a wheel to open it.

1d6

1-2 The door is not locked.

3-4

The door is locked (lock, bolt, or strange box with flashing lights, and so on)—Kittens may try to pick it (Smart test) or break it (Strong test).

5-6

The door is blocked (jammed, swollen, barred by rocks, trees, trash, recycled materials, or old objects, and so on). The way will have to be cleared (Strong test).

pages.name: p.238 - Atmosphere
pages.html:
Atmosphere

Roll d6 to determine the location’s atmosphere, then roll to determine what is found here (see next page). Roll for each result’s subtable.

1d6 The nightmare’s atmosphere…

1-3

1 Ominous shadows bring to life strange stories in the lights the Kittens carry…

2 An invisible presence in the trees whispers words nobody understands…

3

Unmoving animals and beasts are scattered around, motion- less and frozen in time, who do not react to anything…

4 Everything is blurred, as if seen through mist or glass…

5 The air is heavy and humid, as if awaiting a storm that never comes…

6 It is suddenly deathly cold, with a freezing wind that burns the fingers…

4-6

1 All colors disappear, leaving everything drab and gray…

2 Colors are all wrong, strange, and saturated…

3 Sound no longer carries, it is impossible to speak or hear…

4 It gets darker and darker— it’s almost impossible to follow the trail…

5 Insects and small creatures make a huge racket—it is impossible to hear yourself think…

6 Inquisitive eyes appear on leaves, tree trunks, flowers, and stones…

pages.name: p.239
pages.html:
1d6 What is found here…

1-3

1 Nothing in particular: Common plants, brambles, grasses, ferns, and some more or less poisonous fungi…

2

Trash everywhere: Impossible-

to-identify garbage, filthy discharge from cracked pipes, food leftovers, mold, maggots, and unknown, stinking things…

3

Ruined remnants of the

past: Broken electronics, intricate gears, bits of computers, and lumps of rusty metal that are beyond recognition…

4 Tracks and footprints: Beasts and animals, tires and tracks, or odd machinery…

5 Markings: Ancient graffiti, traffic signs, direction arrows, recent scribbles, or carvings in the bark of trees…

6

Food: A big, warm teapot, a table set for tea, bags of fruit and vegetables, a fridge full of pizza and sodas, or an oven with a roast dinner inside…

4-6

1 Writing: A poem, a warning, a cry for help, sinister symbols, or meowgic runes…

2 Bones: Of animals and beasts, maybe even an ancient giant…

3

A breeze: It carries sound of unknown origin, a strange smell, distant words that are hard to make out, or a shiver down the spine…

4 Mushrooms: Shiny, massive, making strange noises, and releasing clouds of spores, etcetera.

5

Ancient walls with small

alcoves: Candles, statues, odd, luminous machines, or small cold or hot springs…

6

One or more pillars: Some engraved with symbols, others luminous, some that play music when approached, or some with levers and switches on the side…

pages.name: p.241 - Adventures
pages.html:
Adventures

It is up to you to determine which adventures the Kittens will come across in the location. To assist this, roll 1d6 for the adventure type below, then roll for each subtable within that adventure.

1d6 Adventures

1 Nothing to report, everything seems to be frozen in time and space. 2 A hazard (see this page). 3-4 A discovery (see page 242). 5-6 An encounter (see page 243).

Hazard

1d6 Hazards

1

A whistling sound is heard and gas starts flowing from a pipe. It spreads everywhere. Quickly, the Kittens must protect themselves (each Kitten must use an appropriate object or be poisoned, with the loss of 1 Heart point). They must flee (Strong test) or come up with a solution (Smart test).

2

A deafening cracking noise. A piece of the ceiling drops down. The Kittens must react to avoid being crushed (each must pass a Strong test or be buried and lose 1 Heart point).

3

A cloud of unknown, aggressive insects comes out of nowhere. They attack the Kittens. Their bites are really itchy (each Kitten must pass a Cute test or lose 1 Heart point). Kittens must flee or chase them away.

4

Strange ropes hang from the ceiling and all over the floor. They make roar- ing and snapping sounds (they are in fact live electrical cables). Kittens must progress and avoiding touching them (each Kitten must pass a Smart test or be electrocuted, losing 1 Heart point).

5

A strange door creaks open and closed by itself. Its pattern and speed are random (it is, in fact, a still-function- ing airlock). The Kittens will have to count carefully and race through at the risk of getting stuck (each must pass a Smart test or lose 1 Heart point).

6

With a thunderous roar, the floor under the paws of the Kittens splits and col- lapses. They must jump or grab some- thing to avoid falling (each must pass a Strong test or lose 1 Heart point).

pages.name: p.242 - Discovery
pages.html:
Discovery

1d6 Discoveries

1

A concealed passageway that

gives access to a secret room:

1d6 How do they get into the secret room? 1-2 Through a collapsed ceiling.

3-4 Through a hole in the ground. 5-6 Through a hole in the wall.

1d6 What does the secret room contain? (Roll below, then go to Atmosphere, page 238). 1-2 A hazard (see page 241). 3-4 An encounter (see next page). 5-6 Treasure (see page 244).

2

A deep, gaping chasm:

1d6 Can you make out some treasure at the bottom? 1-4 No.

5-6 Yes, but you still have to get down to it.

3 A still-functioning water fountain from the olden days. Kittens can fill up.

4 Food, odd but edible, and packed in strange silver bags.

5-6

A metal box: 1d6 Is it locked?

1-3 Yes, it must be picked open

(Smart test) or forced

(Strong test). 4-6 No.

1d6 Does it contain something interesting? 1-3 No, it's empty. 4-5 Yes, some treasure (see page 244).

6 Remnants of a previous expedition; roll again below.

1d6 In the latter case, is there anything to salvage? 1-3 No. 4-6 Yes (roll 1d6 below): 1-2 Food. 3-4 Some treasure (see page 244). 5-6 Tools (roll 1d6 below): 1-2 A rope and a climbing hook. 3-4 A pickax and a shovel. 5-6 Torches and a tinderbox.

pages.name: p.243
pages.html:
Encounter For each result below, roll for its subtable. Adapt the number of creatures encountered to the number of Kittens. Depending on how the Kittens behave, an encounter can lead to a Catfight or a conversation, an information swap, help, and so on. Not every encounter should turn into a confrontation. The Kittens are not the only ones lost in Selene’s nightmare.

When an encounter is over, whether it ended in friction or harmony, the Kittens will probably find some treasure (see page 244)— ideally you plan it in advance and integrate the result into the scene.

1d6 Encounters

1-2

One or more beasts who are panicked by the situation and ready to fight (roll 1d6). 1 A horde of hungry rats. 2 An angry boar. 3 An unkempt bear. 4 Disagreeable ferrets. 5 Aggressive crows. 6 Thieving bats.

3-4

One or more animals who have no idea what they are doing there (roll 1d6). 1 Lost explorer pigs. 2 Treasure-hunting toads. 3 Wanted pirate crabs. 4 Mercenary dogs from the Junkyard. 5 Peasant foxes on the run.

6 Fish in wetsuits looking for an underground lake.

5

One or more nightmar- ish monsters (roll 1d6). 1 A big, hungry eye. 2 Giant centipedes. 3 A man- (and Kitten-) eating plant. 4 Beetle slaves. 5 A voracious gropkin. 6 A bloodthirsty molevamp.

6

A ramshackle robot from the olden days (roll 1d6).

1-2 A caterpillar-tracked robot worker. 3-4 A big, walking, talking robot. 5-6 A small, annoying, flying robot.

pages.name: p.244 - Treasure
pages.html:
Treasure

1d6 Treasure 1 Advanced, good quality tools. 2 A small fortune in strange gems. 3 An extraordinary potion.

4 An incomprehensible book from the olden days, valuable for a scholar or collector.

5 Unknown material, which can be used to make wonderful clothes or amazing armor.

6 A rare, unusable machine from the olden days (roll 1d6 below): 1-2 A telephone. 3-4 A laptop. 5-6 A small robot insect.

pages.name: p.247 - Crimsonfief
pages.html:
Crimsonfief

In the far north of the country, at the end of a wild and steep coastline, tucked away in an invisible cove out of view of the high seas, lies the strangest, most dangerous, and most famous of places: Crimsonfief. The name is legendary, the stories about it are countless. Most of them are pure lies or, worse, the boastfulness of a few braggarts who add to the rumors, but who have never even been near the place.

However, some of the stories are true: Crimsonfief is meowgical. Crimsonfief is deadly. Crimsonfief is unforgiving. All the world’s secrets can be found there: knowledge of the past, the present, and the future. It contains the answers to the simplest or most difficult questions, solutions to the most complex problems… All you have to do is dare to enter and confront the multitude of traps and inhabitants you will find inside.

Those who made it out will confirm that Crimsonfief gave them what they wanted, but they never like to talk about what exactly happened there. In any case, it would be useless, because no two visits to Crimsonfief are ever the same.

Crimsonfief is the most famed dungeon from the title of this game, and the place Kittens will probably visit multiple times, for information and for help. It is an ever-changing place. Every time the Kittens go there, it will be completely different from the last time. Crimsonfief is put together according to the principle of the

“Five Room Dungeon”—a progressive exploration of five places within, each offering their share of danger and mystery before you get to the end. It is enough to take up a good portion of a game session, but without taking up too much of the Kittens’ time.

Note to the Storyteller: Crimsonfief was dreamt up to be a place lost in a temporal anomaly. Crimsonfief is never the same twice, because the place is the reflection of all that it has been and all that it will be, but never all at the same time, never completely whole. It is both advanced and savage at the same time, it is well- looked-after and in ruins, inhabited and deserted. It contains everything you might need, everything you can imagine for your amusement, and everything to encourage more play…

pages.name: p.248 - Getting to Crimsonfief
pages.html:
Getting to Crimsonfief

Kittens will first hear rumors about a mysterious, very dangerous place. Travelers will talk about it, including customers in taverns and inns, friends passing through for an evening, Grandma Scramble, or Mr. Mooner perhaps. It could be Baron Rinswith-Gutrotter who brings it up when the Kittens find themselves in trouble.

Little by little, the Kittens can gather clues and information about the place, by asking questions or encountering animals who have been there.

Crimsonfief is in the north of the coun- try, near the sea, and is a difficult place to access. The place is strange and bizarre. When the sun or moon align in certain ways, people claim to have seen it come and go, disappear and reappear randomly, or react strangely in certain light. Crimsonfief seems to have dozens of different entrances and the tales of those who have been there are always different. When it comes to what it looks like and where it is—going there multiple times changes nothing: All is different each time you visit.

There are many dangers: creatures, traps, riddles, dead ends, and nasty mindgames to contend with. You can literally disappear into the depths of Crimsonfief and never come out again. Those who succeed in a quest there always seem to find answers to their questions or solutions to their problems. It comes in the form of advice, valuable information, useful objects, and even—occasionally— direct help. Crimsonfief always seems to know what Kittens will need and can give it to them without hesitation. To get there, you can follow the coastline all the way, but various dangerous creatures and monsters protect the ways in. It is also possible to go through the GIN network of tunnels (see page 121). Sure, it’s easier and faster that way, but you do have to negotiate with rats from the depths. It is said that some meowges created a spell that instantly teleports you there, or brings you back. But who would have the knowledge of such a secret? And would they agree to teach it to some Kittens? It is said that Crimsonfief’s “chosen ones” may one day find and use a strange communication box. It allows them to call on a magical machine—some kind of flying saucer—that picks them up where they are after summoning it, and takes them to Crimsonfief.

pages.name: p.250 - Constructing Crimsonfief
pages.html:
Constructing Crimsonfief

Every time the Kittens go to Crimsonfief with different questions, the place will never be the same. So we will not give you a definite plan of it, but instead a simple, quick method to construct for yourself the Crimsonfief that the Kittens will encounter (this time).

This tool builds on the principle of the “Five Room Dungeon,” an old-school roleplaying game classic that is used to create short adventures that can be played in an evening, with a good number of twists and turns. As the name above suggests, exploring Crimsonfief takes place through five locations that are linked to each other and at the end comes the quest’s final goal. Theme

Begin by deciding on a general theme. This theme is built around a word that will serve as a common thread for your descriptions of Crimsonfief, the nature of the dangers or encounters inside, and so on. To help with this, roll 1d6 for the row and another for the column to find a word from the table below (or simply choose one).

For example, if you take the word “pipes”, you can build an exploration around pipes (inside and out), complex systems that go in and out of walls, and anything that you can put into pipes (strange liquids, gases, steam, unpleasant stuff, and so on). This makes the dungeon coherent, and helps you to find interesting ideas.

1d6 1 2 3 4 5 6 1 Elevators Color Fragile Laser Soft Rust 2 Arms Crystals Cold Light Shadows Twisted 3 Fog Debris Slippery Music Wavy Swirls 4 Noise Electrical Squeaks Metal Pendulum Pipes 5 Bubbles Balance Wet Mirrors Plants Wind 6 Heat Small Shiny Mold Stinking Faces

pages.name: p.251 - Configuration
pages.html:
Configuration

The five rooms of Crimsonfief dungeon do not necessarily have to come one after the other. There are plenty of possible configurations. Choose one of them and organize the others around it. It is always interesting to give the Kittens choices of direction. To generate each room, roll 1d6 for the row and another for the column to find a description from the table below (or simply choose one).

Note that when we talk about a “room”, it is not necessarily a closed-off cube of small dimensions, with a door in and a door out. It is above all an environment that can be bigger or smaller, and more or less open, such as a huge tropical greenhouse with paths going in all directions, or the buildings of a food production plant with tanks in a large room and many other adjoining places. It could also be a single airlock with all the problems contained inside it.

Each piece of the dungeon is an opportunity to vary the environment, tactics, problems, and solutions.

1d6 1 2 3 4 5 6

1 Spaceport Recycling center Elevator Plant-growing warehouse Open space Amusement arcade

2 Workshop Corridors Warehouse Hospital Indoor park Conference rooms

3 Offices Maintenance tunnels Foundry Laboratory Patio Greenhouses

4 Canteen Crater Hall of mirrors

Underground lake

Subway platform

Thermoelectric unit

5 Barracks Kitchen Hallway Belly of a whale Subway train Food processing plant

6 Data center Particle accelerator Hotel Microfactory Panoramic rotunda

Ventilation shaft

pages.name: p.252 - Rooms
pages.html:
Rooms

Each of the dungeon’s rooms will contain a different feature. They define the type of challenge that awaits the Kittens and, when combined with the dungeon’s theme, should spark your imagination. These features do not have to match the order of the rooms. In fact, you can arrange them in whatever order you like: for example the, guardian before the trap but after the mirror, then the choice, and finally the ordeal. To generate a theme for each ordeal, roll 1d6 for its table (or simply choose one).

Ordeal. The ordeal should involve the abilities and bravery of one Kitten in particular. If he does not survive the ordeal, it is likely that he will not get to the end of the dungeon (he is knocked unconscious, is carried out, or disappears for a while, and so on). 1. Block // 2. Challenge // 3. Technical challenge // 4. Duel // 5. Sacrifice // 6. Transformation

Choice. The choice will concern all the

Kittens at once: They will have to agree on an ethical or moral issue—a sacrifice of one of them or a Purr-ecious item, taking a risk to seize an opportunity or grab some treasure, and so on. In some cases, the choice will be essential in order to move forward; in others it will be a subsidiary question that may lead to opportunities that can be taken or not. 1. Odd alliance // 2. Lesser evil // 3. Opportunity // 4. Wager // 5. Secret passage // 6. Sacrifice

Guardian. The guardian will usually be an encounter with one or more creature(s) who are defending a place and preventing the Kittens from continuing. Some guardians are aggressive and violent; some may be negotiated with; some are like a sphinx and will ask riddles and questions. 1. Interrogator // 2. Machine // 3. Villains // 4. Predators // 5. Refugees // 6. Sentries

Mirror. The mirror lets the Storyteller do whatever they want. If things have been simple thus far (getting to Crimsonfief in the first place), then this should be hellish—difficult and complicated to get through. Otherwise, it can be a haven or refuge, an opportunity to rest, catch a breath, and heal (in this case, skip rolling below). 1. Assassins // 2. Disaster // 3. Rivals // 4. Disease // 5. Treachery // 6. Emergency

Trap. The trap can be a sudden or un- expected event that puts the characters in danger immediately; or it can be the announcement of danger that makes the Kittens reflect and find a way to avoid it. Or both. 1. Anomaly // 2. Environmental hazard // 3. Malfunction // 4. Meowgic // 5. Structural problem // 6. Poison

pages.name: p.254 - Exploring Crimsonfief
pages.html:
Exploring Crimsonfief

Exploring Crimsonfief should not just be a simple series of tests. Each room has a particular situation, an atmosphere, and you have to let the players react to it in their own ways. They will probably have lots of ideas and thoughts, and will often come up with problems by themselves that their Kittens have to solve. The tests should come at that point, based on what they come up with.

You will need to maintain some sort of balance between the progression needed to get to the end, keeping the momentum going, and the mixture of obstacles, challenges, and problems that the players are faced with— without you helping them too much or giving them nothing but test rolls. The Kittens will need to explore their environment and you add detail as they do it. You can let them find equipment (if they remember to look for it), or come up with smart solutions. Always reward clever solutions and good ideas.

Examples

Here are three examples of Crimsonfief dungeons that you can get by mixing up the previous ideas. Feel free to use them if you don’t have the time or the inspiration to create your own.

The big, round tunnel

The theme of this dungeon is “wet”. It is all located in the ruins of a vast particle accelerator. The entrance is in a bunker that’s covered with vegetation. A heavy, metal door opens onto a large, very deep, very dark hole in the ground.

1. Ordeal. A ladder is fixed to the tunnel wall, as well as bits of machinery. The ladder is unstable and rusty. Only one Kitten can go on it at a time and they must be quick—the ladder could break at any moment. The first Kitten on it will have to dare to go down in the dark, alone. No rope is long enough to reach to the bottom. The ladder’s rungs are wet and slippery. It is a very long way down. Bugs are stuck to the wall—different kinds of snails, slugs, and poisonous anemones. The Kitten must pass a Strong test: each success, up to 4, cancels the loss of 1 Heart point (no minimum).

pages.name: p.255
pages.html: Heart point loss is from the bugs, slipping, splinters, and so on. At the tunnel’s very bottom there is a machine that powers an elevator. Kittens there must pass a Smart test (easy) in order to activate it and send it up for the Kittens at the top. Failing this test means that the elevator works but electrocutes the Kitten who activated it a little— everything is very wet down here—and he loses 1 more Heart point. 2. Mirror. If it has been very hard going so far, the Kittens come across a small, cold room with damp walls. In one corner, an old drink and snack dispenser is still switched on and working, with plenty of edible items in it (the expiry dates long since passed but that doesn’t matter). If it has been easy so far, the Kittens instead find themselves at the end of a long, flooded corridor. They will have to dive into the thick, black water, where strange things brush against their coats and slip in and out of their bags. They must be careful not to get too cold or lose equipment en route. 3. Choice. The Kittens arrive in a large, round tunnel leading off both to the right and left. In front of them is some very complex-looking machinery, covered in switches, VU meters, and lights. Some are blinking dimly. There is a huge metal cabinet with a large lever in the upper position. Should they touch it or not? Different things occur if the lever is activated (lights blink on everywhere, the machine comes to life, robotic arms start moving, there are bolts of electricity and disturbing noises because of all the moisture, the tunnel’s inhabitants stop crawling around and seek shelter) or if it is not (the long corridors remain dark and damp, the creepy-crawlies that live there may attack or get in the Kittens’ way). There is significant risk in either case. And the fundamental question remains: Will Crimsonfief answer questions if the machines are not switched on?

pages.name: p.256
pages.html:
4. Guardian. A big-bare-butt lives in the round corridor at its ride side, feeding on snails and anemones. He is dressed in a long shirt that is more or less white. He is writing complicated mathematical formulae on the walls with luminous chalk. When the Kittens show up, he begins to ask them mathematical questions: first, simple operations of addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. Then he asks more logical questions: “How many times do you need to cut a chocolate bar to separate each square?” The Kittens should answer all his questions if they do not want him to follow them down the tunnels, continuing to ask them confusing questions.

5. Trap. At the left side of the round corridor, the Kittens see a big, red button. And a countdown timer that displays random, ominous, numbers. Does the red button stop the countdown? Does it reset it? In truth, it doesn’t really matter: You just want to get the Kittens’ attention. A little further along, the wall has a crack in it, and a torrent of water is spreading out towards the machines, causing a short-circuit. Everything starts to hum and buzz: Look out—particle blasts! Get out of the way! Finally, it is likely that the answer to the Kittens’ questions will be displayed on a screen, along with the results of the particle collision.

pages.name: p.257 - Hilbert's Hotel
pages.html:
Hilbert's Hotel

The theme of this dungeon is “fragile”, and everything takes place in a huge hotel complex. The entrance is buried in the undergrowth: a frosted glass front with the words “Hilbert's Hotel” written in big, black letters. When the Kittens enter the hotel, they quickly realize that the inside seems to be infinitely larger than it looked from outside. However, everything—furniture, wall and floor coverings, fabrics—is incredibly delicate and fragile, about to break or tear. Any slight movement may lead to breakage.

1. Mirror. If everything has gone well so far, the Kittens will be greeted by several large, beautifully polished, black robots. They are not very polite when they demand the Kittens leave immediately (shoes off!) They are strong in a Fang Catfight, but will fall to pieces as soon as soon as Kittens get physical with them. If it has been difficult, the Kittens are greeted by silent but eager, white lacquered robots, who take their belongings and escort them to a dining hall to eat. They whisk their bags off to various hard-to-find rooms and, in general, lavish so much care and attention on the Kittens that it may leave them dizzy!

But be careful, they are also very fragile and can easily fall apart while trying to help the Kittens, which may add to the confusion. 2. Guardian. A big, round, gray robot, with a golden key painted on its body, welcomes the Kittens in an incomprehensible language and starts questioning them, giving them strange forms to fill in, and asking for things in return (without them knowing exactly what). It may become violent if the Kittens do not comply, but, if it is hit hard, they will find that it is not very solid either. However, other black robots will come to its aid.

pages.name: p.258
pages.html:
3. Ordeal. The Kitten with the highest Smart ability score (or the one who is the most curious) takes an interest in some gambling machines. He thinks there is a lot to gain for someone as clever as him. And once he starts he is fascinated by the game and nothing seems to get him away from it. The Kitten gets lost in a vast casino, wandering from game to game, losing and winning, and gradually disappearing into the maze.

4. Choice. Elevator or stairs? If Kittens choose elevator, two things can happen: Whichever button you press, it never really goes where you want it to. And then the elevator breaks down, as you would expect in a place where everything is as fragile as it is here. But once stuck between floors how do the Kittens get out? If they choose stairs, Kittens will have to find the right staircase and will tire themselves out from climbing so many floors. It’s even higher than Cat Tree City! And there are black robots and white robots everywhere to make everything more difficult. 5. Trap. The entire floor is made of glass. It is very, very fragile, of course. So, how to get to the hotel’s only guest—who is sitting on a big bed—when you have to cross a floor that’s ready to split and break? Maybe it is this particular guest, who is lost, lonely, and in a panic, who has the keys that the Kittens are looking for. He is stuck there, unable to leave the bed (the floor is too fragile for him to walk on) and served by a chain of much-too-eager robots. Will the Kittens be able to get the guest out safely?

pages.name: p.259 - Central park
pages.html:
Central park

The theme of this dungeon is “noise” and it takes place in an overgrown urban park. It contains climbing walls, skateparks, little landscaped bridges, colorful concrete statues of dinosaurs, rides, slides, treadmills, huts, and so on. Everything is half ruined, with peeling paint, crumbling concrete, rusting metal, rotting wood, and it is overgrown with grass, brambles, and nettles. Strangely, all the noises of an old-fashioned metropolis can be heard (car horns, wailing sirens, trains, planes) but none of the sources can be seen. And there are wind chimes and wind organs everywhere. The entrance is a rusty gate with strange signs on it (Yardogs are, apparently, not allowed to wee in the park).

1. Trap. When entering the park, a deluge of aggressive noise shocks the Kittens. They are not used to it, and they cannot work out what the sounds are or where they come from. If they do not find a quick way to reduce the noise level, they will be disoriented and become dazed from it. One example solution may be to activate chimes whose soft notes seem to weaken the volume of urban noise. Whatever the solution, they will need to think about it (and be able to repeat it throughout the whole adventure).

2. Choice. When the Kittens have to venture onto a big field without any trees or chimes, they will have to choose between plugging their ears and being able to communicate with each other. Maybe they will attempt to cross through the dizzying noise? And, of course, once in the middle of the field, giant strawberries spring out of the ground and attack the Kittens (and why not? We are in Crimsonfief, after all!) 3. Ordeal. A giant bell tower is seen, located at the top of a high cliff. The Kittens quickly realize that it could be used to protect the entire park from the noise for a while. One of the Kittens will have to climb up there. What are the dangers of climbing? And what about getting up the tower—is only one Kitten allowed in at a time, as stated on the door?

pages.name: p.260
pages.html:
4. Guardian. The park warden is a huge wolfdog, with a coat as black as night a snarling mouth lips, who starts to track the Kittens as soon as they enter. He has gone crazy (as well as being completely deaf) because he’s had to endure the loud noise of the city for so long. His goal is to force the Kittens back to the gate. He harasses and hunts them as much as he can, striking and disappearing immediately, in a very frightening manner.

5. Mirror. If the Kittens have struggled so far, they arrive on the shores of a quiet and peaceful lake where the noise is muted. The warden does not approach here. They can rest and set up camp. If the Kittens have had it easy so far, the noise increases in volume on the lake shore, their ears get sore, and they hear all manner of strange things. They can hear Walter insulting them and telling them to bring treasure back for him! The solution or answers that the kittens are looking for will be written on large horizontal panels that decorate the Belvedere, a large building that overlooks the park. Then they just need to find the exit.

pages.name: p.263 - The book of Adventures
pages.html:
The book of Adventures

Dear Storyteller, here’s everything you’ll need to write your own adventures.

Once again, don't worry

You don’t have to worry at all about this: Writing an adventure is something that's simple—anyone can do it. In fact, you don’t even need to have a very clear idea. You also don’t need to spend hours and hours writing it—some of the best adventures ever were made up only a few minutes before a game was started and were summarized in only three lines at the top of a page. The reason is very simple: An adventure is not what is written on a piece of paper; it is what ends up around the table, with the help of the players and the determination of the dice.

Nor should it be said that a little (or a lot of) preparation is required or always useful. In fact, each Storyteller has different needs, different approaches, and different ways of working. The initial preparation depends on the person, the circumstances, the type of adventure, and so on. As you go on, you will find your feet, but the following tips should help you overcome any worries.

pages.name: p.264 - First, pick a situation
pages.html:
First, pick a situation

An adventure is, above all, the partnership and meeting of a bunch of Kittens with a situation. The adventure stems from the way the Kittens take an interest in a situation or take it over. So what we have to do first is determine the initial situation. For example, in The Disappearance of Grandma Scramble, (see page 207) it is the discovery of an abandoned farm and some panicked chickens; in Three Little Pigs (see page 217), it is the meeting with the mother of the three missing porkers. Situations also fall into different theme categories, which we’ve listed below:

Mystery. Someone has murdered the old cat who lived in the house at the edge of the village. There’s been no news from the beer delivery person who usually comes by once a week. The village harvest has been exceptional this year, but in the next village it has been strangely poor. Some barns in the area have been burned down, because of a fire outbreak every few days. Someone stole the bales of wool that were meant to be left under a tree. Strange people have settled in the neighboring woods (people are always strange if you don’t know them). One night, someone nailed shut all the doors and entrances of the village storeroom.

Necessity. The Kittens have to buy new clothes after a week of crawling through brambles. The Kittens witness a criminal act and must give evidence before a judge, despite threats from the accused’s family. Poisonous catnip has been distributed around the dregs of Corktown , and will hurt people if not found. The pantry is empty, but it is really foul weather outside. Termites have been found in the wood of the village’s storage loft, endangering supplies. Social. The Kittens have been invit- ed to a wedding and they must find a gift. The Kittens have to go to the nearest town to find musicians for a big party. The grandfather of one of the Kittens has died and they need to travel discreetly to the funeral in the Kingdom of Cats. The Kittens have to take an important message to someone. A strange animal follows the Kittens more or less carefully, and it is not easy to work out what it wants. Rude leaflets roasting all the nobles of the area are being clandestinely distributed. Every evening at midnight, Maxel the Bard sings loudly and badly near the village well.

pages.name: p.265
pages.html:
Urgent. Children are in danger some- where on the mountain. Water has stopped flowing into the village fountain. Workers at a construction site all fall ill at the same time. The Kittens’ boat has fallen to bits, they must find a marine repair cat to fix it. All the actors in the troupe have lost their voices at the same time; it is too dodgy to be a coincidence. There is a hailstorm that catches people outside, with hail the size of rats. The house near the river has just collapsed into the riverbed—where are the inhabitants? The herbalist has run out of bandages and at the end of the week it’s the big healing tournament.

Violent. A bunch of weasels attack the Kittens to kidnap them. Walter's soldiers are looking for the Kittens to bring them back to the capital under guard. Dark's troops are said to be on their way to loot the village. A big Persian cat is terrorizing the roads with his “cousins” Serval and Caracal. A huge owl with monstrous claws has settled on the bridge and refuses to let anyone pass. Shaggy Simon has decided to prove his love to Grizelda by chasing all Kittens from the area. A giant snake claims ownership of all the nearby hunting areas.

pages.name: p.266 - Look for explanations
pages.html:
Look for explanations

The initial situation should be followed by an explanation that quickly establishes who is involved and the adventure’s challenges. Who are the bad guys? Who are the good guys? What are the goals of each? What do they have in terms of abilities, skills, or other characteristics? How will they react to what the Kittens do?

In general, the presence of Kittens is not expected and they create chaos for the extras, who already had their own plans.

You have to answer a few simple questions:

What. What is really going on? What are the dynamics of the situation? Why here, why now? Sum up in two or three lines what you think is going on. Think about the possible consequences—what could happen if the Kittens don’t intervene and what could happen if they do.

Who. Make a list of all the animals that are involved in the situation. First describe, those who are directly involved: the bad guys and their victims, those in distress, those who profit or suffer from the situation. Then, describe the animals who are more peripheral to the situation: those who could help the Kittens, provide information, or even hire them; and those who will hinder them, or try to take advantage of them. All you need is a list of names and a line of description for each. Where. Think of the places the adventure’s action will take place. You will not need many, just two or three locations, no more. You can improvise the rest as needed. Try to give personality to the places and imagine interesting details—accessories and objects, noises, smells, particular setups, possible dangers, and so on.

pages.name: p.267 - Critical path or improvisation
pages.html:
Critical path or improvisation

Now you have two possibilities. You can choose to stop your preparation there. This is the most logical choice if play is going to start soon or you are already comfortable as the Storyteller. You have a few ordered notes, you know the ins and outs of the adventure you want to play and, in any case, the players will mess it all up shortly by making decisions!

You may want to do a little more to prepare. The idea here is not to note down every little detail of the adventure as if you were writing a novel. All that will do is establish a rigid time frame from which you will have great difficulty escaping— because the Kittens will do anything other than what you have planned for them in advance—and you will get frustrated.

Instead, it can be useful to establish a critical path: a series of steps and important moments that you identify beforehand, and which you think the Kittens will eventually pass through, in whatever order. Examples of these can be found in the scenes or sections of the two adventures mentioned at the start of this chapter (see page 264). There is no guarantee that the Kittens will follow the precise plan, but you have put in the essential elements which form the basis of the story.

A critical path comes when you play out an adventure in your head and select the moments you want to highlight: the cool places, the ordeals, the dangers, resolutions, and so on. Just choose three or four important moments and write them down quickly. No more needs to be done—these are, in fact, mini-situations within the big situation. If you add too many things, you risk choking the adventure before it even starts.

pages.name: p.268 - An adventure’s natural progression
pages.html:
An adventure’s natural progression

In general, an adventure almost always takes place in the same way— at least, in terms of its dynamic around the table. Forget all the advice from drama and cinematic writing classes requiring three acts and a finale: That’s good for if you want to master writing a linear narrative, but it’s not going to be much help when faced with an improvized collective creation.

What you need is to understand the natural dynamic of an adventure: Identify, understand, and decide.

Identify

At the beginning of an adventure, players need to identify the situation.

What, precisely, is going on? What is happening right now? Do they need to react quickly or not? Does it interest the Kittens and if so, why? Kittens look, they ask questions, wonder, and act instinctively , often without knowing why.

This phase can be long or short: You can let the players carry on and make mistakes (which can take time), or an extra can quickly give them all the necessary information (if you want to speed it up). This is, generally, a somewhat confusing step. The players can be a little lukewarm. They don’t know what to look for, or why. Kittens do what they do, and make mistakes. But that’s a good thing: The more things the Kittens try, the more the knots of intrigue tighten around them— and the more they will feel they want to get to the end of the adventure. What was only previously a minor external situation becomes a personal matter: perfect!

pages.name: p.269 - Understand
pages.html:
Understand

The second major phase of an adventure is the moment when players try to understand what is happening, the ins and outs of a situation, the characters involved, and its secrets. In this phase, Kittens ask a lot of questions, they explore places, and meet people. The goal is to get as much information as possible.

This is almost always the longest phase of an adventure, even if it can (and should) be interrupted by events to keep the pace up. In The Disappearance of Grandma Scramble (see pages 207-215), this phase covers the search of the farm, the trail in the forest, and the arrival at Mr. Mooner’s camp—the meeting with the two baddies is only an encounter to break the continuity and to prepare for the final scene.

And always remember: If players ask questions, give them answers. It is the only way an adventure can keep moving.

Understanding is the central issue in an investigation adventure. In an action adventure, it is only by getting enough information that the last part—decide (and act)—will be effective and successful.

pages.name: p.270 - Decide
pages.html:
Decide

The last part of an adventure is the moment when the players have all the information in hand and can make choices, and take decisions. Note that we do not necessarily talk about actions here: In fact, the Kittens may decide not to do anything and not intervene.

However, most of the time Kittens will decide to act, to solve the initial situation, to restore peace or balance, to chase the bad guys, or to punish the guilty.

The choice, made at the end of the adventure, is not something trivial—that is why you should not “direct” the adventure, but only consider a critical path with a variety of possibilities. Ideally, you should not think about the end of the adventure while you are writing it. You only need the beginning and the objectives. The end is up to the players to decide—no one else, not even you!

Your job at this time is simply to eva luate the logical consequences of their decisions.

And there you go. You have nearly all the “secrets” that will let you to write and lead an adventure in the Dungeons and Kittens universe. All you have to do is gather a few friends and get started! Enjoy your gaming!

entries.name: Appendix: Lighter Rules for Younger Children

pages.name: p.280 - Appendix
pages.html:
Appendix

Lighter rules for younger children

The mechanics of Dungeons and Kittens are not hard to understand and apply, but for very young players—or for those who want to make the game as simple as possible—it can be useful to simplify them.

That is easily done, because the rules of Dungeons and Kittens are simply a set of small mechanics that fit together neatly. You can add them one by one over the course of a few games according to the ages of the participants. Or use only very few.

1. The easiest adjustment is to use only the three abilities and Heart points. For an action to succeed, 1 success is enough from a roll of 3 dice. Don’t worry about the other elements of actions.

2. The triples rule can easily be added: It is very simple, and is immediately visible on the dice.

3. It is possible to add the re-rolling rule later. It applies to both Purr-ecious items and Cattributes—meaning it is a good way to introduce these concepts as well.

4. Finally you can add difficulty levels within a test to succeed, then skills, advantages and disadvantages, and last of all, Furr-endship points.

Meowgic and Catfights are based on these rules. When spells or Catfights first occur, take the time to explain what is happening and how it is resolved in the game. You’ll see: It fits together using common sense.

The rules can be picked up slowly and precisely following this method. The Kittens will progress, and the players will too. It’s rewarding! And of course, you are free to use whichever Dungeons and Kittens rules you like: It’s your game!

Game mechanics quick reference

Action: Roll 3d6; each result less than or equal to the ability score equals 1 success (see page 16). Difficulty level: Number of successes required; Easy 1, Medium 2, Difficult 3, Legendary 4 (see page 48). Triple: Succeed or fail, the Kitten gets a little bonus to his action (see page 52). Character trait: If positively used, gain 1 advantage. If negatively used, gift 1 Furr-endship point (only once per session for either; see page 24). Heart points: Measure of a Kitten’s health and confidence; allows re-casting of a spell (see page 38 and 53). Furr-endship: Measures Kitten morale. May spend 1 point to either make 1 die roll a success or give 1 Heart point to another Kitten (not during Catfight). Must spend 1 point to start a Claw Catfight (see page 54). Cattribute: When triggered, can provide an advantage, a recovery, a success, or another positive effect depending on the situation (see page 22).
